decisions.hook: Race anti-gravity craft using airbrakes to hold tight lines while weapons threaten your position. Clean visual design makes the speed readable, but learning corners and handling is still a demanding part of the appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces title-like praise and personal aside with actual racing decisions.

decisions.hook: Move your dragon around enemies during battles to exploit weak sides and avoid dangerous firing arcs. Dragon customization adds preparation to that positional puzzle, making this a relatively compact RPG with a distinctive combat focus.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies the positional battle system and replaces disc-only local prose where present.

decisions.hook: Move your dragon around enemies during battles to exploit weak sides and avoid dangerous firing arcs. Dragon customization adds preparation to that positional puzzle, making this a relatively compact RPG with a distinctive combat focus.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies the positional battle system and replaces disc-only local prose where present.

decisions.hook: Move your dragon around enemies during battles to exploit weak sides and avoid dangerous firing arcs. Dragon customization adds preparation to that positional puzzle, making this a relatively compact RPG with a distinctive combat focus.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies the positional battle system and replaces disc-only local prose where present.

decisions.hook: Knuckles' Chaotix links two characters with an elastic tether, making momentum and partner positioning the unusual platforming challenge. Chaotix Complete v0.1 is an experimental hack whose exact changes and completeness are not established. Sample it as a variant, not as a verified fix or definitive edition of the original.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes private archive investigation details while retaining unverified-patch warning.

decisions.hook: Race futuristic hovercraft over fast, narrow courses where collisions drain the energy needed to finish. Learning a clean line and choosing when to risk more speed makes this a demanding racer despite its simple presentation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre-only note and private suitability aside.
Editorial review: Replaces an alias-only note with the distinctive speed-and-collection loop.
decisions.hook: The international version of Dangun Feveron combines rapid shooting with racing to catch released cyborgs before they escape. The disco presentation is playful, but maintaining that collection chain demands restless movement rather than staying safely at the bottom of the screen.

decisions.controls: Designed for Wii Remote pointer aim + Nunchuk. Classic Controller and GameCube pad are supported natively, aiming with a stick-driven reticle instead of the pointer. Pointer emulation via touch or mouse is possible in Dolphin but untested.
decisions.reason: Control note referred to the curator's own testing setup.

decisions.hook: Smilebit turns futuristic Tokyo into a skating playground: chain grinds and wall rides, hunt hidden graffiti souls, and tag rival territory without the original game's constant stage timer. Boosts consume spray cans, while police encounters punctuate the exploration. Built for movement mastery and finding your own routes rather than gear-building or stealth simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes local-image and Android-launch bookkeeping from both public and local prose; retains gameplay distinctions.

decisions.hook: Switch between tanks, aircraft and hovercraft while coordinating a wider attack on enemy installations. Captured resources feed research and new hardware, so success depends on managing the war as well as piloting its vehicles.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace the cryptic systemic-sim label with the vehicle-command and resource trade-off.

decisions.hook: Fly through detailed battlefields where hidden enemies can interrupt an otherwise straightforward vertical shooting run. The loop-the-loop works as an attack or an escape, giving you a useful answer when ordinary weaving runs out of room.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expand the AGA label into the shooter's evasive mechanic and ambush pressure.

decisions.hook: Race and fight a rival through steampunk arenas rather than cooperate against the machine. The opponent can be human or computer-controlled, but this is a competitive detour, not a replacement for the first game's shared campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Make the competitive departure from the cooperative original explicit.

decisions.hook: Collect weapon blueprints and visit upgrade bays during the stages to develop your ship's arsenal. Customization gives this tough horizontal shooter more to think about than dodging, but the easiest setting is only a trainer and cannot reach the proper ending.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct between-stage shop to in-stage blueprint development bays; preserve the trainer restriction.

decisions.hook: Explore an alien cave network with a jetpack whose movement is shaped by gravity, wind and inertia. Objects obey physical rules too, making experimentation central to solving obstacles; the freedom is rewarding, but figuring out what to try can be opaque.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove unsupported best-version and no-scripting claims; explain the physics and opacity.

decisions.hook: Control four mercenaries through separate first-person views in a science-fiction dungeon crawl. Equipment and positioning matter across the whole squad, but managing all four alone is a more deliberate undertaking than its guns suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace swamp-biology shorthand with the four-viewpoint coordination burden.

decisions.hook: Mine asteroids and decide whether to sell their resources or spend them on colonies and warships. Pollution, unhappy workers and hostile aliens keep expansion from becoming a simple building spree; choose it for management under military pressure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turn the management list into a clear resource-allocation recommendation.

decisions.hook: Guide a sword-wielding hero through richly drawn fantasy landscapes, alternating platform jumps with close-range fights. The scenery is a major attraction, but this is a direct action journey rather than an open-ended exploration game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove prettiest-platformer superlative and explain the actual sword-and-jump play.

decisions.alias: Midwinter II - Flames of Freedom v1.7.9.1991 (1991-09-07)(Rainbird).m3u
decisions.hook: Choose your route through an occupied archipelago, using different vehicles and sabotage missions to provoke rebellion. The attraction is freedom to plan a campaign across land, sea and air rather than follow a fixed sequence of action stages.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace vast/emergent shorthand with mission planning and vehicle choice.

decisions.hook: Lead a six-character party through a bleak science-fiction world, creating spells with runes and switching between exploration, inventory and turn-based battles. Its strange art and systems are the draw, but the icon-heavy interface asks for patient learning.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace unsupported hex-grid detail with sourced turn-based combat and runic spell creation.

decisions.hook: Direct four cybernetic agents through real-time urban missions, then use conquered territory's income to research weapons and upgrades. Persuading civilians to join you adds another way to reshape an encounter; the appeal is ruthless tactical control rather than careful diplomacy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove native-version claim and explain the link between missions and research.

decisions.hook: Sweep over enormous warships, shooting their defenses while dodging walls built into the decks. Speed makes the strafing exhilarating but leaves little time to correct a bad approach, before reactor-destruction sections change the task.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain the dreadnought obstacle problem instead of relying on author-name shorthand.

decisions.hook: Clear a virus from a virtual amusement park whose zones borrow the look of different game genres. Collecting power-ups funds weapon upgrades, while checkpoints soften failed attempts; the changing scenery gives its robot shooting more personality than a generic corridor assault.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace the unsupported final-Graftgold claim with researched weapons and checkpoint play.

decisions.hook: March a giant combat walker through different time periods while aiming its guns independently with the mouse. Picking off ground troops and airborne attackers is the hook, but the heavy opposition makes this a punishing power fantasy rather than a relaxing stomp.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turn brutal-and-lovely praise into the mouse-aiming decision and difficulty warning.

decisions.hook: Fight through organic enemies in a horizontal shooter whose solo mode sends you back to checkpoints after a death. Two-player play avoids those restarts but restricts most power-ups, so bringing a partner changes the challenge rather than simply making it easier.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace clone dismissal with useful solo/co-op rules and a concrete caveat.

decisions.hook: Launch opponents into air combos or throw your weapon and fight unarmed until you retrieve it. The fantasy cast gives this three-button fighter plenty of personality, though uneven character balance makes it a rougher competitive choice than its attractive sprites suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace obscure/good with researched weapon throws, air combos and a balance caveat.

decisions.hook: Asura Blade's sequel chains ordinary attacks into specials while adding ways to break guards and recover in midair. Spending the Magic Gauge on offense or an aerial escape makes defense an active decision, not just a pause between combos.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct the self-referential sequel label and explain the Magic Gauge's competing uses.

decisions.hook: Take one of two heroes through a monster-filled scrolling sword fight, breaking objects for useful pickups along the way. The draw is a direct fantasy hack-and-slash, not the equipment planning or character building of a role-playing game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace genre-only shorthand and unsubstantiated magic emphasis with swordplay.

decisions.hook: Use a biplane's dangling hook to grab objects and fling them at enemies or obstacles. Losing the plane puts you on foot hunting another ride, so the slapstick destruction comes with a sudden scramble for protection.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace picks-up-anything exaggeration with the hook and vulnerable on-foot transition.

decisions.hook: Choose a cybernetic dragon and use its special breath weapon to turn ground targets into score medals. The three breath attacks change how you approach enemies; keeping the medal chain alive adds a deliberate collection route to the vertical shooting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct generic lock-on characterization to the dragons' differing Banish breath weapons.

decisions.hook: Shoot through branching monster-filled stages with a familiar that provides both offensive and defensive help. The careful platform navigation makes this slower than Metal Slug, but using your companion well gives the measured advance its own appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain the pet's actual role and slower pace instead of only naming Metal Slug.

decisions.hook: Run, jump and shoot through attacks by enemy fleets, then take to the water on a dolphin. Those riding sections give the military run-and-gun a playful change of pace rather than merely copying Metal Slug's soldier-and-vehicle setup.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expand the comparison into the dolphin-riding action and reason to choose it.

decisions.hook: Send your dragon forward as a separate attack while the rider continues dodging enemy fire. That split between movement and damage turns a fantasy vertical shooter into a game of lining up aggressive strikes rather than only staying at the bottom of the screen.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain what throwing the dragon means as an attack decision.

decisions.hook: Aim through an on-rails fantasy shooting gallery with unlimited ordinary ammunition and limited screen-clearing dragon attacks. Saving those stronger attacks for a crowded moment is the useful decision; a comfortable pointer setup matters more than ordinary directional controls.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retain pointer warning while describing infinite shots and the limited dragon attack.

decisions.hook: Choose among eight fighters and clear crowded streets with special moves and airborne combos. The unusually broad move sets reward learning how attacks connect, making this a better choice for experimenting with a character than simply repeating one punch string.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace underrated label with the eight-character move-set and air-combo attraction.

decisions.hook: Pilot a revolver-shaped aircraft through a science-fiction western, collecting gold to strengthen your bombs. Your movement directs the larger blasts, so a bomb is something to aim and prepare, not merely a panic button.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace bomb-variety shorthand with the researched movement-directed blast.

decisions.hook: Run and jump through enemy defenses, taking control of vehicles when you can rather than fighting the entire war on foot. The appeal is that change in firepower and movement within a straightforward military action game, not a deep campaign simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expand Contra comparison into a clear vehicle-based run-and-gun recommendation.

decisions.hook: Collect floating energy molecules to strengthen the Black Fly's gun before confronting bosses in enormous beam duels. Its bleak science-fiction imagery is memorable, while the shared energy focus gives it a different rhythm from shooters built around swapping weapon pickups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain Newalone collection and beam confrontation rather than use art-shooter shorthand.

decisions.hook: Fight through monster crowds as heroes who can transform into powerful animal guardians. The transformations and mythological spectacle distinguish an otherwise direct scrolling brawler; choose it for exuberant creature combat rather than a complicated progression system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expand beast-transformation shorthand into its brawler premise and expectation.

decisions.hook: Ride a broom through ghost-filled fantasy stages, mixing ordinary fire with charged shots for stronger targets. The fairy-tale setting lightens the presentation, but positioning and deciding when to charge still drive this horizontal shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace charming label with the charged-shot decision and fantasy presentation.

decisions.hook: Beat up an army of undead monsters with a cyborg, vampire hunter or martial artist. Horror-film enemies and bloody combo-driven fights are the attraction; it is an exuberant monster brawler, not a game of cautious survival horror.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace gore-and-combos shorthand with a clear horror-brawler recommendation.

decisions.hook: Robotic baseball ninjas batter living mitts, balls and other sporting absurdities with combos, throws and dash attacks. The expressive animation sells the joke, while moves that catch several enemies make crowd control more satisfying than the premise alone suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Ground the animation praise in the baseball enemies and crowd-control move set.

decisions.hook: Fight through Journey to the West's monsters while learning the reach of your attacks and making good use of pickups. The mythological cast is appealing, but loose-feeling combat makes this a less polished choice than the setting first promises.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace classic label with spacing and pickups, including a supported precision caveat.

decisions.hook: Launch your supporting bits at enemies instead of relying on R-Type's usual detachable Force pod. Sending firepower away from the ship changes how you line up attacks, making this a useful variation for someone who wants familiar biological scenery with a different shooting rhythm.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain the detached-bit mechanic without leaning on sequel shorthand.

decisions.hook: Build a combat mech by choosing a body, arms and legs that determine its secondary weapon, melee attack and mobility. Those choices give the side-scrolling shooting a reason to try another configuration instead of treating every run as the same armored march.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain mech parts as choices rather than merely saying mech-flavoured.

decisions.hook: Samurai, a kappa and other eccentric fighters meet in bouts where grapples become button-mashing contests. The cast is more distinctive than the combat: strict special-move timing and awkward grabs make this a curiosity rather than a strong alternative to more precise fighters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace obscure label with researched grappling and a supported control-quality warning.

decisions.hook: Mix flying melee attacks with shooting and limited magic as fantasy warriors battle through a short campaign. The spell selection is interesting, but crowded close-range exchanges and unclear hit boundaries make this a messy alternative to Psikyo's cleaner shooters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace weird label with melee/spell decisions and supported criticism.

decisions.hook: Build a charge meter through sustained attacks, then spend it on your plane's special shot or save for a stronger burst. Fast bullets and changing early-stage order reward practiced routes and timely bombs rather than leisurely reactions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove unsupported best claim and explain charge-meter management and speed.

decisions.hook: Modern jets face dense attacks, but the most tempting scoring opportunity asks you to fly closer to danger. Approach an exposed boss core until it turns vulnerable for a quick kill and Technical Bonus; learning that opening adds a sharp risk-reward target to survival.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace modern-jets label with the distinctive close-range boss bonus.

decisions.hook: Build long martial-arts combos and juggle enemies through a lavishly drawn Chinese sword-fighting adventure. An expanding special-attack menu and mechanically different characters give repeated runs more to learn than another straightforward march through crowds.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expand air-juggle shorthand into move learning and character variety.

decisions.hook: Clean up monster-infested streets by turning scenery into weapons, from steel girders to concrete columns that break on impact. You cannot simply take every enemy's weapon, so spotting usable objects gives the familiar scrolling brawler a satisfying improvised edge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace gritty label with the environmental weapon distinction.

decisions.hook: Fight through a post-apocalyptic city with punches, kicks and crowd-clearing special attacks that cost health. That price makes escaping a mob a small resource decision, while three-player play turns the street fighting into a lively shared rescue mission.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove unsupported best-brawler claim and explain the health-for-crowd-control decision.

decisions.hook: Choose a mech's body, arms and legs to set its secondary weapon, close-range attack and movement style before heading into battle. Mixing those parts is the appeal: a new build changes how you tackle the side-scrolling firefights rather than merely changing the robot's appearance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct mech construction categories to body, arms and legs; explain why they matter.

decisions.hook: Detach the tentacled Flint to attack away from your ship while navigating elaborate horizontal stages. This overseas version uses an energy bar and a restricted main-weapon selection, so it does not offer the same weapon variety or survival rules as the Japanese release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Add the important overseas-version energy-bar and restricted-weapon caveat.

decisions.hook: Separate offense and defense gauges let you budget attacking techniques and defensive responses independently. Visible battle damage gives the fighters personality, but learning when to spend each meter is the stronger reason to explore this technical one-on-one game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace SNK-ish shorthand with the practical significance of separate meters.

decisions.hook: Shoot through six aerial stages, collecting stronger weapons while keeping a limited supply of evasive loops for emergencies. Unused loops earn a bonus, so safety and scoring pull in opposite directions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre shorthand with the loop-versus-bonus decision.

decisions.hook: Dash into gangs, turn dropped guns and melee weapons against them, and give enraged dinosaurs room to lash out. The loose, scrappy crowd control makes it a lively cooperative brawler, especially when you use that unruly space instead of trading stationary punches.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported best-in-system praise with weapons and crowd control.

decisions.hook: Four very different heroes fight through futuristic street gangs, occasionally climbing into armed mechs. The appeal is a crowded cooperative romp with oversized attacks and absurd characters, rather than a fighter built around subtle duels.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the cooperative brawling and mech appeal beyond a feature fragment.

decisions.hook: Choose a fighter and buy special weapons before each side-scrolling sortie, then keep an eye on fuel as well as enemy fire. Damage drains that same reserve, making a slow, cautious approach costly too.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how the weapon shop and draining fuel affect sorties.

decisions.hook: Fight from horseback through massed armies in a Three Kingdoms setting, choosing one of four generals. The mounted perspective is unusual, but the stiff exchanges make it a less inviting brawler than the later Warriors of Fate.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the clunky verdict into a clear mounted-combat comparison.

decisions.hook: Choose a quick striker, a balanced fighter or a powerful wrestler and keep street gangs from surrounding you. Throws and crowd positioning give the simple controls their depth; careless aggression is punished much harder than the premise suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces title-only canon shorthand with character and spacing decisions.

decisions.hook: Move through scrolling battlefields while rotating your aim independently, then spend collected money on equipment at shops. Its appeal depends on controlling direction and aim together, so learning the rotation controls matters more than simply holding fire.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains independent aiming and the practical control demand.

decisions.hook: Guide a fragile knight through traps and monsters, choosing firing positions carefully because a committed jump leaves little room for correction. The cruelly precise stages reward memorization, but the required second trip through the game makes this a poor choice for a relaxed platforming tour.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the difficulty and repeat-clear demand rather than calling it brutal.

decisions.hook: Arthur, Lancelot and Perceval cut through crowds while timed blocks create openings to counterattack. Weapons and armor improve automatically as you level up, so the real decisions are in defense and spacing rather than building a character.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Distinguishes automatic levels from actual defensive decisions.

decisions.hook: Climb a fifty-floor monster tower, spending keys to free allies with different attacks and abilities. Choosing and protecting a useful companion gives the brisk sword fighting more texture than simply collecting a stronger weapon.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why recruitable allies matter to the tower climb.

decisions.hook: Skip the platform stages and choose bosses to fight as Mega Man, Proto Man or Bass, collecting their weapons as you win. Working out a useful weapon order supplies the strategy, but the short boss rush cannot replace a full Mega Man adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes boss selection and the lack of platform stages useful buying guidance.

decisions.hook: Sword-wielding twins jump through colorful monster-filled stages in a brisk arcade platform adventure. Cooperative play and the bright fairy-tale setting are the draw; this is direct action rather than a long quest built around exploration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces alternate-title shorthand with action and scope.

decisions.hook: Push up the battlefield on foot, grab stronger guns and commandeer vehicles while enemies close in from several directions. The wide overhead view makes controlling space the pleasure, with explosive bosses punctuating the advance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sequel label with the overhead combat and vehicle loop.

decisions.hook: This Slam Masters revision concentrates on tag-team wrestling, with bodies sharing the ring instead of waiting for a clean one-on-one exchange. Pick it for the crowded team bouts rather than a conventional singles championship.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the tag-focused revision instead of naming the sport.

decisions.hook: Nemo and Flip blast animated toys with magic through the strange scenery of Slumberland. This arcade game is a direct, tough platform shooter, not the animal-riding adventure of the NES Little Nemo.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies arcade Nemo's shooting identity and distinguishes the NES game.

decisions.hook: Fire harpoons upward to split bouncing balls into smaller, increasingly awkward threats. Different characters change the tools for managing that crowd, while the artwork backdrops give the familiar Pang routine a fresh setting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the splitting-ball risk and character choice.

decisions.hook: Join same-colored jelly pieces, but include two stars in a connected group before it can disappear. That delayed trigger makes planning the final connecting piece more important than simply building the largest patch of color.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Puyo shorthand with Pnickies' actual clearing rule.

decisions.hook: Brawl around the ring, work into a grapple and finish with a pin or submission using an exaggerated cast of wrestlers. It borrows the immediacy of an arcade fighter without abandoning wrestling's positional scramble for a finish.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands the control comparison into wrestling objectives and appeal.

decisions.hook: Champion Edition makes the four bosses playable and lets both players choose the same fighter. Pick it for a measured Street Fighter II duel with the expanded cast, before Hyper Fighting speeds up the exchanges.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the edition's roster and mirror-match changes.

decisions.hook: Faster movement and attacks tighten Street Fighter II's familiar contest over jumps, fireballs and close-range pressure. Added special moves broaden some characters' options, but the quicker pace gives you less time to recognize and punish a mistake.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces fast-one shorthand with the consequence of increased speed.

decisions.hook: Eight playable fighters turn spacing, anti-air attacks and special-move timing into sharply different duels. This is the original Street Fighter II: the bosses are opponents rather than selectable characters, so later revisions offer more choice.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces original-version label with fighting decisions and roster limitation.

decisions.hook: Slash through a spectacular science-fiction obstacle course, climbing walls and hanging from ledges to reach the next attack. The joy is making its acrobatic set pieces flow together, though blind rushing quickly becomes a lesson in enemy placement.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces cryptic Cypher and Soviet-moon references with traversal appeal.

decisions.hook: Choose among five fantasy classes, from close-range fighters to ranged attackers, and push through monster crowds as equipment and levels improve. The different reach and attack styles give cooperative parties a purpose, without slowing the adventure into a full RPG.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces weak public shorthand and local duplicate-of-ZIP note.

decisions.hook: The Punisher and Nick Fury beat through criminal gangs, mixing throws and improvised weapons with bursts of gunfire. The shifts between close combat and shooting give the crowd control its energy, making this more than a license pasted onto street fighting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported excellent with the brawler's combat distinction.

decisions.hook: Choose between Midnight Wanderers' platform shooting, Chariot's flying shoot-outs and Don't Pull's block-pushing monster puzzles. The appeal is three distinct short-session rhythms, with the gentler-looking puzzle game demanding its own careful positioning.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains all three games instead of listing unexplained genre abbreviations.

decisions.hook: Choose one of three pilots and buy special weapons before flying through hostile side-scrolling missions. The shop turns each sortie into a small loadout decision, while the military scenery and constant pressure keep it firmly an arcade shooter rather than a flight simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands shop-based-shmup shorthand into loadout decisions and scope.

decisions.hook: Guide a fighter through dense vertical battlefields with support pods adding coverage around your main guns. The pods make protecting your firing position part of the appeal, but the busy screens still demand deliberate movement rather than trusting firepower alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why the pods matter instead of listing a shooter feature.

decisions.hook: Fight through Three Kingdoms armies on foot or horseback, using dropped weapons to break up crowded encounters. The changes in reach and mobility give this historical brawler its personality, especially when partners work together to stop enemies surrounding them.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands the historical label into mounted and weapon-based crowd control.

decisions.hook: Willow's magic and Madmartigan's sword carry you through a linear platform-action version of the film. Collect gold for shop upgrades, but expect a compact arcade journey rather than the exploration of the unrelated NES adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains shop progression without implying a full RPG.

decisions.hook: Switch a fighter's Stand on or off to change attacks, reach and defensive options in this flamboyant one-on-one brawler. The expanded Heritage for the Future roster rewards learning those paired styles, but its unusual rules take more adjustment than the familiar Capcom buttons suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Stand switching instead of calling it deep.

decisions.hook: Fighters summon supernatural Stands to alter their attacks and spacing, giving JoJo's duels a different rhythm from Street Fighter. This earlier release has less character choice than Heritage for the Future; choose it to explore the original version rather than for the broadest roster.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the original game's mechanics and version limitation.

decisions.hook: Choose one of four heroes and fight a sequence of enormous monsters, earning levels that expand your capabilities. The boss-focused quest is the draw; its small playable cast makes it a different proposition from a broad tournament fighter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Warzard shorthand with the boss-quest and roster tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Hugo, Urien and Akuma join Street Fighter III's cast in a faster revision of its parry-centered fighting. Timed defensive inputs still let you turn an opponent's attack into an opening, so learning the rhythm matters more than simply choosing a new face.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the missing Akuma context and explains parry-centered play.

decisions.hook: Timed parries can turn an apparently safe attack into a punishable mistake, making every jump and poke a question of prediction as well as spacing. Expressive animation and a varied cast make the duels compelling, but the precision demanded can be unforgiving to casual button-mashing.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces animation-benchmark shorthand with the parry risk and learning demand.

decisions.hook: Street Fighter III's debut lets well-timed forward or downward taps parry attacks instead of merely blocking them. The small, mostly new cast gives that defensive idea room to stand out, though later revisions offer more characters and refinements.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what parries do and why this early revision differs.

decisions.hook: Explore open space in a top-down starship, take missions and turn combat rewards into upgrades for the next expedition. The appeal is steadily building a stronger ship between bouts of shooting, rather than clearing a fixed arcade stage list.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces breezy-loot shorthand with the exploration and upgrade loop.

decisions.hook: Dying shifts you into a parallel route through the stage, changing enemies and terrain instead of merely subtracting a life. A high enough stage score lets you regain a lost life, making route knowledge and scoring useful survival tools rather than separate challenges.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the claim that death always sends you to a harder route; rank falls on death, and the options menu is English.

decisions.hook: Dash, circle and trade ranged attacks in one-on-one mech duels, choosing when to close in rather than firing constantly from a distance. Fast movement is the pleasure and the learning barrier; getting comfortable with its twin-stick-style controls matters more than the promise of instant giant-robot spectacle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported best-ever praise and explains movement and control demands.

decisions.alias: Fatal Fury - Mark of the Wolves (USA).chd
decisions.hook: Precisely timed Just Defend blocks reward defensive timing, while choosing a T.O.P. segment of the life bar determines when your fighter gets extra power. Those systems make life management part of the duel without burying the compact roster beneath elaborate controls.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes best-SNK and arcade-perfect claims; explains Just Defend and T.O.P.

decisions.hook: Build a fantasy mech from parts with different weights and elemental properties, then fight one-on-one duels. The attraction is testing those equipment trade-offs against an opponent; this edition includes a fan translation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the build trade-off in complete sentences while retaining the fan-translation distinction.

decisions.hook: Airborne movement and fast attack strings give Guilty Gear X its aggressive rhythm, while the Tension gauge supplies powerful ways to cash in an opening. The sharp high-resolution art is immediately appealing, but following the action takes practice and the menus are Japanese.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces anime-fighter shorthand with aggression, meter and accessibility.

decisions.hook: Race around compact arenas with an arsenal of outsized weapons, using first- or third-person views to track opponents. Short solo challenges provide practice, but four-player split-screen is the stronger reason to visit; comfortable aiming controls matter more than the simple premise suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns frantic-short shorthand into modes and aiming guidance.

decisions.hook: Fight through enemy-filled areas, collect weapons and repeat runs to strengthen your character, with Ver. 2 adding a tougher Ultimate difficulty. Solo play preserves the equipment hunt, but without companions the repetition is much harder to disguise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains the negative solo-grind judgment while explaining the actual loop.

decisions.hook: Scramble for weapons and power stones while four fighters send multi-level arenas into chaos. Item crafting adds something to pursue between bouts, but this is strongest as an improvised party fight rather than a precise one-on-one contest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the arena scramble behind the party-game verdict.

decisions.hook: Cut through crowds, return to safety and use runes to improve your equipment before venturing out again. The detailed item tuning is the attraction; the slow, repetitive fighting makes this easier to recommend to equipment tinkerers than to anyone seeking nimble action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the slow-combat criticism and crafting appeal concrete.

decisions.hook: Spawn's comic-book cast trades gunfire and close-range attacks in crowded arenas, with team battles letting you share the mayhem. The collision of very different characters is the draw, but the disorder suits a noisy multiplayer diversion better than a carefully readable duel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains chaotic fun as a specific arena-combat strength and limitation.

decisions.hook: Pilot giant robots that borrow from very different strands of mecha anime, from lumbering weapons platforms to extravagant super robots. Branching stories and the Hero Challenge give the duels a solo framework, while finding a machine whose fighting style suits you is the lasting appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands genre homage into robot-style choice and solo structure.

decisions.hook: Each new dungeon sends your hero back to level one, making preparation and the companions you bring more important than accumulated levels. That reset is an interesting roguelike idea, but repeatedly rebuilding strength can make the dungeon crawl feel like work rather than progress.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces dull-execution dismissal with the specific reset-related friction.

decisions.hook: Raise terrain into walls to contain falling water, then evaporate it for points before leaks overwhelm the basin. Too much raised ground risks an earthquake, so building higher is not always safer; the pleasure is balancing a landscape rather than merely stacking blocks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces oddly-deep shorthand with terrain and earthquake tradeoffs.

decisions.hook: This American variant of 1943 Kai keeps the aircraft's energy reserve at the center of its air-and-sea battles. Emergency attacks spend that same resource, so clearing a dangerous screen can leave you closer to defeat; choose it for a revised campaign, not a wholly new sequel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague variant advice with the energy-versus-emergency-attack decision.

decisions.hook: Build a fighter's weapon strength by collecting sets of four power-up capsules, choosing between spread fire, lasers, missiles and support drones. Death strips away those gains, and the two bomb types trade broad protection for concentrated damage, making recovery and emergency timing more important than the military setting suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims a long feature list and removes unsupported staffing and creator-disavowal claims.

decisions.hook: This three-game collection includes straightforward paddle-and-brick action alongside its other puzzle challenges. Penta limits thinking time and Heuk Sua Baek Sa penalizes help, so the menu offers variety without guaranteeing a relaxed puzzle session.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the collection beyond unexplained game names, retaining evidenced timer and help costs.

decisions.hook: A moving paddle launches colored balls in only three directions, so positioning replaces Puzzle Bobble's freely adjustable aim. Detaching a cluster is satisfying, but the restricted angles make apparently simple matches surprisingly awkward. Stage rewards show women in underwear, making this a less neutral choice than its colorful board suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the evidenced underwear-photo rewards to an otherwise useful explanation of restricted aiming.

decisions.hook: Arrange colored pieces into matching groups without letting the board become too crowded. Despite its name, this is a block puzzle rather than Pang-style balloon shooting; choose it for quick visual sorting, not action-platforming novelty.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the matching activity and space-management decision explicit while preserving the Pang distinction.

decisions.hook: This King of Fighters 2001 bootleg retains the choice of splitting four characters between active fighters and supporting Strikers. Giving up a playable teammate buys more assist possibilities, so the most interesting decision arrives before the first punch: depth of roster or concentrated pressure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Identifies the KOF 2001 bootleg rather than allowing its unrelated title to imply a separate original fighter.

decisions.hook: This boss hack of Double Dragon is a one-on-one fighter, not the scrolling street brawler, with attack buttons organized by strength rather than fixed punches and kicks. Its super meter becomes easier to fill as your health shrinks, keeping a losing round dangerous.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves the boss-hack identity and makes the distinction from the identically named brawler explicit.

decisions.hook: Movable satellite weapons turn a whimsical vertical shooter into a small formation puzzle. Arrange their fire to cover awkward angles; losing a powered-up setup makes recovery much more demanding.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague cute-shooter advice with the evidenced satellite-formation and recovery decisions of the same game.

decisions.hook: Clear matching sets of three from layered mahjong layouts, planning which removals will expose the tiles you need next. Helper powers can rescue a poor sequence, but the satisfying part is dismantling the board in a useful order rather than merely taking the first available tile.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects pair matching to sets of three and explains the available helper powers.

decisions.hook: Move exposed mahjong tiles into a holding rack, where matching threes disappear. Taking a tile can uncover something useful but also clog the rack, so removal order matters more than spotting an immediately available match.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic solitaire advice with Dragon World II's distinctive triple matching and limited holding rack.

decisions.hook: Arrange falling tiles into matching groups while leaving room for the next pieces. Egg Hunt offers compact visual sorting rather than an exploration game: the useful challenge is keeping an awkward pile manageable, not searching a world for hidden eggs.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces publisher-led genre shorthand with an explicit placement and space-management recommendation.

decisions.hook: A five-scene space adventure switches from fuel-conscious scrolling shooting to underwater retrieval and defending a city from bombs. That changing set of jobs makes this recovered Spanish arcade game more interesting than its rarity alone, though it asks you to relearn the immediate objective as each scene begins.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces historical-only recommendation with the documented five-scene structure and changing objectives.

decisions.hook: Answer personal yes-or-no questions while Enma theatrically judges whether you are lying. This Japanese novelty attraction was built around a hand sensor, not a test of trivia knowledge; without that cabinet gimmick, much of its appeal rests on understanding the questions and enjoying the joke.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects ordinary trivia-quiz framing to a personal-question lie-detector attraction with a hand sensor.

decisions.hook: Shoot through waves of hostile space flowers and destroy chains of them for power-ups. The botanical enemies give this vertical shooter a genuinely odd visual identity, even when the immediate task is the familiar business of finding a safe firing lane.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Botanical shooting is clear, but the narrative comparison is irrelevant.

decisions.hook: Colored capsules change the balance of your three weapons, while dropping a medal breaks your scoring streak. A bomb that converts bullets into rewards connects defense to collection, so a strong run means choosing which risks are worth taking rather than merely surviving.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Weapon balance and score conversion are useful but jargon-heavy.

decisions.hook: Shoot through waves of enemies in an Italian variation on Exerion's space-combat formula. It is a detour for someone who already enjoys this sort of formation shooting, rather than a strong reason to abandon the better-known game that inspired it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Regional provenance dominates; needs a more direct shooting recommendation.

decisions.hook: Choose when your T.O.P. power-up activates by assigning it to a section of the health bar, then time Just Defend blocks at the last moment. The result is a fighter built around active defense and planned comebacks; this version also makes the hidden characters available.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Just Defend is explained, but T.O.P. and the hidden-character hack need context.

decisions.hook: Chase aircraft through different historical periods in a vertical shooter whose time-travel premise keeps changing the backdrop. Choose it for straightforward shooting and the pleasure of seeing the scenery transform, rather than for a radically different combat system in every era.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Time-travel scenery is useful context, but the narrative comparison adds little.

decisions.hook: This horizontal shooter lets you keep your weapons after a death, but strips them away at the start of the next stage. Each level becomes a fresh equipment problem rather than a long punishment for one early mistake.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Equipment-reset rules are useful but the scrolling-shooter format is omitted.

decisions.hook: Arrange falling colored pieces into matching lines to clear stages and reveal pictures of women. The adult reward loop is its clearest distinction from a neutral matching puzzler, so choose it because that presentation appeals rather than expecting the familiar formula to be reinvented.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adult image rewards are candid, though the comparative quality claim is thin.

decisions.hook: Direction-sensitive combo finishes, throws into other enemies and a separate special-move energy bar give Guardians unusually flexible crowd fighting. Field Edition is a fan hack, so choose it to explore a variation rather than to learn the original game's exact rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Good combo explanation omits the Field Edition hack caveat.

decisions.hook: Direction-sensitive combo finishes, throws into other enemies and a separate special-move energy bar give Guardians unusually flexible crowd fighting. LBS Edition is a fan hack, so choose it to explore a variation rather than to learn the original game's exact rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Good combo explanation omits the LBS Edition hack caveat.

decisions.hook: Direction-sensitive combo finishes, throws into other enemies and a separate special-move energy bar give Guardians unusually flexible crowd fighting. Evil is a fan hack, so choose it to explore a variation rather than to learn the original game's exact rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Good combo explanation omits the Evil hack caveat.

decisions.hook: Direction-sensitive combo finishes, throws into other enemies and a separate special-move energy bar give Guardians unusually flexible crowd fighting. Reverie is a fan hack, so choose it to explore a variation rather than to learn the original game's exact rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Good combo explanation omits the Reverie hack caveat.

decisions.hook: Different stages put you in a speedboat, helicopter or motorcycle while you shoot through military targets. Pickups improve firepower and replenish limited bombs, making this a straightforward cooperative option whose changing vehicles provide more variety than its generic battlefield setting suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Generic military-shooter wording omits stage-specific vehicles and pickups.

decisions.hook: Fight through ten stages of military targets, then face a harder loop in this Korean bootleg vertical shooter. It is a straightforward dodge-and-fire pick rather than a simulation, and the title does not indicate a sequel to an earlier Gulf War game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Generic shooter wording omits the bootleg context and concrete run structure.

decisions.hook: Match colored pieces in a low, compact field while keeping an eye on the prominent guts meter. Its squat board makes a change from the towering stacks of conventional falling-block games; approach it as an unfamiliar matching puzzle rather than assuming Tetris habits will transfer.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Describes the appearance more than the matching task; clarify the action.

decisions.hook: Switch between free-firing and locked-on gunner attacks to turn nearby bullets into rings and jewels. Destroying the right enemy at the right moment links scoring to survival, but Red Label is a fan-made Progear hack rather than the original arcade ruleset.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Base Progear mechanics are clear, but fan-hack status is missing.

decisions.hook: Pilot a helicopter with separate attacks for ground and airborne targets, plus a bomb for emergencies. This unreleased prototype sends you back to checkpoints after a death, so learning where to position and which weapon to use matters more than its rarity.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Rarity displaces gameplay; separate air/ground attacks and checkpoints are more useful.

decisions.hook: Fight from behind your boxer, choosing strikes through controls originally built around two movable punch handles. Reading opponents remains the point, but ordinary buttons cannot fully reproduce the cabinet's physical sparring appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Incorrectly calls the behind-the-boxer presentation first-person.

decisions.hook: Fruit, bells and other slot-like symbols fill a small timed puzzle field. Its original token-prize setting is important context: choose it as a brief payout-oriented amusement, not a deep competitive falling-block game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Slot imagery is described, but the token-prize framing needs acknowledgement.

decisions.hook: This bootleg cartridge conversion brings the Neo Geo CD mahjong game into an arcade format, with adult imagery framing the table play. Knowing Japanese mahjong is the main requirement; the conversion is not a separate new game or a beginner-friendly introduction to the rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Conversion caveat is useful, but the filename reference is not public-safe prose.

decisions.hook: Play a short arcade football tournament, looking for a passing lane instead of dribbling straight into the opposition. This is Jaleco's game, not the home-computer Kick Off series, so its name is not a promise of that other game's ball-control model.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Jaleco identity prevents confusion, but another generic tournament comparison adds little.

decisions.hook: Read the card layout and free useful cards in an arcade take on solitaire. It offers a quiet sequencing puzzle rather than a betting contest, making it a better choice for deliberate planning than reflex-driven play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Solitaire is clear, but the surrounding arcade-library comparison is unnecessary.

decisions.hook: Keep groups of enemies in front of your fighter and learn which attacks give you enough reach to avoid being surrounded. Qun Xiong Luan Wu 2020 is a Knights of Valour Plus hack, best approached as a variation for brawler enthusiasts rather than a guide to the original game's rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Hack identity is clear but needs more actionable crowd-fighting guidance.

decisions.hook: Crowded weapon fights reward arranging enemies on one side before committing to an attack. Yi Tong Zhong Yuan Qing Ban is a fan revision of Knights of Valour Super Heroes, so familiarity with the original helps without guaranteeing that every tactic will transfer.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Fan identity is clear, but comparison with a strategy game is unhelpful padding.

decisions.hook: Control a screenful of enemies with a Three Kingdoms fighter, using positioning to stop a crowd from surrounding you. The Best Firepower in 2020 is a Super Heroes Plus hack; it is a variation for players already interested in the brawling, not an official new installment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The misleading shooter comparison displaces actual brawler guidance.

decisions.hook: Keep the mob in front of your warrior and use jumps to escape being boxed in. This Tian Wang variant is a Super Heroes Plus hack, making it a better comparison for experienced players than a baseline for learning the official game's rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Useful positioning is weakened by editorial-process wording about undocumented rules.

decisions.hook: Keep enemies on one side and use your fighter's reach to control crowded weapon battles. The Road to Survival True King is a Super Heroes Plus fan variation, best chosen to explore a familiar brawler in altered form rather than to learn the standard version.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The survival-management comparison is less useful than combat advice and hack caveat.

decisions.hook: Control crowded weapon fights by keeping opponents in front of your warrior instead of letting them surround you. This is a bootleg revision of Knights of Valour Super Heroes, worth comparing once you know the original rather than using as your introduction to its exact rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Filename commentary displaces useful bootleg-specific selection advice.

decisions.hook: Keep groups of enemies within your weapon's reach while avoiding attacks from behind. Ao Shi San Guo belongs to the Knights of Valour Super Heroes bootleg family, making it a comparison for existing brawler fans rather than an official separate sequel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Bootleg identity is useful, but an imagined strategy-game misconception is filler.

decisions.hook: This unreleased vertical aircraft shooter offers a look at an abandoned arcade design. Hiroshi Iuchi's background work makes it a particular curiosity for players interested in the visual history of arcade shooters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Prototype status is useful, but does not establish inferior polish or a sequel comparison.

decisions.hook: Fight along a narrow horizontal lane as a female martial artist, answering approaching enemies with attacks at the right height. Its small combat vocabulary puts the emphasis on timing and spacing rather than an elaborate move list.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The female lead alone is a weaker recommendation than explaining fight spacing.

decisions.hook: Race a cyclist against a pack of rivals and the clock, with a side-on view that keeps the slopes and nearby riders prominent. This three-button prototype is an unusual arcade take on road cycling, worth sampling for the race itself rather than expecting a team-management game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The prototype note needs a clearer account of the race on screen.

decisions.hook: Keep enemies on one side while working through crowded weapon fights in this Knights of Valour Super Heroes Plus hack. Wu Shuang Edition is another variation on that 2D brawler, not a Dynasty Warriors game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The hack identification is useful but the combat recommendation needs an actual decision.

decisions.hook: Pilot a fighter through vertically scrolling attack waves, collecting power-ups without letting the next upgrade lure you into incoming fire. Bombs provide an emergency escape, making this a direct shooting challenge about preserving space as well as building firepower.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Useful shooter advice lacks context identifying what Mad Shark actually plays like.

decisions.hook: Guide a fighter through vertical military battlefields, collecting weapon pickups while lining up the larger mechanical targets. The immediate challenge is balancing a clean attack position against the space you need to dodge, rather than simply chasing every upgrade.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The shooter description leans on an unsupported absence of scoring complexity.

decisions.hook: Throw weapons in eight directions, but keep moving to maintain a sideways aim: letting go returns your fire upward. Single-use special weapons can remove enemies your ordinary attack cannot reach, giving this repetitive Viking march more resource planning than its costume suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The costume-led description misses the distinctive aiming reset and consumable weapons.

decisions.hook: Rotate falling pieces to complete lines while watching the timer and remaining bomb stock. This Mosaic is a timed stacking challenge, not the picture-reconstruction puzzle of F2's later game with the same name.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The title distinction is useful, but the actual line-clearing task needs explaining.

decisions.hook: Move a paddle beneath the ball and use its rebounds to break blocks. This rotary-controlled game is a straightforward choice for practicing shot angles, but smooth analog movement matters more than its sparse theme.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The phrase about the paddle being a conversation is obscure rather than useful guidance.

decisions.hook: Aim at cartoon targets, including woodland animals, in a timed shooting gallery for one or two players. The appeal is quick target acquisition; a comfortable pointer setup matters more than learning a complex move list.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The note describes input mapping but omits the actual cartoon target-shooting presentation.

decisions.hook: Two-player gunfire and scenes moving into the distance expand Operation Wolf's military shooting gallery. Keep supplies and hostages in view as well as enemies: accurate target selection matters more than simply holding the trigger.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Generic controller advice misses the sequel's two-player pressure and supplies.

decisions.hook: Character transformations let you change fighting tools within Oriental Legend's crowded side-scrolling battles. This One Key hack belongs to the Super Plus branch, not the later PGM2 sequel also called Oriental Legend 2.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The lineage correction needs an explicit reason that changing fighters matters in combat.

decisions.hook: Pick up and drop colored marbles to connect groups of three, setting off explosions that turn nearby boxes into more marbles. The pleasure is arranging a clear that feeds another clear, rather than merely spotting the nearest matching group.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace generic recognition advice with marble handling and chain mechanics.

decisions.hook: Keep the magic ball rebounding into barriers while steering your paddle to catch its return. The slime-rescue story gives the block breaking a playful wrapper, but reading rebound angles matters more than following the fantasy plot.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove the misleading claim that every barrier hit requires a paddle return.

decisions.hook: Roll a trackball to pitch and swing, then use power-up moves to turn baseball into an exaggerated duel. The fielding is less convincing: watching the outfield while checking a small base map can make the action feel disconnected. This surviving prototype is worth trying for its physical batting and pitching rather than expecting a polished baseball simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace vague comic-baseball praise with trackball mechanics and fielding friction.

decisions.hook: Maze chasing, falling-block stacking and Snow Bros. enemy clearing share this bootleg compilation's selection screen. It is a way to sample contrasting arcade challenges, but labels such as PacMan 2 and HyperMan 2 should not be mistaken for official sequels.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Add gameplay categories so the compilation note is more than labels and provenance.

decisions.hook: Robot wrestlers mix conventional holds and throws with impossible aerial attacks, including the Sky High move available when three red lamps flash. The appeal is exploring that varied move set in short bouts, rather than simply admiring mechanical bodies trading punches.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace generic robot-theme praise with documented wrestling techniques and Sky High.

decisions.hook: Sand Scorpion is a vertically scrolling space shooter for one or two players, with a separate stock of emergency bombs. The useful survival decision is when to spend one rather than keep squeezing through shrinking gaps; saving every bomb does little good if the next burst destroys your ship.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Name the shooter and its cooperative scope instead of offering only generic bomb advice.

decisions.hook: Chunky robots trade blows with a dedicated guard button alongside punch and kick. The compact input set puts the emphasis on when to defend and when to answer, making this an approachable mechanical alternative to more elaborate fighting-game controls.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove a hollow comparison to interchangeable martial artists; retain guard timing.

decisions.hook: Rescue hostages across two-level stages, using shuriken at range and close attacks when guards get too near. Careful positioning is Shinobi's appeal; this Korean FZ-2006 bootleg is an alternate release, so choose the standard Sega version if learning the original rules is your priority.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Release-history advice crowds out Shinobi's actual hostage-rescue gameplay.

decisions.hook: Move the puck into a shooting position while keeping the opponent away from your own goal in Sega's early arcade ice hockey. The two-player contest is the reason to choose it: a direct sports rivalry rather than the spaceship shooting of the similarly named Slap Fight.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Title disambiguation displaces the more useful competitive hockey appeal.

decisions.hook: An armed heroine fights upward through beasts and cyborgs, stealing enemy flying vehicles while pursuing escaped prisoners. That switch from fighting on foot to commandeering transport gives the overhead shooting a stronger hook than its unusual setting alone; this is the export version of Sei Senshi Amatelass.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Alias explanation dominates; replace it with evidenced vehicle-stealing gameplay.

decisions.hook: This early version of 1945k III sends selectable aircraft through overhead shooting stages. Try it to compare the developing game with its later revision, but expect rough edges such as the second player's incorrect selection graphic rather than a separate polished sequel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Historical-variant commentary needs an explicit description of the aircraft combat.

decisions.hook: Destroying complete enemy waves reveals weapon upgrades, while each stage's boss must be beaten against a timer. That combination rewards staying on the attack rather than merely dodging until the danger passes, giving Sega's military vertical shooter a clear, aggressive rhythm.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Generic aerial-pattern language misses the evidenced wave-clear and boss pressure.

decisions.hook: Table tennis turns each return into a quick decision about timing and placement, with little room to recover from a badly judged shot. Best treated as a short rally duel rather than a sports game to settle into for hours.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Identify table tennis explicitly rather than leaving the sport implicit.

decisions.hook: Moving the soldier and lining up the crosshair compete for attention while enemies fill the background. Evasive rolls and destructible scenery make this shooting gallery unusually physical; this release is the US prototype rather than the finished World version.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove internal shortname commentary while retaining prototype status and dual attention.

decisions.hook: Choosing when to jump, throw or hold your ground gives Champion Edition its appeal. Magic Delta is an unofficial variation, best sampled as a comparison bout rather than used to learn the standard game's matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Magic Delta's provenance needs a concrete fighting decision, not only comparison advice.

decisions.hook: Threaten with a projectile, catch a jump or move close enough to throw: Champion Edition makes distance the heart of a bout. Tu Long is a Chinese bootleg variation, worth exploring for altered matchups rather than treating it as an official step between Champion Edition and Turbo.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Tu Long's lineage dominates; add a readable spacing-and-anti-air play hook.

decisions.hook: Threaten with a projectile, catch a jump or move close enough to throw: Champion Edition makes distance the heart of a bout. Tu Long is a Chinese bootleg variation, worth exploring for altered matchups rather than treating it as an official step between Champion Edition and Turbo.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Tu Long's lineage dominates; add a readable spacing-and-anti-air play hook.

decisions.reason: Editorial review: Tu Long's lineage dominates; add a readable spacing-and-anti-air play hook.

decisions.hook: Well-placed attacks deny space, while an ill-timed jump can hand the opponent an easy answer. V004 revisits Champion Edition's fighting through an unofficial variation; choose a standard Capcom version when consistent matchup practice is the goal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: V004's release classification needs actual attack and positioning decisions.

decisions.hook: Well-placed attacks deny space, while an ill-timed jump can hand the opponent an easy answer. V004 revisits Champion Edition's fighting through an unofficial variation; choose a standard Capcom version when consistent matchup practice is the goal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: V004's release classification needs actual attack and positioning decisions.

decisions.hook: Champion Edition's punches, throws and special moves make each approach a choice about reach and risk. Xiang Long is a Chinese bootleg variation, so familiar moves should not be taken as a promise of familiar timing or matchups; try it for experimentation rather than tournament practice.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The hack warning is useful, but add the underlying attack-risk decisions.

decisions.hook: Champion Edition's punches, throws and special moves make each approach a choice about reach and risk. Xiang Long is a Chinese bootleg variation, so familiar moves should not be taken as a promise of familiar timing or matchups; try it for experimentation rather than tournament practice.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The hack warning is useful, but add the underlying attack-risk decisions.

decisions.hook: Fireball spacing, anti-air timing and the threat of a throw give Champion Edition its readable back-and-forth. YYC is an unofficial offshoot: a comparison bout for the curious, not a dependable reference for standard competitive play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace short-name commentary with a direct explanation of fighting decisions.

decisions.hook: Champion Edition's contest of attack range, jump timing and throws underlies this unofficial variation. Magic Delta Turbo is not Capcom's Hyper Fighting; choose it for an experimental bout rather than to practice that official game's matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Magic Delta Turbo's version warning needs an actual combat hook.

decisions.hook: World Warrior's contest of pokes, throws and anti-air attacks meets a boss-enabled variant. The appeal is comparing how the expanded selection changes the original's matchups, not assuming this is the same ruleset as Champion Edition.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove archive-oriented wording while retaining the boss-enabled comparison and combat hook.

decisions.hook: Trap enemies in bubbles and pop them to clear compact platform rooms, with round selection letting you choose where to begin. This unofficial Sun Mixing variation runs on Mega Drive-derived hardware; sample it for another take on bubble-platforming, not as Taito's original with a new subtitle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Hardware provenance outweighs play; add bubble-clearing and round-selection appeal.

decisions.hook: Defend Earth from alien raiders while preserving its three layers of shielding; losing all three ends the defence. Remaining shields also earn a bonus, giving this spare early shooter a reason to intercept threats before they get through rather than merely chase whatever is easiest to hit.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Generic cassette-era shooting misses the evidenced Earth-shield defence objective.

decisions.hook: Pick three fighters and learn when to approach, hold your ground or intercept a jump. The Random Combo hack is an alternate rules experiment, not a reliable baseline for practicing standard KOF '97 matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces misleading team-wide damage phrasing with readable spacing and jump-defense decisions.

decisions.hook: Build a three-fighter team around different attack ranges, then use short hops and grounded attacks to find openings. Combo Plus is a fan-made KOF '98 variation, so learn the original first if you want a dependable reference for its matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces an irrelevant Capcom disclaimer with concrete three-fighter spacing decisions.

decisions.hook: Build a three-fighter team whose different ranges give you answers to awkward opponents, then learn when to hop in or hold your ground. Despite its Ultimate Match label, this is a Neo Geo hack of KOF '98 rather than the official later remake.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds actual team-fighting decisions instead of recommending only a familiar cast.

decisions.hook: Choose three active fighters and a fourth teammate to call in as a Striker assist, giving team selection a role in how you create openings. Evolution Ultra Remix is a fan revision of KOF '99, best explored after its movement and assist timing feel familiar.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the offscreen fighter's assist role explicit instead of relying on a coy metaphor.

decisions.hook: A fourth teammate supplies Striker assists instead of fighting an ordinary round, so choosing support matters alongside choosing your three active fighters. Summer Revolution is a KOF '99 hack for exploring that assist-based combat, not a standard-rules reference.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the confusing fourth-member phrasing and unnecessary summer-theme disclaimer.

decisions.hook: Omega builds on KOF 2002's three-person teams and cancel-heavy combos, rewarding practice with a small group of fighters rather than constant roster switching. This early hack revision's number is uncertain, so do not assume changes from later Omega releases are present.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes catalogue-facing phrasing while preserving uncertainty about the Omega revision.

decisions.hook: KOF 2002's hops, rolls and MAX-mode combo extensions give this Omega revision a demanding team-fighting foundation. This is the beta-labelled Omega 0.9 hack, not the later revision without that suffix; choose it to explore the variation rather than learn stock matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds a meaningful combat reason to try the beta while retaining its exact revision caveat.

decisions.hook: Fluid punch-and-kick strings and health-costing special attacks give this cooperative brawler satisfying moment-to-moment decisions. The familiar weapon pickups and crowd fights offer little surprise beyond those combos, while garbled story text and an abrupt ending make the journey less rewarding than the combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces compressed feature-list fragments and uncertain licensing history with grounded combo strengths and narrative weaknesses.

decisions.hook: Seven stages of vertical aircraft shooting survive in this unreleased Korean game's late debug build, which displays position values during play. Worth trying for a recovered full-length arcade run, provided visible development readouts do not distract you from the shooting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the inference that an unreleased debug build means unfinished game design; the developer said the seven-stage game was finished.

decisions.hook: Rotate and position shapes to change a pattern of colored squares, using XOR placement to remove occupied cells while filling empty ones. Each move can repair one part of the pattern while disrupting another, making this unreleased Gaelco prototype more of a planning puzzle than an ordinary block-stacking exercise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported prototype-polish criticism with the designer-described XOR placement puzzle.

decisions.hook: Guide a remotely operated robot through combat and exploration to uncover the Magma Project conspiracy. This substantially reworked adaptation of Hacker is a science-fiction RPG, so choose it for an investigative adventure rather than a terminal-hacking puzzle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the unsupported superiority comparison with Hacker while retaining the robot-led RPG distinction.

decisions.hook: Donald takes a hammer or throwing discs into compact platform stages, making attack reach part of each jump. The simple weapon choices give this treasure hunt a firmer action focus than its cheerful presentation suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague QuackShot comparison with the evidenced weapon-reach decisions already described for the matching western release.

decisions.hook: Dizzy the Adventurer combines object puzzles with a small world to revisit, while Go! Dizzy Go! offers maze collecting and slippery ice routes. Those two are the stronger reasons to choose this collection; Panic Dizzy's repetitive horizontal shape matching is a weaker diversion, not an equally compelling third attraction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Restores Go! Dizzy Go! to the recommendation and gives a supported reason to prefer the adventure and maze games over Panic Dizzy.

decisions.hook: Combine weapon types to tackle crowded run-and-gun stages and oversized bosses, experimenting with the coverage each pairing gives you. The combinations remain the attraction, but this handheld adaptation is single-player only and suffers slowdown, so it is no replacement for the Mega Drive game's cooperative spectacle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague cutbacks with verified single-player-only and slowdown limitations while retaining weapon combinations.

decisions.hook: Arle explores a first-person tower and fights with spells in turn-based encounters, with expressions and text replacing numerical health readouts. The lively monsters are appealing, but repetitive-looking corridors and punishing early fights make this a demanding introduction to the Puyo characters rather than a gentle one.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects Mega Drive-style directional spell inputs misattributed to Game Gear; adds supported navigation and early-battle cautions.

decisions.alias: Moldorian - Hikari to Yami no Sister (Japan).zip
decisions.hook: Each character's turn gives you a short window to enter a direction-and-button command for an attack or spell. Hesitate and the turn is lost: this fantasy RPG rewards memorised inputs, but that pressure makes it a poor choice if you prefer time to consider your party's options.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies timed turn-based commands rather than free real-time combat and explains the penalty for hesitating.

decisions.hook: Two-on-two basketball cuts away much of the rulebook and lets outrageous dunks take over. Choose a partner whose strengths complement yours; this putative prototype should not be assumed to match the final retail release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the local-file reference while preserving uncertainty about this putative prototype revision.

decisions.hook: A timed swing meter makes the shot simple to start but difficult to place precisely around hazards. Course planning carries the interest; the putative-prototype designation does not establish how this revision differs from the retail release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves golf and uncertain-prototype caveats without referring to a local file.

decisions.hook: Grab ledges and ropes to work through the city's platform stages while shooting down enemies. The Phantom's mobility matters alongside his gun, so look for a route above trouble rather than always trading shots from the floor.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the confusing phrase 'shooting platforms' with a clear action-platforming description.

decisions.hook: Choose clubs or national sides for football matches with adjustable pitch presentation. The large team selection offers variety, but the unlicensed names are only approximations: choose it for the matches rather than an authentic roster.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces circular football praise with the already stated unlicensed-roster limitation.

decisions.alias: 2467 - Super Robot Taisen - Original Generation (U)(Jam Project).gba
