decisions.hook: Build a force of Banpresto's original robots, swapping pilots and equipment before sending them into turn-based grid battles. The lengthy anime story demands patience, but tuning a machine around its pilot makes the preparation as absorbing as the fighting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands shorthand into the robot-customisation decision and long-story commitment.

decisions.hook: Upgrade robots and exchange their weapons before committing your squad to turn-based battles. The appeal is developing a larger force across a long anime campaign; this GBA sequel does not have the Twin Battle system introduced in the later PlayStation 2 Original Generations.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the false GBA Twin Battle claim and removes unsupported best-of-pair ranking.

decisions.hook: Link adjacent letter tiles into words, clearing space before burning tiles work their way down the board. Longer words earn more and help control the danger, making vocabulary useful under pressure rather than merely a way to chase a score.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre shorthand and removes the incorrect homebrew-port label for the commercial GBA release.

decisions.hook: Collect enemy souls to equip new attacks and abilities, then use them to explore more of the castle. Experimenting with Soma's loadout gives familiar rooms and enemies new possibilities, though obtaining particular souls can mean repeated fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the soul system, removes unsupported best-in-series praise and avoids implying every kill guarantees a soul.

decisions.hook: Combine magical cards to change attacks and defensive effects while exploring a demanding castle. The combinations reward experimentation, but hunting the cards can turn that promise into repeated enemy grinding.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns DSS shorthand into readable mechanics and retains the grinding warning.

decisions.hook: FireRed becomes a comedy puzzle adventure in which rewritten characters, altered Pokémon and hidden clues make completing the Pokédex the main goal. Built-in hints help with the secrets, but the creator designed it for group problem-solving and warns that Nuzlocke restrictions are frustrating; v1.0.91 is the finished release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses the comedy hack on puzzle-solving and preserves its Nuzlocke caveat.

decisions.hook: Place arrows to herd mice into rockets while steering them away from cats. The puzzle is indirect control: one arrow can rescue a stream of mice or send the whole group into trouble, with an editor available when solving preset boards is no longer enough.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands mouse-herding shorthand into the actual routing decision.

decisions.hook: Travel between duels and rebuild a Duel Masters deck, deciding which cards to sacrifice as mana and which to keep for later plays. That trade-off gives each hand a useful tension: the creature you want to summon may also be the resource needed to play anything at all.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why mana-as-cards matters instead of merely calling it neat.

decisions.alias: Duel Masters - Shadow of the Code (USA).gba
decisions.hook: Build a Duel Masters deck and battle through another card-RPG adventure, balancing cards spent as mana against creatures kept for combat. The expanded card pool is the reason to return, but the same resource trade-off remains at the centre rather than a wholly new battle system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sequel-only text with the card economy and reason to choose it.

decisions.hook: Move across a strategic map, then fight the enemy forces in small action skirmishes. The mixture offers a different rhythm from the console Dynasty Warriors games, but anyone seeking their sprawling crowd battles should expect a much more compartmentalised experience.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the map/action structure and gives a concrete limitation instead of 'curiosity'.

decisions.hook: Race futuristic machines through high-speed circuits, with a story mode following different drivers alongside the Grand Prix competition. Learning the corners is the substance; the character missions give that practice more context than a bare championship ladder.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces 'Racing' with high-speed circuit play and the distinctive story structure.

decisions.hook: Learn tight corners and well-timed boosts on futuristic tracks built specifically for this GBA outing. Clean racing lines matter more than spectacle, so expect practice laps and repeated attempts rather than instant mastery from knowing the Super NES courses.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces 'Racing' with course-learning demands and GBA-specific tracks.

decisions.alias: Final Fantasy I & II - Dawn of Souls (USA).gba
decisions.hook: Two early Final Fantasy adventures offer very different party-building rules: choose fixed classes in the first, or develop the second game's characters through what they actually do in battle. They are useful for comparing those systems, but repeated encounters and old-fashioned progression can make both feel grindy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the two systems without cryptic stat shorthand or an unsupported short-runtime claim.

decisions.hook: Follow a largely fixed cast through a story-led adventure, choosing commands as each character's battle timer fills. Late-game party swaps add some flexibility, but this is a directed journey rather than a sandbox for building any party you like.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands ATB shorthand and replaces vague 'not systemic' with a meaningful limitation.

decisions.hook: Develop a clan through changing jobs and grid battles, while judges impose laws that can forbid particular actions. Building a versatile squad helps you work around those restrictions, though a law that blocks your favourite tactic can feel more obstructive than interesting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes job-building and judge-law friction understandable without FFT shorthand.

decisions.hook: Switch between jobs and mix learned abilities to build combinations that solve battles in unexpected ways. The Advance edition's extra jobs give you more to experiment with, making party construction the strongest reason to choose this adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the false exclusivity of tinkering and explains the job-system appeal.

decisions.hook: A large cast with distinct abilities carries a story that eventually opens into a much freer search for allies and unfinished business. The Advance edition adds bonus dungeons, but the changing shape of the main adventure is the attraction; expect a substantial story commitment rather than a quick campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces absolute praise and fixed playtime with the story/structure appeal.

decisions.hook: A frontier-sailing Fire Emblem campaign lets every unit move again after acting, with shoves and free trading opening up flexible turns. Quest-filled towns and boat maps add variety across 31 chapters, while start-of-turn saves make tactical experiments less costly; v2.11 is a post-2.0 bug-fix build.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Selects movement freedom and save flexibility from an overlong feature inventory.

decisions.alias: Fire Emblem - Dream of Five (Definitive Edition v1.7.6).gba
decisions.hook: Build an army through a long original Fire Emblem campaign whose route split changes more than the next few maps. Extensive character supports give the large cast a reason to matter beyond statistics; v1.7.6 is the intended final patch, with mGBA recommended by the project.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts chapter arithmetic and feature stacking while retaining route consequences and edition advice.

decisions.hook: A 37-chapter original Fire Emblem war keeps skills relatively restrained, so unit roles and class choices remain readable. Multiple difficulty and optional-rule settings help tailor the campaign, but only two characters have written supports despite the completed main story and endings.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces stat abbreviations and feature lists with tactical identity and the missing-support caveat.

decisions.hook: The Binding Blade gets retuned units, enemies and classes, giving familiar maps different tactical possibilities. It is balanced around Hard and the added Maniac difficulty rather than a gentle first playthrough; minor known bugs remain in v1.85.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves FE6 identity and difficulty/bug caveats while removing unexplained combat abbreviations.

decisions.hook: An original Fire Emblem campaign follows House Olva's war, with fully written supports giving the army relationships beyond its battle statistics. Turn rankings encourage efficient clears, but the creator warns that the opening chapters are rough and the overall difficulty is above the usual baseline; v1.4.1 is final.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces chapter bookkeeping with tactical motivation and preserves the creator's difficulty warning.

decisions.hook: Personal axes and an unusual bomb weapon class give this 33-chapter Fire Emblem campaign distinctive unit roles without covering everyone in skills. An Easy mode offers a softer entry, but save points replace suspend saves, so stopping mid-battle follows different rules from the original game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Prioritises personal weapons and the meaningful save-system caveat over a long feature list.

decisions.alias: Fire Emblem - Souls of the Forest (v9.3.2).gba
decisions.hook: Mostly single-weapon classes and a stronger weapon triangle make positioning the right unit against the right enemy central to this tactics hack. Difficulty and growth modifiers invite experimentation, but v9.3.2 is unfinished: only one route through chapters 1–24 is playable, and supports are unwritten.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the tactical constraint and retains unfinished-route/support warnings.

decisions.hook: A mid-campaign split makes you alternate between two fixed armies sharing one convoy, so distributing equipment becomes a campaign-level decision. Personal weapons give most units a distinct role across the main story and postgame trials; the creator warns that save points in chapters 8 and 19 can crash.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes shared-convoy planning the recommendation and preserves the crash warning.

decisions.hook: Build an army through a long original Fire Emblem campaign, with route choices and time-sensitive side chapters rewarding more than simply surviving each map. The old-school structure suits deliberate campaign play rather than a short tactical diversion; v2.1 is the final 2013 release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns chapter and release lists into a clear campaign commitment without losing sidequest conditions.

decisions.alias: Fire Emblem - The Morrow's Golden Country (Complete).gba
decisions.hook: A lengthy original Fire Emblem campaign alternates grid battles with free-movement base interludes and conversations. Combat arts and unusual items give you tools to experiment with, while the side-party chapters and postgame trials make this a substantial commitment rather than a compact story.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces dense feature enumeration with battle/base rhythm and campaign scope.

decisions.alias: Fire Emblem - The Road to Ruin (v3.0.3).gba
decisions.hook: Lead mercenaries through a compact original Fire Emblem war with custom maps and music. Each unit has only one support partner, limiting relationship choices; v3.0.3 is the final bug-fix release of a project its creator still described as closer to open beta than final.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains restricted supports and beta-quality qualification while reducing production trivia.

decisions.alias: Fire Emblem - The Sacred Stones (USA, Australia).gba
decisions.hook: Choose between promotion branches and shape your army through grid battles, with a world map that allows extra training when a fight feels too hard. Two story routes encourage another run, but optional grinding can soften the pressure that gives stricter Fire Emblem campaigns their bite.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands 'Comfortable FE' into promotion choice, optional grinding and its trade-off.

decisions.hook: A farmer's turn to banditry begins a long Fire Emblem campaign with escape maps, fog and flexible item trading. Restrained skills keep attention on positioning and the promotion choices; v3.0 is the final polish patch, with Normal the recommended starting point.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported best-fan-game praise and abbreviations while retaining difficulty guidance.

decisions.hook: Build a deck whose cards determine attacks, recovery and what you can counter in real-time battles. The deckbuilding gives this Kingdom Hearts detour a genuine tactical identity, but repeatedly fighting through similar Disney rooms can wear down the novelty.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains card-battle decisions and retains repetition criticism.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings, The - The Return of the King (USA, Europe) (En,Fr,De,Es,It).gba
decisions.hook: Fight through the film's battles as an action-RPG, collecting equipment and choosing skills to shape your hero. The steady loop of fighting and improving a build is the attraction, rather than the cinematic combo-brawler experience of the console versions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects genre-only brawler framing to the GBA loot-and-skills action-RPG.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings, The - The Two Towers (USA, Europe) (En,Fr,De,Es,It,Nl).gba
decisions.hook: Choose a hero, cut through Middle-earth's enemies and turn new equipment and experience into a stronger build. This GBA adaptation is closer to a Diablo-style action-RPG than the console combat game, so repeated fighting for useful loot is part of the appeal and the commitment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands genre shorthand and distinguishes the GBA adaptation from misleading console metadata.

decisions.hook: Train at the tennis academy, improve your player's abilities and carry those gains into tournaments. The RPG progression gives practice a purpose beyond winning the next rally, while special power moves keep the matches from feeling like a straight tennis simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands 'Tennis RPG' using the supplied academy and progression evidence.

decisions.hook: Arrange battle chips before a match, then watch the selected sequence play out with only limited opportunities to intervene. Planning the deck is the point, but players who enjoy Battle Network's direct movement and dodging may find the automatic fights too passive.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the deckbuilding-versus-passivity trade-off rather than 'set and watch'.

decisions.alias: Mega Man - Battle Network 6 - Cybeast Gregar (USA).gba
decisions.hook: Dodge attacks on a small grid while choosing battle chips from a customised folder. Building combinations that work under real-time pressure is the attraction: a powerful chip is only useful if you can survive long enough to use it well.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported best-tuned ranking with the action/deckbuilding interaction.

decisions.hook: Explore the original Metroid's world rebuilt around sharper movement and new abilities, then use those tools to open old routes. Its compact campaign rewards learning shortcuts and experimenting with sequence breaks, making repeat runs more interesting than simply checking every room once.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands tight/short shorthand into exploration and replay decisions.

decisions.hook: Follow directed missions through a research station, gaining abilities that open new routes while the powerful SA-X threatens your safety. The tension is effective, but frequent orders make this a more guided Metroid than an open-ended hunt for your own path.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains both stalker tension and the cost of linear direction.

decisions.hook: Move an Onimusha-themed squad across grid battles, choosing who should attack, support or hold back. The relatively light challenge makes it an approachable tactics detour, but players seeking demanding encounters may find too little resistance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces skin/easy shorthand with an understandable accessibility-versus-challenge judgment.

decisions.hook: Build a team through Hoenn's badge journey, then take it into the Battle Frontier's varied battle challenges. That demanding postgame is the strongest reason to choose Emerald over a straightforward replay of Ruby or Sapphire.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generation shorthand with team-building and the Frontier's purpose.

decisions.hook: Build a team through the same Kanto journey as FireRed, with a different selection of version-exclusive Pokémon. Choose it for those encounters rather than a different campaign; a complete collection still depends on trading.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what FireRed's sibling actually changes and retains the collection limitation.

decisions.hook: Explore a new region where Oak's grandson rules through eight altered 'tyrant' Pokémon. Only Surf and Fly remain as field-move requirements and trade evolutions are removed, making this a more self-contained solo adventure, though its design belongs to an older generation of hacks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts plot and feature stacking to focus on the campaign and solo-play convenience.

decisions.hook: Explore a restyled Kanto and Sevii without the usual field-move gates, choosing the order in which to challenge gyms. Scaling and level-cap options help shape the difficulty, but rebalanced bosses mean the familiar map does not promise an easy nostalgic tour.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns graphical/option lists into a clear nonlinearity-versus-difficulty recommendation.

decisions.hook: Build your team from Game Corner prize machines rather than ordinary catches, with casinos replacing the usual shops. Optional dice, coin and slot effects can push chance into the battles too, making this a deliberately gambling-driven remix rather than a reliable test of conventional team planning.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the consequence of the casino rules instead of ending with vague systemic praise.

decisions.hook: Kulure's gyms test battle concepts such as terrain and status rather than assigning every leader one type. That gives team-building a different target, while three difficulty modes let you choose how hard those ideas bite in this complete new-region adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Selects concept-based gyms and adjustable challenge from a crowded feature list.

decisions.hook: Replay Ash's anime journey through a FireRed campaign built around the episodes rather than a new regional story. This patch repairs serious bugs in Ash Gray beta 4.5.3, but the story remains unfinished and PC boxes 2, 3 and 6 are locked to avoid save corruption.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains the incomplete story and important locked-PC-box caveat while simplifying patch prose.

decisions.hook: Revisit Hoenn with new regional forms, unfamiliar starter choices and tougher boss teams. Reusable move-teaching items and training tools encourage rebuilding your party, while Hard Mode's badge-based level caps stop extra grinding from solving every problem.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a feature inventory with the roster experimentation and capped-difficulty decisions.

decisions.hook: Build a team from 386 original creatures across Fochun and the post-league islands, facing smarter opponents and soft level caps. The constant imageboard humour is a substantial taste barrier, not a minor decoration; v1.3.3 also leaves the Battle Channel unfinished and its saves will not carry into 2.0.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains content and save-compatibility warnings while reducing version and feature clutter.

decisions.hook: Pokémon are retyped to match their sprite colours, so familiar appearances invite new team-building mistakes and discoveries. Reworked opponents make the change matter in battle; the Classic option preserves original stats if you want the type puzzle without the full statistical rebalance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why colour-based retyping matters and distinguishes the Classic option.

decisions.hook: Explore Enpale with a curated 300-Pokémon roster and a rock-and-metal soundtrack, building a team for a new-region story. Mining and field travel without dedicated HM carriers leave more room for exploration, but v1.1.1 is an early release rather than a long-mature revision.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces plot/name lists with exploration appeal and preserves early-build context.

decisions.hook: Replay Crystal through the battle with Red in a FireRed-based remake with a larger roster and changing days and seasons. Faster battles and optional shared experience reduce some repetition, but the attraction is revisiting Johto rather than discovering a wholly new campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Prioritises remake scope and pacing instead of protagonist and engine inventories.

decisions.hook: Start with a fully evolved dragon and build a powerful team for the Omni-region sequel, now with move-specific physical and special attacks. Bosses escalate into excessively strong legendary lineups, so the apparent head start does not remove the grinding; the story also leans heavily into bleak melodrama.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains difficulty criticism, explains battle terminology and removes an unnecessary ending spoiler.

decisions.hook: Worlds Collide mixes Pokémon and Digimon in a Ferrum-region campaign against the Seven Great Demon Lords, making crossover team-building its main draw. Despite the Origins name it is not a conventional prequel; the abbreviated title leaves the exact release identification uncertain.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces 'almost certainly' and a feature list with useful conditional identity guidance; does not claim release verification.

decisions.hook: Kanto's gym order and cast are reworked around a new version of the original journey, with later-generation moves and move-specific physical and special attacks changing team choices. It offers more than a graphical remake, but the deliberately edgy writing may be less appealing than the battle changes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies the reboot's gameplay difference while retaining the writing caveat.

decisions.hook: Investigate a missing professor and the Dreamstones in a new region, with a quest tracker helping you follow the story. Freely adjustable training and field travel without HM requirements favour trying different teams instead of keeping an inconvenient party solely to get around.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the story and convenience inventory into a concrete exploration/team-building reason.

decisions.hook: Follow a tournament-bound trainer through a story-led new region, using a quest log to keep track of side errands. This is only Part A: v2.5.0 ends aboard the S.S. Challenger, so choose it knowing the story continues in a separate Part B.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the crucial Part A boundary while cutting plot and mechanics abbreviations.

decisions.hook: Draft a team and race through a compressed Emerald with randomised gyms and an expanded final gauntlet. Hard level caps, no battle items and tightly limited stat boosts keep the focus on fast decisions rather than grinding; it was designed for roughly 90-minute Nuzlocke races, not a normal story campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the race constraints instead of listing every replacement item.

decisions.hook: Hoenn gets a Gold-and-Silver-inspired visual makeover alongside a broader roster and reworked Pokémon types. Modern battle categories and party experience sharing make team experiments easier, while optional Hard Mode gives the familiar journey more resistance than its cosy appearance suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces acronym-heavy feature lists with the visual/mechanical contrast.

decisions.hook: Give each Pokémon up to four abilities and build combinations far beyond ordinary Emerald teams. Difficulty, randomiser and sandbox options make this a system-heavy experiment, better suited to learning unusual interactions than preserving the original game's balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses on multi-ability builds rather than an overwhelming list of additions.

decisions.hook: Explore a mountain community from before Poké Balls existed, investigating hostile Pokémon with a single partner. Wild encounters and bosses replace trainer battles, making this a short, different kind of adventure rather than another badge-and-League campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the absence of trainer battles the meaningful distinction and trims background lore.

decisions.hook: Play a Team Rocket recruit, stealing Pokémon from defeated trainers as you climb the organisation and uncover another side of Kanto. Side jobs and expanding theft opportunities make the criminal perspective more than a costume change; v1.0.2 is the completed release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces best-reskin praise and mechanical abbreviations with the distinctive theft loop.

decisions.hook: Explore a Netherlands-inspired region of canals and polders, using a quest log to follow the fight against a flood-plotting faction. Followers and campsites give the journey character, but v0.1.9 is a buggy beta covering only about four gyms, not a finished regional campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves demo scope and bugs while reducing feature stacking.

decisions.hook: Collect Yu-Gi-Oh! cards that fight as Pokémon-style monsters in a retelling of Forbidden Memories. The novelty is rebuilding your team around that crossover roster rather than playing the original card game's rules; v0.9.5.2 remains a pre-1.0 release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what the crossover actually plays like and retains pre-release status.

decisions.hook: Revisit Johto through redesigned events and maps, with a broader roster and smarter trainer teams. Riding Pokémon replaces the old HM burden, but v2.7.6 is still a beta ending after eight badges and the League; Kanto is not included yet.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the remake's practical changes clear and retains the missing-Kanto boundary.

decisions.hook: Explore Orbtus's ruins in a new-region Pokémon journey with modern battle rules and Mega Evolution. It suits a fairly traditional adventure with unfamiliar places to search, but v3.2 ends at the League and has no postgame.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unqualified polish praise and a feature list with campaign shape and completion limit.

decisions.hook: Explore a decayed Kanto using an entirely Ghost-type roster, including many redesigned regional forms. Removing individual training stats and offering unlimited Rare Candies puts more emphasis on choosing a team than raising its numbers; the horror setting makes this a different mood from a comforting Kanto replay.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the all-Ghost constraint and reduced training friction without vague time-respect praise.

decisions.hook: Build a team across Tunod, Johto and Rankor in a long, traditional Pokémon adventure. The v9.2.0 update speeds battles and strengthens later opponents, but old Pokédex and cry glitches remain; the extensive journey is the draw, not a polished short campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains meaningful update and bug caveats while cutting plot and roster inventory.

decisions.hook: Revisit Johto and its Kanto postgame with following Pokémon and optional modern battle rules. Level caps and challenge modifiers let you reshape the difficulty, but the familiar story remains the point; choose it for a configurable remake rather than a new adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported best-GBA-Johto ranking and explains configurable familiarity.

decisions.hook: Explore a quiet region inspired by pre-modern Japan and China, taking quests and watching characters follow daily routines. The relaxed pace is the appeal, but v0.1.27 is a demo that stops at the third gym, so do not start it expecting a complete campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces 'mostly vibes' with the town-routine appeal and a clear demo limit.

decisions.hook: Try an artist-built roster of original creatures either by exploring abandoned regions or drafting rentals for a Battle Factory gauntlet. Reworked types, moves and opponents reward inspecting unfamiliar monsters rather than relying on remembered Pokémon matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the choice between exploration and rental drafting instead of listing contributors and features.

decisions.hook: Explore a story-driven mystery through randomised floors, adapting to the enemies, items and upgrades each run provides. Unlockable characters and team synergies give repeat attempts different possibilities, while permanent progress makes this a compact roguelike adventure rather than another long badge chase.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unexplained 'Start here' directive and makes run variation the recommendation.

decisions.hook: Follow Ash, Brock and Misty through the opening stretch of the Johto anime, catching the Pokémon associated with Ash's journey. Alpha 2.1 covers only a short section and the creator declared the project abandoned, so skip it if you want a complete story rather than an unfinished adaptation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the negative recommendation but explains exactly why the abandoned alpha is a poor campaign choice.

decisions.hook: Explore a Greece-inspired region with a large roster redrawn in the Game Boy Color-style art of Emerald Seaglass. Version 2.0 revises the adventure and adds Mega Evolutions, but the underlying appeal remains a traditional Pokémon journey in unfamiliar surroundings rather than a new battle format.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces developer and count lists with the traditional-play/new-setting distinction.

decisions.hook: Investigate aggressive Pokémon in an industrial-era Hoenn prequel, choosing between two protagonists. The altered setting is the reason to visit, but this beta is only a roughly one-to-two-hour demo, not a complete historical campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the prequel setting useful while keeping the short-demo warning prominent.

decisions.hook: Explore Nendios through time-based events and side quests in a visually reworked FireRed adventure. This discontinued alpha is best approached as an unfinished curiosity, and blacking out ends the game, making frequent saves more important than in ordinary Pokémon.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains the severe blackout behaviour and discontinued status while reducing the feature list.

decisions.hook: Explore Waikai from a hub and build teams for legendary biome bosses instead of conventional gyms. Mandatory level caps and the removal of individual training stats keep attention on choosing the right tools rather than outlevelling the problem, while regional forms make old favourites less predictable.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the boss structure and training constraints instead of listing them.

decisions.hook: Revisit Crystal in FireRed's engine, with additional events and an Orange Islands excursion beyond Johto and Kanto. The expanded itinerary is tempting, but the final Live Beta was left unfinished and the creator confirmed it will not be completed; choose another remake if closure matters more than historical curiosity.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the unfinished-status warning into a clear reason to choose or skip.

decisions.hook: Replay routes, gyms and events across several regions for scaling rewards, assigning Pokémon to classes and developing them beyond level 100. This is a repeatable progression sandbox: experimenting with builds and difficulty modifiers matters more than treating each location as a one-time story stop.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains replayable progression without an overloaded economy/feature inventory.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mega Mirage of Tales - A New Age Dawns (v2.1u2).gba
decisions.hook: Graduate from an academy and choose a career such as trainer, researcher or criminal, each with different missions. That branching premise is intriguing, but this early beta was later disowned by its creator as poorly planned and unpleasant to play, making it a risky choice for a sustained campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves the creator's negative assessment and connects it to the player's choice.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Red Rescue Team (USA, Australia).gba
decisions.hook: Explore changing dungeon floors with a Pokémon partner, managing moves, food and supplies one turn at a time. Its forgiving opening and sincere rescue-team story make it an inviting introduction to dungeon crawling, though repeated rescue trips can feel routine.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces 'easy with sincere story' with dungeon decisions and a concrete repetition caveat.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Rogue Rescue Team (v3.0.0).gba
decisions.hook: Choose a hero, partner and seed for a ten-dungeon gauntlet that reveals its challenges as you advance. Harder modes restrict carried items and recruiting, forcing better use of what a run provides; v3.0.0 adds the broader NatDex roster option rather than a traditional story campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes must-try and cheese jargon while explaining the resource pressure.

decisions.hook: Follow Chronya through a darker four-region story, building teams for Battle Arenas and a tournament instead of the normal gym-and-League sequence. Exploration becomes partly open after Shedir Town, while selectable difficulty lets you decide how much pressure to put on the battles.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses on campaign progression and freedom instead of roster and feature counts.

decisions.hook: Build teams for a heavily reworked Emerald aimed at experienced Nuzlocke players, with mandatory level caps and demanding double battles. Visible training values reduce guesswork, but this is a challenge campaign rather than a comfortable revisit, so prior knowledge of Pokémon battle interactions matters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported fairness praise and explains who the mandatory challenge excludes.

decisions.hook: Descend an Etrian Odyssey-inspired labyrinth where every fight is a double battle and dungeon exploration replaces the badge-and-League journey. Gathering and dangerous roaming enemies make preparation important between fights; choose it for coordinated pairs and deliberate expeditions, not a conventional regional tour.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains FOE shorthand and selects the distinctive dungeon/pair-planning loop.

decisions.hook: Rebuild Kanto teams around an enormous range of Eevee evolutions covering different type combinations. Reworked opponents make those combinations matter, while a tough postgame gives the joke room to become a real team-building challenge rather than only a sprite replacement.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the Eevee gimmick and feature list into a concrete reason to experiment.

decisions.hook: Escape a battle puzzle with one Pokémon that starts without moves and cannot gain levels. Four prayer actions steal an enemy's species, item, ability or move permanently, so progress comes from exploiting interactions rather than grinding; the rules also rig luck against you.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the mechanics-first puzzle and preserves the no-level/luck constraints.

decisions.hook: Revisit Emerald with redesigned scenery, battle weather, following Pokémon and music drawn from later games. Presentation is the main reason to choose it over the original, but the creator lists real-hardware stutter and unfinished battle backgrounds, so the makeover is not uniformly polished.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands presentation shorthand and retains both concrete limitations.

decisions.hook: Run Petalburg Gym instead of travelling between badges: choose its type, build a roster and defend against a season of generated challengers. Injuries, staffing and finances make team management extend beyond the next battle, but there is no conventional overworld journey if exploration is your main pleasure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the management loop and absent exploration explicit rather than ending with generic systemic praise.

decisions.hook: Aim pinball shots to trigger catches and evolutions, building a Pokémon collection across the Ruby and Sapphire tables. Those objectives give repeated games a purpose beyond high scores, though completing them demands controlled shots rather than merely keeping the ball alive.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces hollow 'good pinball' praise with catching objectives and shot-control demands.

decisions.hook: Explore a remapped Hoenn with a mixture of familiar Pokémon and new creatures, learning revised moves and abilities along the way. The team explicitly aims for a tough adventure, so choose it for relearning matchups under pressure rather than a gentle tour of new scenery.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the value and difficulty of the new roster rather than listing additions.

decisions.hook: Choose your own route through Hoenn and Sevii, tackling gyms in any order while opponents scale with badge progress. Broad early access to Pokémon encourages building the team you actually want, while optional battle and difficulty modes turn the familiar geography into a flexible replay space.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains open-world team-building without overwhelming the note with mode names.

decisions.hook: Revisit Sapphire through redesigned maps and demanding trainer teams while keeping generation-three battle rules. Cheap Rare Candies reduce preparation grinding, so the appeal is solving hard fights with a deliberately restricted ruleset rather than collecting every modern mechanic.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes comparison shorthand and feature stacking while retaining strict Gen 3 mechanics and anti-grind tools.

decisions.hook: Explore Colen in a new FireRed-based story with modernised battle categories and a postgame visit to part of Hoenn. This is the 2020 bug-fix release, but the creator still describes the game as flawed; choose it for the new journey rather than expecting the author's later polish.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the edition and creator caveat while replacing acronym-heavy feature listing.

decisions.hook: Return to Johto twenty years after Gold and Silver, assembling a broader team for a new conflict over Celebi. Leaders use items and setup strategies, so the familiar region comes with moderately harder battles rather than simply a nostalgic walk through old towns.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the sequel setting and tactical difficulty clear without an engine/feature inventory.

decisions.hook: Explore a zombie-ravaged Hoenn with altered creatures, ruined gyms and deliberately absurd humour. The appeal is the strange transformation of Ruby's world, not a faithful sequel; fast-forward can break scripts, so rushing past the oddities can also cause technical trouble.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves the fast-forward warning while prioritising tone and changed-world exploration.

decisions.hook: Follow a story-led tournament journey through Hupest, building teams around special Solar and Lunar Pokémon forms. A quest log helps organise the side content; for mGBA, use the creator's Emulator Fix variant rather than assuming the ordinary v1.3 release is compatible.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Selects the form-building hook and keeps the meaningful emulator-variant caveat.

decisions.hook: Explore an expanded Johto with hidden grottos, achievements and legendary bosses whose multiple health bars demand more sustained plans. Optional level caps let you tune the journey, while postgame multi-ability builds reward continued team experimentation rather than merely collecting another badge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains boss and postgame build decisions instead of a dense feature list.

decisions.hook: Revisit Kanto through stylised graphics, new regional forms and a broader choice of Ghost and Dark Pokémon. Reworked moves and stats add some resistance, but this is intended as a somewhat harder familiar adventure rather than a dedicated challenge hack.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands vanilla-plus shorthand and preserves the intended moderate difficulty.

decisions.hook: Take quests in your chosen order to earn enough local reputation for Veldan's gym leader to face you. The structure makes community tasks part of progression, but v0.1.1 covers only the first area and first gym, so it is a substantial demo rather than a finished open-world campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains reputation gating and keeps the first-area/gym boundary.

decisions.hook: Climb a hundred-floor trainer gauntlet with random starters, planning around shops and healing stops every five floors. Boss victories periodically add recruits, so keeping a workable team alive matters more than following a story; optional endless play extends the run beyond the original goal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns floor arithmetic into the resource-planning decision and distinguishes it from a campaign.

decisions.hook: Collect the Unown alphabet to decipher inscriptions and find a path through an ancient temple. Field tools and sturdy single-Pokémon bosses turn that language hunt into a compact exploration puzzle, not a standard gym journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Prioritises deciphering and exploration instead of soundtrack and quantity lists.

decisions.hook: Follow an expanded Gold-style journey across several regions with a much broader Pokémon roster. Its enormous scope is the attraction, but v1.5.1 still labels some areas unavailable despite its bug fixes, so a long itinerary should not be mistaken for a fully completed remake.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a sprawling feature inventory with the scope-versus-incompleteness trade-off.

decisions.hook: Complete the original-generation-three collection in one FireRed adventure, with version exclusives combined and trade evolutions removed. A new island houses additional encounters, but the main Kanto story stays familiar; choose it for self-contained collecting rather than a new plot.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the solo-collection purpose without listing every encounter mechanism.

decisions.hook: Explore Borrius through a new story and a large set of tracked side missions, building teams around modernised battle rules. Four difficulty settings let the same journey range from approachable to highly demanding, while field moves without dedicated HM carriers make experimenting with your party less awkward.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Selects mission structure and configurable battle challenge from the flagship/feature list.

decisions.hook: Explore a Levant-inspired region in a Celebi-centred story, using familiar early-generation Pokémon with modern battle categories. Version 4.3.0 reaches the LAVAN League and Lilycove harbour, but the planned Hoenn half is absent, so this beta does not yet deliver the whole advertised journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the precise campaign boundary while reducing engine and plot naming clutter.

decisions.hook: Explore Vega's original-creature roster through a modified Vega Minus build that adds Fairy typing and further creatures from related hacks. The appeal is experimenting with a revised roster and matchups rather than a new campaign; v1.4 is the final balance patch for this edition.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the layered hack's practical purpose and preserves final-edition context.

decisions.hook: Explore an alien planet on limited oxygen, learning how its altered creatures and environment fit together. Knowledge and environmental puzzles drive progress rather than gym victories, making this a short Pokémon detour for people who enjoy discovery more than a conventional championship climb.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces author and genre references with oxygen-constrained exploration and learning.

decisions.hook: Pursue Jirachi through Shin-Tokyo while stealing Shadow Pokémon from trainers and purifying them for your team. That capture-and-recovery loop gives the short story a distinct identity, but v1.2.2 predates later fixes for serious progression bugs, including being unable to leave the Shinkansen.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses on Shadow capture and adds the creator-documented train progression bug affecting this older build.

decisions.hook: Follow a character-focused story through a new region, stepping off its linear main route to find optional areas and unfamiliar creatures. The baseline challenge stays near the main series, with scaling and alternative battle modes available if you want more variation rather than mandatory punishment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the balance of directed story, optional exploration and adjustable challenge.

decisions.hook: Descend into a turn-based dungeon, identifying unfamiliar items and deciding when to spend a useful wand or trust a god. The goal includes getting back out alive, so survival and learning the rules matter more than clearing every enemy; this is a compact-looking game with a demanding traditional roguelike underneath.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces NetHack-adjacent shorthand and empty excellence praise with item uncertainty and survival decisions.

decisions.hook: Spend action points to move and shoot, using cover and overwatch to control where enemies can safely advance. The squad-level decisions are the draw, making this a focused tactical campaign rather than a full X-COM-style management simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains action-point and overwatch tactics instead of relying on underrated/X-COM-lite labels.

decisions.hook: Switch between Gundams with different movement and attack abilities across side-scrolling fights and flying stages. The changes of role give the action some variety, but repeated enemy-clearing sections make it a simpler combat diversion rather than a deep robot-building game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces dismissive kids'-brawler shorthand with the GBA-specific role/stage structure.

decisions.hook: Choose a class and work through action-heavy dungeons, improving your character through combat and new equipment. Building a specialised fighter is the attraction, but repeated enemy clearing makes the progression grind part of the deal rather than a brief interruption.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the class-and-equipment loop while retaining the grinding criticism.

decisions.hook: Fight in small arenas while teaching Emerl a customised set of attacks copied from other characters. Choosing how the robot moves, strikes and defends gives repeated bouts a building goal, so its appeal depends as much on assembling a moveset as winning the next fight.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why copied skills matter instead of merely repeating that Emerl is the hook.

decisions.hook: Explore a reconstruction of Super Metroid's map inside Zero Mission's engine, with rails replacing Grapple Beam traversal and reworked boss arenas. It is a reinterpretation rather than a straight port: the Super Metroid soundtrack is absent and Crocomire remains rough even in the final 4.0 release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the conversion differences into two sentences and retains the rough-Crocomire caveat.

decisions.hook: Revisit the first Mana adventure through two protagonists, real-time fighting and a forge for improving equipment. The attractive presentation and crafting invite a longer stay, but easy, repetitive combat can make those preparations feel more elaborate than the battles require.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces pretty/button-mashy shorthand with the crafting-versus-combat trade-off.

decisions.hook: Read a tiny visual instruction and act within seconds before the next completely different microgame arrives. Simple controls make individual tasks easy to grasp, but the accelerating switches test recognition as much as reflexes; the humour comes from being surprised again and again.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands quick/funny shorthand into the actual rapid-rule-reading challenge.

decisions.alias: Yggdra Union - We'll Never Fight Alone (USA).gba
decisions.hook: Choose a card to set your army's shared movement and available abilities, then arrange units so several can join one attack. Those linked decisions give the tactics a distinctive shape, but unusual rules and unskippable battle animations create a steep learning curve and slow later fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains cards and union positioning and replaces vague opacity with researched friction.

decisions.alias: Zone of the Enders - The Fist of Mars (USA).gba
decisions.hook: Command robots in turn-based grid battles, then take part in timed attack minigames instead of leaving every hit to the numbers. That hands-on interruption is the distinctive choice here: appealing if you want reflexes mixed into tactics, less so if you want to plan without execution tests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the timing/tactics trade-off and removes empty 'decent' judgment.

decisions.hook: Shoot through Bond missions with driving sequences breaking up the first-person action. The changing pace gives it a movie-spy flavour, but choose it for a straightforward action outing rather than expecting its gunplay alone to carry the whole adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces FPS/filler shorthand with the on-foot/driving structure and a qualified reason to play.

decisions.hook: Third-person shooting, gadgets and elaborate set pieces turn Bond into a playable action film. Choose it for cinematic variety rather than a free-form spy simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces an unsupported best-of-series verdict with the actual appeal of Bond set pieces.

decisions.hook: Sean Connery’s Bond anchors a third-person shooter with lock-on gunplay and gadgets, rather than a recreation of the film’s restrained espionage. The period atmosphere is appealing, but passive enemies and awkward vehicle controls let down the action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands opaque EoN shorthand and gives supported criticism of enemy behavior and vehicle controls.

decisions.hook: First-person gunfights alternate with gadget work and driving missions, giving Nightfire the rhythm of a globe-trotting Bond adventure. Choose it for those changes of pace rather than uninterrupted corridor shooting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the vague GoldenEye comparison and solid verdict with concrete campaign variety.

decisions.alias: Baten Kaitos - Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean (USA) (Disc 1).iso
decisions.hook: Build decks of weapons, defenses and items, then combine matching card numbers or numerical runs for battle bonuses. Items also change as they age, making your inventory an evolving puzzle; the unusual systems reward patience with a slow-moving RPG.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies that number combinations form sets and runs rather than spelling numbers.

decisions.hook: Hunt block-shaped animals and choose what to eat to change your creature’s colors, limbs and abilities. Discovering mutations is the draw, but this is a structured action game with breeding and progression goals, not an unrestricted evolution sandbox.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the misleading pure-sandbox label and explains mutation choices.

decisions.hook: Build a small combat robot from interchangeable parts, then test it in compact arena battles. The garage gives you plenty to experiment with, but the long, chatty story repeatedly slows access to the fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the remaining clipped Custom Robo fragments into complete explanatory sentences.

decisions.alias: Legend of Zelda, The - The Wind Waker (USA, Canada).ciso
decisions.hook: Sail between islands, solve tool-based dungeon puzzles and fight through a vividly animated ocean adventure. The expressive characters and dungeons are the reward, but long voyages give this original GameCube version a noticeably leisurely pace.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns clipped sailing shorthand into a clear exploration recommendation with its pacing caveat.

decisions.hook: Build a deck of creatures and summon them during real-time battles, making preparation as important as dodging the next attack. Its short, unusual adventure is worth choosing for that collision of card planning and immediate action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why the creature deck matters instead of ending with cryptic short-and-strange shorthand.

decisions.hook: Build a deck of creature cards for real-time battles, with transformations letting you become some of the creatures yourself. The larger card pool and extra side quests make this the broader adventure, especially if experimenting with a loadout is the attraction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the sequel note understandable without knowing Lost Kingdoms.

decisions.alias: Phantasy Star Online Episode III - C.A.R.D. Revolution (USA) (En,Ja).ciso
decisions.hook: Build decks of weapons and creatures, then use them in grid-based tactical battles rather than Phantasy Star Online’s usual real-time combat. The offline campaign gives deck experimentation a purpose even without online opponents; choose it for deliberate planning, not action-RPG loot runs.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands unexplained PSO shorthand and makes the genre change explicit.

decisions.hook: Double battles ask you to coordinate two Pokémon at once while rescuing corrupted Shadow Pokémon from opposing trainers. That team-focused combat and darker adventure are the draw, rather than the familiar routine of roaming grass to build a collection.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains snagging and the double-battle appeal instead of relying on franchise shorthand.

decisions.hook: Rescue and purify Shadow Pokémon through a story built around two-on-two battles. A broader selection to catch makes this an appealing continuation of Colosseum’s team-building idea, but the focus remains a directed adventure rather than a traditional gym journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sequel-only shorthand with the rescue loop and team-building distinction.

decisions.hook: This Sunshine overhaul adds 120 Shines, new areas and playable characters while opening Isle Delfino to less linear exploration. Choose it for a much larger adventure and new movement options rather than a faithful replay; version 1.1 also addresses 60 FPS bugs and balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Compresses a feature inventory into the exploration appeal while retaining the edition fixes.

decisions.hook: Sunburn loosens Sunshine’s mission structure with freer travel, out-of-order Shines and fewer forced returns to the hub. Autosaving and more accessible coin collecting reduce interruptions, making this a smoother revisit rather than a wholly new campaign; version 2.0 uses a newer engine build.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how the quality-of-life changes affect play instead of listing every feature.

decisions.hook: Knock opponents off interactive stages rather than emptying a health bar, using fast movement, recoveries and well-timed attacks. Local battles are the lasting attraction, while Adventure and Event modes provide structured challenges when playing alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces competitive-Smash shorthand with the actual fight objective and solo options.

decisions.alias: Super Smash Bros. Melee - Akaneia Build (v1.0.1).iso
decisions.hook: Akaneia expands Melee with seven bonus fighters and eighteen stages while preserving the original cast’s familiar handling. Choose it for new matchups in Melee’s style, not a replacement combat system; version 1.0.1 adds item toggles and experimental custom saves alongside crash fixes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the claim that every bonus fighter came from Brawl: Tails did not, and trims the roster list.

decisions.hook: Bomb on Basic City turns repeated bombing passes into a compact arcade challenge. Its appeal is timing releases against the city below rather than flying a realistic aircraft; do not expect the extra features of the separately released Special Edition.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes filename commentary while retaining the important Special Edition distinction.

decisions.hook: Marketed as a five-in-one poker collection, this unlicensed Taiwanese cartridge is a curiosity for card-game collectors rather than a clear starting point for learning poker. Its individual rules are poorly documented, so do not assume a standard Texas Hold’em game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Uses consulted packaging to identify the compilation premise without inventing undocumented rules.

decisions.hook: Early EA ice hockey keeps the focus on finding passing lanes and getting a clean shot through traffic. Choose it for the relatively spare on-ice contest rather than elaborate roster management or later games’ presentation features.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes database housekeeping from an otherwise useful hockey recommendation.

decisions.hook: This Swedish-league edition brings NHL 96’s on-ice contest to Elitserien clubs. Pick it for that roster context and the familiar passing game; this is the 16-bit release, not a polygonal or CD-enhanced hockey game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves platform-specific guidance without referring to erroneous database summaries.

decisions.hook: This FIFA Soccer 95 hack refreshes the familiar angled-pitch football with 2019–20 club squads, revised presentation and added commentary. Choose it for updated teams within the old match engine rather than modern football mechanics; the documented 2020 release does not establish what changed specifically in version 2.3.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces an overlong feature list with the roster-update appeal and keeps the undocumented-version caveat.

decisions.hook: The Gryphon hack adds a playable Gryphon to Golden Axe III's story mode, lets both players choose the same hero and removes friendly fire. Those changes make cooperative crowd-fighting less prone to accidental sabotage; version 9 also fixes Gryphon bugs found in version 6.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses patch bookkeeping into two useful sentences while retaining all documented co-op and version caveats.

decisions.hook: Hire troops before battle, then keep commanders and their soldiers working together as spells and unit matchups reshape the front. This Chinese-language translation of Langrisser II offers the original game's linear campaign and class development, not the branching allegiances of Der Langrisser; reading Chinese is important for following its story and menus.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces registry shorthand with troop-command decisions, preserving Chinese-language and original-campaign distinctions.

decisions.hook: Build up three colour-selected weapons and supporting orbs in this unlicensed vertical shooter, whose title does not make it an official Raiden sequel. Generous health pickups make it approachable, but repetitive enemies and bland stages give experienced shooter players little reason to choose it over stronger alternatives.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague collector-curiosity recommendation with researched weapon choices and grounded criticism of repetition.

decisions.hook: Late-era Genesis Madden is chiefly a playbook game: disguise intentions, find the favorable matchup and manage the clock. Choose it for sustained football tactics rather than a dramatic change to the established 16-bit formula.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes irrelevant computer-networking comparison while retaining the playbook-centered recommendation.

decisions.hook: Activate resonators to stun roaming zombies, then reach them and jump on their heads before they recover. That brief window turns a simple platformer into a route-and-timing challenge, giving this irreverent homebrew a clearer attraction than its unclothed heroine or Spectrum ancestry alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces presentation-only summary with the developer-documented resonator, stun and stomp loop.

decisions.hook: A fan modification of Mortal Kombat 3, whose Run button and preset combos favor closing distance and committing to an attack. The Mini hack's specific changes are not reliably documented, so treat it as a variant to investigate after learning the original, not a proven upgrade or the separate Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 Mini hack.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces file-size and registry prose with the fighting premise while preserving uncertainty about undocumented hack changes.

decisions.hook: An angled court and brisk five-on-five play keep passing lanes and quick attacks at the center of the action. The appeal is learning to work the ball into space and sustaining that teamwork across a season, rather than the exaggerated dunks and shoving of NBA Jam.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes metadata-source commentary and describes the actual passing-and-season appeal.

decisions.hook: An angled court and brisk five-on-five play keep passing lanes and quick attacks at the center of the action. The appeal is learning to work the ball into space and sustaining that teamwork across a season, rather than the exaggerated dunks and shoving of NBA Jam.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces computer-version metadata aside with the same useful gameplay recommendation as the equivalent NBA Live 95 release.

decisions.hook: An updated roster sits on a modified Prime Time NFL engine, keeping the emphasis on choosing plays and executing them on the field. Choose it for its period matchups; the familiar football offers less reason to return if you already have a favorite entry in Sega's series.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes meaningless futuristic-title comparison and gives a concrete reason to choose or skip another annual football entry.

decisions.alias: Rock n Roll Racing Hack v16.zip
decisions.hook: Missiles, mines and paid upgrades turn isometric racing into a contest of sabotage as well as driving. Ti's v16 overhaul expands that loop with six-car races, 208 new tracks and revised opponents; choose it for a much larger combat-racing campaign rather than a faithful recreation of the original balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Excessive feature list and unsupported deepest-version claim need a gameplay-led rewrite.

decisions.hook: Sonic 3 Complete joins Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles into an exploratory platform campaign where each character's movement opens different routes. Tiddles' v130810 build restores Sonic 3 presentation details and the Big Arm fight, with options to reverse many changes or play the component games separately; its attraction is a configurable combined adventure rather than entirely new stages.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Dense restoration checklist needs a clearer reason to choose this combined Sonic campaign.

decisions.hook: Familiar Sonic 3 & Knuckles stages become timed challenges, from collecting 200 rings to protecting Tails. ColinC10's remix rewards solving a particular objective instead of merely reaching the exit, with a hub and saved unlocks making it easy to tackle one challenge at a time.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Timed objectives are useful, but shorthand and archival details crowd the recommendation.

decisions.hook: Streets of Rage 2 supplies the foundation of this fan-made brawler: lining up enemies and using throws are more important than blindly trading punches. Kratus' Bare Knuckle 3 Boss Edition v1.1 is an experimental alternative, but the available release information does not establish its exact roster changes; choose the original first if you want a clearly established introduction to the combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Research-status prose needs useful brawling guidance without inventing the undocumented roster.

decisions.hook: Ryu, Ken, Guile and Dhalsim bring Street Fighter-style special moves into Streets of Rage 2's crowd fights. Kratus' Version 1 changes damage and speed and enables cheats, so it is a crossover power trip rather than a faithful test of the original game's balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Roster and moves are useful but need a player-facing reason to try the crossover.

decisions.hook: Cammy, Dee Jay, Chun-Li and Fei Long bring Street Fighter-style special moves into Streets of Rage 2's crowd fights. Kratus' Version 2 changes damage and speed and enables cheats, so it is a crossover power trip rather than a faithful test of the original game's balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Roster and moves are useful but need a player-facing reason to try the crossover.

decisions.hook: Balrog, M. Bison, Sagat and Vega bring Street Fighter-style special moves into Streets of Rage 2's crowd fights. Kratus' Version 3 changes damage and speed and enables cheats, so it is a chance to take the bosses through a street brawl rather than preserve the original balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Roster and moves are useful but need a player-facing reason to try the crossover.

decisions.hook: Blanka, E. Honda, Zangief and T. Hawk bring Street Fighter-style special moves into Streets of Rage 2's crowd fights. Kratus' Version 4 changes damage and speed and enables cheats, so it is a crossover power trip rather than a faithful test of the original game's balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Roster and moves are useful but need a player-facing reason to try the crossover.

decisions.hook: The four Ninja Turtles replace Streets of Rage 2's heroes, putting familiar characters into its street fights and crowd-control rhythm. The documented TMNT Edition changes character graphics rather than creating a new campaign; this 2017 build also credits M3tro, but further changes are undocumented, so approach it as a visual crossover rather than a new Turtles adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Character replacement caveat should remain while research-log wording is removed.

decisions.hook: Extreme Edition pushes Streets of Rage 3's crowd fighting toward harsher difficulty and more brutal player attacks. Gsaurus' v0.42 remix is for veterans seeking a more aggressive challenge, not an easier introduction to running, rolling and managing special attacks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Difficulty warning is useful but the research-log framing obscures the recommendation.

decisions.hook: A Portal Zone hub leads into four new zones in redhotsonic's Sonic 2 Recreation, with several playable characters offering different ways to explore. This 2013 contest build is Part One of a subsequently cancelled project, so choose it for an unfinished alternate Sonic adventure rather than a complete replacement campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Dense technical checklist should become a concise recommendation retaining the unfinished-project caveat.

decisions.hook: Rescuing and escorting Flickies still makes this an isometric search-and-rescue game rather than a sprint. Jon Burton's Director's Cut revises the controls and adds a map and password saves, making the unusual formula easier to revisit without turning it back into side-scrolling Sonic.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Director's Cut note omits the actual control and saving improvements that distinguish it.

decisions.hook: Extended layouts and a Spin Dash make this Sonic 1 remix an invitation to relearn familiar routes rather than simply admire replacement artwork. JK.Fox's 2013 Ultimate Version completes the earlier Pixel Perfect demo, but the changes are front-loaded: the opening zones have four acts each, while later stages stay closer to the original.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Art and layout checklist should explain the uneven extent of the remix.

decisions.alias: Sonic the Hedgehog - The Lost Worlds.zip
decisions.hook: Explore fan-built versions of Sonic 2's discarded zones, with new layouts inspired by prototypes, concept art and contemporary coverage. ExecByte's 2009 Lost Worlds is a speculative alternate adventure, not a recovery of Sega's finished missing levels; curiosity about what might have been is its strongest appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cut-zone feature list needs a clearer distinction between fan reconstruction and original content.

decisions.hook: Sonic 1, Sonic 2 and Sonic 3 share a selection menu in vladikcomper's 2011 compilation, but Sonic & Knuckles is not included. The added Spin Dash and removed speed cap in Sonic 1 make familiar routes feel different, so this is a convenient modified collection rather than three untouched originals.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Compilation checklist relies on unexplained EHZ shorthand and obscures movement changes.

decisions.hook: Esrael Neto's Sonic 2 Delta v0.25 mixes prototype zones, art and enemies with new boss fights, giving familiar momentum-based platforming an alternate route through Sonic 2's development ideas. This 2015 work-in-progress build supports saving, but it is a fan reconstruction to explore rather than a finished official lost edition.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Filename explanation should become a public-safe identification and gameplay recommendation.

decisions.hook: Spacing, anti-air attacks and punishing missed moves remain the heart of Special Champion Edition. This patched version combines Pyron's arcade-style recoloring with Stephane Dallongeville's clearer voice playback, making it a presentation-focused alternative rather than a new fighting system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Visual and voice-driver improvements are concrete, but the note should also explain unchanged fighting.

decisions.hook: Sixteen fighters offer different answers to the same questions of spacing, anti-air defense and when to commit to an attack. This Mega Drive patch combines Pyron's arcade-style recoloring with Stephane Dallongeville's clearer voice playback; choose it for a cleaner presentation of Super Street Fighter II, not new characters or a redesigned fighting system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Technical asset counts and unsupported best-version praise need replacement with useful patch context.

decisions.hook: The original Super Monaco GP career still rewards learning braking points and beating rivals to reach stronger teams. TA Marcos' HE Returns hack dresses that climb in 2019-season teams, drivers and a revised calendar, making it a period-themed refresh of the old racer rather than a modern Formula One simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Long roster-and-presentation checklist should explain the racing appeal and retain the 2019-season distinction.

decisions.hook: Running, rolling and spacing out special attacks remain central to this revised US Streets of Rage 3 campaign, with bug fixes and expanded stage-six hidden areas giving veterans reasons to return. Gsaurus' v0.3 Project from 2018 has fixes absent from the Bare Knuckle III branch but does not add Adam or Max; it also predates the later v1.0 release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Bug-fix inventory needs a fighting recommendation while preserving the missing Adam/Max distinction.

decisions.hook: This unofficial UEFA Euro 2004 rebranding keeps International Superstar Soccer Deluxe's arcade football beneath a changed title screen. It offers no established football improvement over the original, so choose ISS Deluxe unless the bootleg presentation itself interests you.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces bootleg provenance shorthand with a clear reason to prefer the original football game.

decisions.hook: Ultimate Mortal Kombat Trilogy brings fighters from the first three Mega Drive Mortal Kombat games into UMK3's combo-driven combat, making unusual cross-game matchups its main attraction. Revision 5149 expands the arenas and moves as well, but its oversized 10 MB format needs compatible emulation such as Genesis Plus GX or PicoDrive.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the expanded roster as a playing choice rather than a list of abbreviations; preserves compatibility warning.

decisions.alias: Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 Hack Ver. 0.71 (By Nemesis_c).zip
decisions.hook: This v0.71 UMK3 Arcade hack restores Sheeva and missing arenas while adding playable bosses and an in-game move list. It is a useful way to explore a fuller version of the Mega Drive fighter, but its 6 MB format is incompatible with Regen, Kega and Gens Plus.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the crowded patch inventory into a readable arcade-restoration recommendation while retaining compatibility limits.

decisions.hook: UMK3 miniHack v13 expands the selectable cast with Khameleon, Chameleon and playable bosses while retaining the stock 4 MB cartridge size. Unlocked options and palette and move fixes make it a convenient variation on the same combo-heavy fighter, rather than an entirely new Mortal Kombat game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a feature-list sentence with the practical appeal and limits of the compact patch.

decisions.hook: Search corridors for keys and supplies while clearing guards from the route to the elevator. Gasega68k's Mega Drive homebrew preserves Wolfenstein 3D's direct maze-shooting appeal, but this 'fv11 fix' build contains the shareware episode rather than the full commercial campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the actual maze-shooting appeal instead of relying on technical praise and release history.

decisions.hook: Yoshi's Island-style moves change how you traverse Sonic 2, with Baby Sonic floating away in a bubble when you take a hit. The crossover is an appealing movement experiment, but this unfinished hack has reports of an impassable boss, so do not choose it expecting a complete campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Shortens contest history and explains the movement contrast while preserving the unfinished boss caveat.

decisions.hook: Choose one of eight rulers, recruit armies and use diplomacy before committing them to tactical battles in Bahamut Senki. Supper and TheMajinZenki's English patch opens up this involved fantasy strategy game, but its mix of political management and several battle systems makes the included translated manuals valuable preparation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces compressed credits and mode listing with strategic choices and the translation/manual benefit.

decisions.alias: barver battle saga - tai kong zhan shi (english translation).zip
decisions.hook: Brave Battle Saga follows a linear fantasy journey across a connected world, with party battles presented in the style of Breath of Fire II. This English translation makes Chuanpu's Taiwanese RPG approachable, but its familiar structure is a better reason to choose it than expecting an open-ended adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Centers the translated RPG on its structure rather than patch-removal history.

decisions.hook: Guide a physics-driven ball around bumpers and black holes to brighten Brunni's hand-drawn artwork. Revealing each picture gives the puzzle a distinctive reward, while the completion-time score encourages finding a more efficient path rather than merely browsing the drawings.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces art-only puzzle description with the creator-confirmed bouncing-ball and image-lighting mechanics.

decisions.hook: Knuckles' glide, wall climb and spin dash open new approaches to Sonic 1's familiar stages in Stealth's v1.1 character hack. Exploring routes with that expanded movement is the attraction, rather than a new campaign; an optional cheat also enables Super Knuckles.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes blanket hardware-safety praise and explains the movement remix in full sentences.

decisions.hook: PGA Tour Golf II makes club choice, wind and swing timing part of every shot. It suits deliberate course management and learning how to recover from a poor approach, rather than the quick novelty holes of an arcade golf game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes local ROM-marking narration while preserving the PGA Tour Golf II identification.

decisions.hook: Deliberate jumps and sword fights carry this restored version of the unreleased Mega Drive Prince of Persia 2 port. Linkuei's v1.5 patch fixes the Level 9 horse bug and revises the controls, graphics and sound, making it a more practical way to explore the lost conversion rather than the untouched prototype.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces an absolute endorsement and dense fix list with a clear remaster benefit.

decisions.hook: Build speed and judge the landing before curling into a roll through this Sonic 2 hack. Its appeal is familiar momentum-driven platforming; the scope of this v0.5 SMTP revision is uncertain, so later versions' additions should not be assumed here.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps version uncertainty without making the blurb a comment about a filename.

decisions.hook: Onion rings make Sonic heavier, reducing his speed and jump until overeating becomes fatal; running or finding '?' monitors reverses the effect. Sonic 2 XL turns the usual collecting habit into a route-planning trap, a joke that changes play substantially even if its central gag wears thin.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the ring-avoidance challenge without dismissing an actual mechanical remix as not real.

decisions.hook: Syndicate Wars lets you take Streets of Rage 2's enemies and bosses through its brawling, with survival and CPU-partner options extending the experiment. The appeal is discovering how those unusual fighters handle crowds, but this 2016 build has incomplete CPU support for the main heroes and reported crashes with some bosses.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves CPU-partner and crash limitations while making the roster experiment the recommendation.
