decisions.hook: Puyo Wars replaces Streets of Rage 2's cast with Puyo Puyo characters and changes the graphics, sound and text. The joke is seeing that cast in a crowd-brawling game; the underlying combat remains Streets of Rage 2 rather than introducing puzzle mechanics or a new fighting system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces release-database shorthand with the unchanged-combat caveat.

decisions.hook: Manage speed and corners through Super Hang-On's motorcycle racing with an arcade-inspired palette and more detailed roadside scenery. Pyron's Enhanced patch is a visual alternative, not a new set of handling rules or courses, so choose it for the presentation rather than a fresh racing challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces blanket better-look praise with the visual patch scope and unchanged racing.

decisions.hook: Choose actions in cinematic football duels, spending special shots on the moments that matter rather than steering every player directly. Rulez Translation's Italian patch makes the unreleased Tecmo Cup football RPG accessible to Italian readers, but its story and menu-driven matches are a poor fit if you cannot read the language.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes menu-led football and the Italian-language requirement readable without curt dismissal.

decisions.hook: Real-time weapon combat and equipment hunting connect the compact dungeons of King Colossus. Jon Najar/MIJET's English translation makes the story and menus accessible, offering an action-first RPG rather than a deep character-building system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported no-issues guarantee and secondhand score shorthand; preserves translation identity.

decisions.hook: Grid battles tie attacks and spell range to character positioning, with experience earned during the fight rather than only afterward. Tactical party growth is the draw, but the Chinese-language story and menus require more reading commitment than the combat alone might suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes a reference to the generic local filename and retains the language barrier.

decisions.hook: Enemy formations fund shop upgrades, making spending decisions as important as collecting power-ups in flight. The heavy ship and backward scrolling favor careful positioning; the 'Amiga Colors' edition should be approached as a visual variation, not an established overhaul of those mechanics.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces local filename commentary with a cautious edition statement.

decisions.hook: Street objects reveal themselves as aliens, forcing you to watch the scenery as you fight through the invasion. Close-range brawling gives way to shooting-gallery scenes, making this a lively two-player action choice rather than a game built around an especially deep move list.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces engine-name shorthand with the alien ambush and changing combat formats; avoids three-player claim for this two-player set.

decisions.hook: Climb walls and ceilings, then launch kicks into enemies as Kirin moves through sprawling action stages. The acrobatics are the draw: learning where you can cling and when to drop into striking range is more rewarding than treating it as a conventional run-and-gun game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the Strider comparison with Kirin’s actual movement and close-range attack decisions.

decisions.hook: Shoot loose a midboss's control orb and collect it to gain a temporary ally while navigating branching routes through mechanical sea creatures. Black-hole bombs offer a spectacular escape from danger, but choosing a manageable route and preserving your upgrades give the spectacle its lasting challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies that capture applies to midbosses and explains the route and survival choices.

decisions.hook: Circle opponents across a deep arena while sprite scaling creates a surprisingly three-dimensional fight. The experiment is fascinating, but overlapping fighters and special-move directions that change with your position make precision frustrating; choose it to explore an unusual design, not for an immediately readable duel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague curiosity label with a supported explanation of its spatial-control problems.

decisions.hook: Steer the dragon so its indestructible body shields its vulnerable rider, or curl it into enemies while charging a stronger shot. That moving shield makes positioning unusually expressive, while dismounting to collect supplies adds a risk beyond ordinary bullet dodging.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands dragon-shield shorthand into the central positioning decision.

decisions.hook: Let off the fire button to charge a stronger blast, then decide when to trade that stored power for steady flame as your dragon flies through enemy formations. Two-player cooperation gives this Dragon Spirit sequel a shared survival appeal, while charging adds a useful pause to the usual constant-fire rhythm.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre-only text with the charged-shot decision and cooperative appeal; avoids erroneous scraped ground-target claim.

decisions.hook: Choose a fighter, archer or wizard and explore branching dungeon rooms instead of following one straight brawling lane. Crates can be steps to hidden routes rather than things to smash immediately, giving the treasure hunt real decisions, though lingering too long brings pursuing enemies.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how exploration and object placement distinguish the isometric brawler.

decisions.hook: A stranded time patroller and a wolfman fight through dinosaur-filled platform stages, breaking chests for weapons and health. The prehistoric setting gives the shooting its exuberant appeal, especially with a second player, rather than offering a slow exploration of a lost world.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the caveman-only description and supplies the dinosaur run-and-gun loop.

decisions.hook: Mix punches and kicks into combos, then use collected magic to break up crowds of demons. A powerful emergency attack costs health, so the useful tension is deciding whether clearing space now is worth weakening yourself for the next encounter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces developer-family shorthand with combo, magic and health-cost decisions.

decisions.hook: Choose a fantasy hero and fight through isometric rooms full of monsters, treasure and traps. Moving around hazards while keeping enemies in reach gives the action its shape; two-player cooperation makes this a better shared dungeon romp than a substitute for a detailed role-playing campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces an alias-and-genre fragment with trap navigation and cooperative play; does not repeat erroneous four-player metadata.

decisions.hook: Four distinct heroes cut through fantasy crowds with weapons and magic, while branching routes let a return visit take a different path. The sprawling four-player battles are the attraction: this is a fuller cooperative Golden Axe outing, not simply the original stages with a new villain.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns roster and branching-route fragments into reasons to replay the brawler.

decisions.hook: Chain ordinary and heavy attacks, then spend stored power on spectacular martial-arts specials. Branching chapters and coordinated two-player summon attacks give Seven Spirits reasons to replay beyond the army-brawling spectacle, though the loosely translated dialogue is less compelling than the combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsubstantiated levelling shorthand and generic original-game metadata with Seven Spirits-specific mechanics.

decisions.hook: Throw shuriken across the screen, then use a sword when enemies close in during this ninja run-and-gun rescue. Up to four players can join the barrage, making the shifting platform battles a strong cooperative spectacle rather than a stealth exercise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces polished shorthand with ranged/close combat and group-play appeal.

decisions.hook: Choose an aircraft and use its supporting wingmen while racing through dense vertical shooting stages. Letting medals combine and chaining quick kills turns score-chasing into a demanding routing game; in Normal mode, performance also changes which stages you reach, so survival alone does not reveal everything.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unexplained slave/miclus jargon and an unsupported peak claim with concrete scoring choices.

decisions.hook: Possess enemies during a side-scrolling ninja brawl and turn their abilities against the next crowd. Separate high and low punches and kicks give the combat more to learn than a typical two-button beat-'em-up, while experimenting with borrowed bodies supplies its strongest novelty.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the implication of a versus fighter and possession only after defeat.

decisions.hook: Weapon-bearing outlaws face off in duels where blocking too much can break your weapon and leave you fighting bare-handed for the rest of the round. That pressure gives defense a useful cost, making the weapon system a better reason to try it than the familiar special-move exchanges alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported rough dismissal with the distinctive weapon-durability decision.

decisions.hook: Charge into enemies with a melee strike to release red gems, then collect them to build a stronger Vasara attack. This vertical shooter rewards aggressive positioning as well as dodging, with ordinary bombs available when the risk of closing in becomes too high.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Separates melee charge attacks from bombs and explains how gems power the Vasara attack.

decisions.hook: Fight through isometric monster crowds and time the cycling spellbook to transform into a useful magical form rather than a helpless pig. The vivid fantasy scenery and cooperative play are appealing, but punishing bosses and status effects make this a rougher dungeon romp than its simple controls suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the alias-and-items fragment with transformation timing and supported difficulty criticism.

decisions.hook: Alternate forward and sideways fire to meet enemies approaching from different directions; the guns cannot cover both at once. That deliberate coverage choice gives Astro Force's vertical stages their identity, with memorizing enemy entrances helping more than simply holding down fire.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic shooter praise with the developer-confirmed front-versus-side firing decision.

decisions.hook: Monster opponents and animated dunk close-ups dress up otherwise conventional basketball, without supernatural powers changing the rules. The presentation is worth a look, but two-player mode switches to ordinary human teams, losing much of the nightmare theme's appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the empty reminder to win with the important limitation of the monster theme and versus mode.

decisions.hook: Five-card draw asks you to judge an opponent and decide whether to bet, fold or replace a weak hand, while slots and pinball offer simpler diversions. Choose it for a few familiar table games rather than expecting the casino setting to supply a deeper management game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Casino framing is clear, but the pinball praise is vague.

decisions.hook: Overtakes buy bike upgrades as you pick a clean route through ramps and rough terrain. This improvement patch makes upgrades cumulative and unlocks a superjump after buying them all, but reaching 99 damage wipes those improvements away, making repairs a serious investment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The patched edition needs its cumulative upgrades and damage consequence stated.

decisions.alias: Lucky Dime Caper Starring Donald Duck, The (Europe, Brazil) (En).zip
decisions.hook: Donald uses a hammer, frisbee or well-timed stomp to cross this separate eight-bit adventure, rather than QuackShot's routes. Taking a hit strips away his weapon, and uneven collision detection makes some jumps frustrating; unlimited continues help, but patient hazard-learning matters more than charging ahead.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Original copy relies on a QuackShot comparison instead of explaining Donald's attacks and fragility.

decisions.hook: Pitch, bat and guide a Japanese high-school team through the Koshien tournament, with animated interludes giving the matches their personality. Slow fielders and hands-on baserunning make it a fussy choice for casual baseball; the school setting is more distinctive than the action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The school setting alone undersells the actual controls and fielding friction.

decisions.hook: Remove exposed matching tiles, choosing pairs that open access to the rest of the stack. An easy match can use up the partner another tile will need later, so the pleasure comes from planning a complete dismantling rather than grabbing every available pair.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removing tiles cannot literally bury another tile; clarify the blocked-match risk.

decisions.hook: The eight-bit Sonic's bridges and jungle ledges reward measured jumps and exploration as much as speed. This modified edition includes FM music, making the changed soundtrack a concrete reason to revisit those stages rather than expect a new Sonic sequel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The combined modified edition needs the documented FM change stated rather than generic copy wording.

decisions.hook: Pass through the overhead soccer match or switch to a behind-the-kicker penalty contest. The Sports Pad trackball offers movement beyond the ordinary pad’s eight directions, making the control method a better reason to sample this edition than expecting a different football game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The passing and penalty modes are useful, but the alternate control explanation is vague.

decisions.hook: Choose a national side and play through group matches and knockout rounds, with team abilities making that initial selection matter. Exhibition and two-player matches offer a quicker route to the pitch if you want a single contest rather than the full World Cup structure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Tournament rules alone are thin; connect team selection with match formats and a reason to choose.

decisions.hook: Your soldier dodges along the near edge while the aiming cursor ranges across the battlefield, making movement and shot placement competing jobs. This FM modification restores access to Double Hawk's hidden FM soundtrack rather than changing that shooting setup.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces copy-label language with a researched FM-patch distinction.

decisions.hook: Portuguese multiple-choice questions turn the television quiz into a ladder of increasingly valuable answers. This Master System prototype is primarily a language-and-trivia curiosity, so skip it if reading the questions would be more work than pleasure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes filename commentary while preserving Portuguese quiz and prototype caveats.

decisions.hook: Two-on-two mech battles make protecting your team leader as important as attacking the enemy's: losing a leader ends the match. Coordinated covering fire is the draw, but the slower movement makes Force less appealing if you want Oratorio Tangram's fast duels.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre-only shorthand with team-leader tactics and a supported pace caveat.

decisions.hook: Mech duels mix ranged fire with close combat, and aerial dashes or mid-dash turns let you change an approach before the opponent can punish it. The many movement and weapon options reward practice, but the twin-stick control system demands more learning than a straightforward arena shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported benchmark praise with dash choices and learning demands.

decisions.hook: Break an opponent's armor to leave them vulnerable to heavier damage, then use the enclosed arena's walls for crushing follow-up attacks. Fighting Vipers turns its three-button fighting system toward exaggerated launches and wall impacts rather than Virtua Fighter's restrained martial-arts presentation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a one-line comparison with armor consequences and wall tactics.

decisions.hook: Explore a screen-by-screen world, gather equipment and take that growing arsenal into monster-filled dungeons. The Japanese text adds a hurdle to an already tangled adventure; an English translation is available as a separate patch, not part of the original release.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes filename-based uncertainty while retaining the Japanese-language caveat.

decisions.hook: Top-down hockey offers three difficulty settings but a fixed match length, keeping the choices focused on the opposition rather than match customization. Pick it for a basic puck-and-goal contest, not an elaborate sports simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the unsupported implication that the match clock equals real-time commitment.

decisions.hook: Send balls through a pin-filled pachinko table and watch which rebounds reach the paying pockets. The appeal is the little mechanical gambling loop; skip it if you want direct control over the action after each launch.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes catalog-listing trivia to foreground pachinko's limited agency.

decisions.hook: Search side-view stages for the equipment needed to overcome their enemies and barriers. Compile's early Crusader mixes fighting with item-led progression, so working out what you need next matters as much as surviving the next encounter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes database-cleanup commentary and keeps the item-led action identity.

decisions.hook: The neat alien formation is deceptive: attackers peel away and dive toward your ship. Choose between thinning the ranks and stopping an immediate dive; that simple target-priority problem gives the score chase its staying power.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces an abstract closing phrase with a plain target-priority recommendation.

decisions.hook: Return a ball across an angled Pong court, judging its approach in a less familiar perspective. The appeal is learning to read familiar rebounds from an unfamiliar viewpoint, so expect a small reflex exercise rather than much variety.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove the irrelevant table-tennis-career comparison.

decisions.hook: Keep a fish alive by reaching its food, alone or with another player. The straightforward feeding chase offers a small survival challenge without a complicated set of rules to learn.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace unrelated fishing comparison with a concise survival premise.

decisions.hook: Aim the cue ball and time the shot strength to pocket colored balls, building score multipliers with consecutive successes. Three fruitless shots cost a cue ball, so this is a pressured clearance challenge rather than leisurely regulation pool.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace generic relaxation language with manual-backed scoring pressure.

decisions.hook: Long rallies build your score as well as helping you win the match, so patient returns have their own reward. Nine escalating skill levels turn the simple table into a focused test of consistency.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Distinguish rally score bonuses from winning match points.

decisions.hook: Spoken calls give this baseball game character, while rapid directional taps let you urge the runners along. Limited differences between players make the matches repetitive, so the lively baserunning and voice effects are stronger reasons to try it than roster strategy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace sound-only praise with baserunning and supported repetition caveat.

decisions.hook: Choose among twelve Central and Pacific League teams for a baseball match against the computer or another person, with spoken umpire calls adding a little stadium atmosphere to the contest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove tautological final praise while retaining teams and spoken calls.

decisions.hook: Run and shoot through a monster-filled platform course, upgrading your weapon for tougher enemies and bosses. Fixed-height jumps can be steered in midair, but the chunky movement makes careful takeoffs important; boss weak spots demand timing rather than constant fire.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct misleading midair-control implication using MSX movement documentation.

decisions.hook: Keep a pinball alive with independently controlled flippers, timing each return to extend the run and improve your score. Its straightforward table play makes it a compact reflex challenge rather than a game of elaborate rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove the irrelevant menus-and-campaign comparison.

decisions.hook: Explore Egyptian pyramids by finding your way through complex mazes. Keeping track of passages is the central demand, making this a better choice for methodical navigation than for players who want a direct route through the adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace opening fragment and costume comparison with clear maze recommendation.

decisions.hook: Aim the cue ball and time the shot strength to pocket colored balls, building score multipliers with consecutive successes. Three fruitless shots cost a cue ball, so this is a pressured clearance challenge rather than leisurely regulation pool.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace generic pool description with manual-backed scoring and miss penalties.

decisions.hook: Choose among three winged heroes before tackling three long shooting stages and their bosses. The compact stage count keeps the campaign focused, with different weapons supplying variety within the airborne fighting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove the unsupported dismissal of advertised storylines.

decisions.hook: Fly a carpet through twisting diamond gates, then repeat the genie's musical patterns on colored pipes. Switching between spatial timing and musical memory gives the trials variety, but also means both skills must hold up as the patterns grow harder.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces metadata-label commentary with the practical challenge of its two alternating tests.

decisions.hook: Adjust the shooting pressure and watch pachinko balls find their way through the pins. A large choice of boards offers variety, but the largely passive play leaves little tactical control once the balls are loose.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the personal-library reference while retaining the meaningful limitation of passive pachinko play.

decisions.hook: Alternate between horizontal and vertical shooting through organic corridors, building firepower while keeping clear of the scenery. Two-player play gives this demanding campaign a cooperative angle; the original true-ending route requires Nemesis 2 in the second cartridge slot as well as the hidden quest items.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a filename-based warning with the actual Salamander true-ending requirement, without claiming this reissue bypasses it.

decisions.hook: Pilot a helicopter through a snowy battlefield, firing ahead while threading the gaps between threats. The stark white-and-blue scenery is the distinctive attraction in this otherwise straightforward vertical shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the pointless winter-sports comparison with a clear description of the shooting and visual appeal.

decisions.hook: Explore randomly generated dungeons one turn at a time, combining gathered materials into weapons and other useful items. Crafting gives the small-scale roguelike its identity, while permanent death makes a careless encounter more costly than the simple presentation suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands crafting and turn-based decisions; removes an unsupported fixed run length and the claim that every item must be crafted.

decisions.hook: A tabletop-styled RPG where chaining skills earns bonus dice that you can spend to improve crucial rolls. The miniature presentation and dense story make this an unusual, compact campaign, but reading and deliberate combat take priority over exploration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces age, price and four-hour shorthand with the dice economy and intended pace.

decisions.hook: Build a card deck, summon creatures onto a board and turn controlled territory into an economic advantage. The appeal is balancing land investment against the cards needed to defend it, not expecting a quick match or a conventional combat-only card game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes newest/best-portable claims and misleading quick-match promise; explains the board economy.

decisions.hook: A fast 2D Dragon Ball fighter where assist choices complement the active fighter's combos and super attacks. Building a team around useful support is the interesting part; the flashy spectacle is a better reason to play than expecting a sprawling role-playing adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands the genre fragment and unexplained slight verdict into assist-team play and scope.

decisions.hook: Take a four-person party with Etrian classes into turn-based, randomly generated dungeons, then build forts to stand against roaming bosses. Party skills and positioning add planning to the dungeon crawl, though managing a whole group is a different challenge from steering one adventurer.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the Etrian/Mystery Dungeon combination without assuming knowledge of Shiren.

decisions.alias: Etrian Odyssey IV - Legends of the Titan (USA).3ds
decisions.hook: Draw maps as a custom-built party explores hostile forests, using an airship to seek out the next destination. Class choices make building a team rewarding over a long campaign, and the more forgiving difficulty option offers room to learn without removing the mapping work.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns mapping, classes and forgiving-options shorthand into a usable recommendation.

decisions.alias: Etrian Odyssey V - Beyond the Myth (USA).3ds
decisions.hook: Build a party from different races and classes, map the labyrinth and eventually specialize characters through master promotions. It concentrates on party construction and dungeon exploration rather than an elaborate story, making it a strong choice when those decisions are the main attraction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported hardest/least superlatives while retaining the class-specialization appeal.

decisions.hook: Stock shops and send residents on errands between real-time dungeon expeditions, recruiting allies whose abilities help solve obstacles. The pleasant rhythm comes from bringing resources home and seeing the oasis grow, so expect town upkeep alongside the adventuring.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how Ever Oasis links shop management and dungeon abilities instead of simply calling it light.

decisions.hook: Switch among twelve jobs to fight, gather and craft in a gentle fantasy world. The professions feed into one another, making an ordinary materials trip useful to several projects, though the sugary tone and leisurely errands will not suit a player seeking urgency.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains job interdependence and retains a concrete tonal reservation.

decisions.hook: Choose a Final Fantasy job and take on action-combat missions against familiar monsters and summons. Changing roles gives the equipment hunt some variety, but repetitive assignments make this easier to recommend for the setting and job experiments than for constantly new encounters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the Monster Hunter comparison and why the repetitive missions may be worth skipping.

decisions.hook: Command the Hoshido army in turn-based battles, pairing units for support and developing relationships between missions. Optional grinding makes this a gentler Fates route, but the castle visits and plentiful dialogue still separate it from a tightly paced string of tactical maps.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands route-specific difficulty and pacing rather than leaving pair-up and chatter unexplained.

decisions.hook: Fight through dungeons for stronger equipment in an action RPG built around teaming up with other players. The loot chase supplies the motivation, but solo play lacks much of that social appeal and can feel like a flat succession of fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a five-word dismissal with the action/loot loop and a specific solo-play limitation; makes no current online-availability promise.

decisions.hook: Alternate on-rails aerial shooting with ground combat, then fuse weapons and wager on the next stage's difficulty. That combination makes repeated runs rewarding, but the aiming controls demand adjustment before the combat's variety can really shine.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Connects weapon fusion and difficulty wagers to replay value while retaining the control caveat.

decisions.alias: Legend of Zelda, The - Ocarina of Time 3D (USA) (En,Fr,Es) (Rev 1).cci
decisions.hook: Explore Hyrule, discover dungeon tools and solve puzzles that use them to open new paths, with a cleaner presentation and touch-screen inventory than the original. Master Quest supplies rearranged dungeon challenges for a second pass, making this more than a cosmetic return to the adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces remake/nicer shorthand with the dungeon loop and the specific Master Quest attraction.

decisions.hook: Steer a flying mech while using the stylus to lock onto enemy swarms and tear through giant mechanical targets. It is a brief action spectacle built for concentrated shooting rather than a long campaign, and the touch-aiming setup is central to the experience.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains lock-on shooting and preserves brevity without an unsupported one-hour guarantee.

decisions.hook: Assemble a small fighting robot from interchangeable parts, then test the build in compact real-time arenas. Tuning the machine is the draw, but a long, child-oriented adventure sits between bouts, so it is not simply a quick robot-combat sandbox.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies part-building and story friction without relying on a Custom Robo comparison.

decisions.hook: Learn a monster's attacks, hunt it for materials and turn those rewards into equipment for the next challenge. Vertical terrain, mounting and the insect glaive broaden the combat, but repeated hunts are fundamental to the appeal rather than incidental grinding.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes deepest-portable superlative and explains the hunt/craft loop and repetition.

decisions.hook: Explore changing dungeons in turn-based steps, building connections that let you recruit a huge range of Pokémon. The cheerful cast hides demanding encounters, so careful party choices matter more than assuming every familiar creature makes the journey easy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes hardest/most-systemic claims and explains the recruitment and challenge instead of using PMD shorthand.

decisions.hook: Catch Pokémon, build a team and choose attacks by type advantage in a colorful 3D journey. The relatively gentle campaign makes experimenting with favorites inviting, but it is a weaker pick if demanding battles are your main reason to play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Gen 6/easy/pretty shorthand with the collecting, battle decisions and difficulty caveat.

decisions.hook: Pick one of four classes and explore a compact dungeon one turn at a time. Its straightforward rules suit a quick dose of tactical exploration, though players looking for elaborate character building may find the simplicity limiting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the genre label into a recommendation with a clear simplicity tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Move between branching timelines to change events, while grid-based battles make enemy positioning part of your attack plan. The story is the main reward, but this expanded edition still asks for the measured pace of a substantial, dialogue-heavy role-playing adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why the time branches and grid matter rather than listing JRPG features.

decisions.hook: Grow crops and build relationships in town, then take weapons and magic into real-time dungeon expeditions. The pleasure is balancing a productive rural routine with adventure, provided the anime-style cast and courtship are as welcome as the farming.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the alternating farming/dungeon rhythm and turns very-anime shorthand into a useful caveat.

decisions.hook: Cut through demon crowds in a fantasy version of Japan's Warring States period, collecting equipment between real-time battles. The short-term pull is another useful drop or stronger build; repeated combat is the main offering, not a richly varied adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Diablo-lite shorthand and little-else dismissal with the loot loop and its limitation.

decisions.alias: Shin Megami Tensei - Devil Summoner - Soul Hackers (USA).cci
decisions.hook: Negotiate with demons, earn their loyalty and fuse them into a stronger party while investigating a cyberpunk conspiracy. The atmosphere and unruly allies are the attraction, but the older dungeon-crawling structure can feel rigid compared with later Shin Megami Tensei games.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains negotiation, loyalty and fusion while retaining the dated-crawl reservation.

decisions.hook: Exploit weaknesses to gain extra actions, manage the advantages of the Smirk state and fuse demons into a party that covers its own vulnerabilities. The refined combat is the draw, while the more overtly anime-style cast gives this follow-up a different tone from Shin Megami Tensei IV.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands press-turn jargon into the actual combat decisions and preserves the tonal distinction.

decisions.hook: This Super Mario 64 hack turns coins, card pickups and fast star clears into ways to build a deck for Bowser's Gauntlet. Unlockable decks and a large card pool make route knowledge useful to a new kind of challenge, rather than simply supplying another set of platform courses.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Compresses the author/count feature list into the deck-building and platforming connection.

decisions.hook: Explore Rare's unfinished Dinosaur Planet adventure with the Dinomod Enhanced patch dated 26 January 2025. Fixes remove many bugs and progression blockers, opening substantially more of the game, but this remains a rough prototype rather than a finished retail adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains exact patch and prototype caveats while emphasizing the exploration experience rather than leak provenance.

decisions.alias: Legend of Zelda, The - The Missing Link (v2.1).z64
decisions.hook: A short Ocarina of Time interquel sends Link through unfamiliar dark forests in search of Navi, with a new item shaping the puzzles. Its focused scope makes it an appealing side adventure rather than a replacement for a full Zelda campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces creator/runtime feature listing with the new-item appeal and short-adventure scope.

decisions.alias: Legend of Zelda, The - The Sealed Palace (World) (v1.3) (Pirate).z64
decisions.hook: A full-length Ocarina of Time hack built around new areas and dungeons, with custom music and cutscenes. Dungeon exploration is the attraction, but cryptic puzzles and the lack of a minimap can turn finding the next step into a prolonged search.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes stale latest-version wording and collectible inventory while preserving cryptic-puzzle and minimap caveats.

decisions.hook: Swap adjacent panels to make matches, then arrange falling blocks into chains that dump garbage onto the opponent. The Pokémon theme supplies a friendly wrapper, but reading several moves ahead under pressure is what makes this puzzle game worth returning to.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Panel de Pon shorthand with the matching, chain and versus decisions.

decisions.hook: Smash Remix expands the original Nintendo 64 platform fighter with new characters, stages and single-player challenges while retaining the original twelve fighters' mechanics. The appeal is discovering new matchups within the familiar game, rather than expecting the controls and systems of a later Smash entry.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the long fighter inventory and time-sensitive final-big-version claim; explains what the expansion preserves.

decisions.hook: The unofficial +EXTRA 0.5.0 pack adds community fighters and stages on top of Smash Remix 2.0.1, offering more experimental matchups than the main expansion. This early release has character-select crash issues addressed in 0.6.0, and its oversized cartridge image requires compatible support for games larger than 64 MB.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the four-sentence fighter list while preserving unofficial status, exact version, crash caveat and compatibility requirement.

decisions.hook: Take over robotic animals and use their different abilities to solve open-ended puzzle levels. Working out which body can reach or operate something is the delight, with the strange wildlife giving each change of character a practical purpose.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces weirdest-systemic-toy praise with the ability-switching puzzle appeal.

decisions.hook: Built in Ocarina of Time rather than Star Fox 64, this survival hack puts Fox on one open map against 32 days of escalating monster waves. Random loot and between-day shops make equipment choices central to surviving; version 1.4 adds a new-game-plus mode that carries gear forward.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Reduces four sentences and engine shorthand while preserving identity, wave structure and version-specific carryover.

decisions.hook: Explore compact 3D worlds for Power Stars, using Mario's jumps, dives and climbing to turn scenery into possible routes. The enduring pleasure is experimenting with movement rather than following one fixed corridor, though judging a landing in depth takes practice.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces perfect-to-hold praise with concrete movement and exploration guidance.

decisions.alias: Super Mario 64 - Beyond the Cursed Mirror (v1.3.1).z64
decisions.hook: Explore fifteen new courses and hunt 120 stars in a story-led Super Mario 64 adventure with original characters and new mechanics. The substantial campaign is the attraction rather than a small challenge pack; this version requires the Expansion Pak.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes decomp/latest-build jargon and plot inventory while preserving the hardware requirement.

decisions.hook: Damage familiar Nintendo characters until you can knock them out of the arena, using platforms and items to change the fight. The small roster makes learning matchups approachable, while battles with other players offer more lasting variety than the brief solo ladder.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the title-only original/second-player recommendation with the actual platform-fighting objective.

decisions.hook: Build a team within a four-point strength budget, choosing between more weaker fighters or fewer powerful ones from Capcom and SNK. The ratio system makes team selection part of the contest before the one-on-one bouts begin, rewarding a plan beyond picking every favorite.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the arcade title stub with the distinctive fixed-ratio team-building decision.

decisions.hook: A fast 2D fighter whose Roman Cancel system lets you spend meter to interrupt an attack and extend pressure or a combo. The expressive characters and heavy-metal presentation are immediate attractions, but getting much from the combat means practicing its timing rather than relying on spectacle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the arcade title stub with the defining cancel mechanic and its learning demand.

decisions.hook: Choose not just a fighter but one of three moon styles that alter how that character fights. That extra layer makes experimenting with matchups rewarding, though learning a character's options is a larger commitment than the familiar-looking 2D bouts initially suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands moon-style shorthand into the choice and its learning cost.

decisions.hook: Ride waves and perform aerial tricks or tube rides in Sega's surfing arcade game. The original cabinet uses a physical surfboard controller, so much of its novelty comes from balancing and steering with your body rather than from a conventional sports-game campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the one-word genre stub with tricks, tube riding and the cabinet's defining control distinction.

decisions.hook: Rotate a helicopter around a pivot to aim at enemies approaching from different directions. Choosing where to turn while still dodging fire gives this shooter a distinctive spatial challenge; it asks for more than holding a forward firing lane.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the unsupported most-inventive superlative with the aiming-versus-evasion decision.

decisions.alias: Age of Empires - The Age of Kings (USA).nds
decisions.hook: Build an economy, research technologies and command historical armies in turn-based battles rather than the PC game's real-time warfare. Civilisation strengths and hero units give the scenarios variety, though long enemy turns can slow the momentum.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the incorrect hex-grid claim and explains the economic and tactical adaptation.

decisions.alias: Animal Crossing - Wild World (USA) (Singleplayer Nookingtons v1.1.1).nds
decisions.hook: Fish, collect, decorate and get to know neighbors in a village that follows the real calendar. SporyTike's Singleplayer Nookingtons 1.1.1 patch removes the visiting-player purchase requirement for the final shop upgrade, making the slow daily routine more self-contained without making time pass faster.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands village-simulation shorthand and retains the specific single-player shop-upgrade patch behavior.

decisions.hook: Combine weapons to solve compact shooting challenges where missiles can fill the screen. More than 160 stages and an editor provide plenty to experiment with, but the attraction is figuring out an effective loadout and attack plan rather than simply surviving one continuous campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague Treasure praise with weapon experimentation and puzzle-stage structure.

decisions.alias: Castlevania - Dawn of Sorrow (USA) (DE+ v2.3 Original Art).nds
decisions.hook: Collect enemy souls to expand Soma's attacks and exploration options in a connected castle. Definitive Edition+ 2.3 removes stylus Magic Seals, fixes Luck and makes boss souls obtainable again, alongside combat and Julius-mode adjustments; this Original Art build retains the stock anime portraits.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the underlying soul/exploration appeal and trims cryptic patch inventory while preserving key edition and art caveats.

decisions.hook: Equip attack glyphs and combine them into powerful union attacks while exploring separate areas linked by a world map. Demanding combat makes learning attack reach and finding effective glyph combinations more important than simply pushing onward with higher stats.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the unsupported toughest claim and misleading open-world implication; explains glyph choices.

decisions.hook: Build a fighting robot from interchangeable weapons and movement parts, then test how those choices work together in compact arenas. The combat rewards thoughtful combinations, but the child-oriented tournament story can be a barrier if you only want to tinker and battle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains part synergy and preserves the story-pacing reservation without kiddy shorthand.

decisions.hook: Create a four-person party and explore a hostile first-person dungeon, spending experience to develop skills and stronger classes. The optional wireframe look suits its old-fashioned structure, but the severe challenge makes it a poor choice for a guided or forgiving role-playing journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Wizardry/brutal-honesty shorthand with party development and a practical difficulty warning.

decisions.hook: Raise and develop Digimon for turn-based battles in Dawn's side of the paired adventure. The DWDDRandomizer 0.2.1 quality-of-life treatment targets faster text, movement and battles, lighter encounter pressure and better rewards, with additional progression options; the underlying monster-development grind remains the main commitment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the patch-tool feature inventory into readable gameplay and pacing guidance, without promising every optional setting is enabled.

decisions.hook: Raise Digimon and develop a team for turn-based battles in Dusk's side of the paired adventure. The quality-of-life edition's exact changes are unconfirmed, so do not assume a particular encounter rate or progression shortcut; expect monster development and repeated battles to remain central.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes speculative attribution to a named patcher and unverified speed/EXP promises while preserving the unknown-options caveat.

decisions.alias: Dragon Quest IX - Sentinels of the Starry Skies (USA) (En,Fr,Es).nds
decisions.hook: Build a party around changeable vocations and take on a long, approachable turn-based adventure. Randomized grottoes give the equipment and character-building loop more room to grow, but this is a patient journey rather than a compact story to finish quickly.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains vocations and grottoes instead of relying on classic-Dragon-Quest shorthand.

decisions.hook: Customize insect-shaped war machines and choose weapons, positioning and counterattacks in turn-based grid battles. Cards offer powerful special effects, but the stylus microgames needed to get their full combat benefit can interrupt otherwise satisfying tactical decisions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the implication that every attack resolves as a card minigame; cards are special effects layered onto normal combat.

decisions.hook: Three original fighters clear crowds and capture bases in a smaller-scale Dynasty Warriors offshoot. Up to seven officer cards supply disruptive roulette effects and help defend captured territory, giving the loadout a tactical role; try it for that compact mix rather than the console games' battlefield scale.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses four sentences into three while preserving the original-fighter roster, card limit and limited-scale caveat.

decisions.hook: Assemble wanzers from interchangeable parts and command them through turn-based battlefield missions. This remake includes both sides' campaigns, giving the equipment decisions a political story to serve rather than treating robot building as a separate toy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands wanzer jargon and explains why part assembly and dual campaigns matter.

decisions.hook: Possess nearby objects and rewind the moments before a death, arranging small actions into a rescue. Expressive animation and a tightly written mystery make the linear puzzle sequence compelling, though there is little room to solve the story in a different order.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the rescue-puzzle loop and what linear means for the player.

decisions.hook: Take on brisk top-down crime missions while buying and selling drugs across districts with different prices. The trading economy gives wandering the city a profitable second purpose, but the criminal theme and repeated supply runs are integral rather than incidental.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes most-systemic-GTA superlative and explains the economy's appeal and repetition.

decisions.hook: Fit modules into ship hulls, assign crew to useful roles and command a growing fleet through a long space adventure. Range and attack choices matter in battle, but much of the satisfaction comes from preparation; expect dense systems and substantial reading between confrontations.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces rock-paper-scissors and adult shorthand with fleet preparation, range and pacing.

decisions.hook: Direct fallen knights while steering a stylus-controlled wisp through enemy bullet patterns. The unusual mixture makes tactical planning and dodging happen together, rewarding patient learning but offering a steep barrier if you want familiar, immediately readable strategy rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the bullet-hell/tactics interaction rather than merely calling the systems strange.

decisions.alias: Legend of Zelda, The - Spirit Tracks (Dpad Patched) (QoL).nds
decisions.hook: Solve dungeons alongside a controllable Phantom and travel between them by train. This patched edition adds D-pad movement and actions, faster train travel with optional boosts, and buttons for microphone-blowing actions, but items and route drawing still require touch input.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the underlying cooperative-dungeon appeal and retains the essential patch input limitations without a speed-feature list.

decisions.hook: Spend limited resources and preparation time building defenses, then join the battle yourself when the enemy wave arrives. The satisfaction is seeing a plan survive contact and deciding where your own intervention is most useful, rather than passively watching towers do everything.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre shorthand and unsupported short-campaign claim with the preparation/action decision.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings - Conquest, The (USA).nds
decisions.hook: Choose a class and fight across isometric Middle-earth maps to capture command points that become spawn locations. The good-and-evil campaigns offer recognizable battles, but sluggish performance and the thin sense of battlefield scale make this a weak choice for anyone seeking a convincing mass battle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects vague licensed-tactics labeling to real-time capture-point action and supplies sourced reasons to skip.

decisions.hook: This action-RPG reimagining of Lufia II replaces turn-based combat with real-time fighting and character switching. Puzzle-filled dungeons remain central: different party members' abilities solve obstacles and support platforming, making it a different adventure rather than a version that discards the puzzles.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the false claim that the remake loses puzzle dungeons; character-specific puzzles and platforming are central.

decisions.hook: Follow class-specific stories and collect equipment in an offline, single-player take on MapleStory's side-scrolling combat. The 16 December 2025 English patch uses an LLM draft with community proofreading, so it opens the adventure to English readers but can still sound stiff; expect plenty of loot grinding.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps offline identity, exact translation provenance and language caveat while removing stale final-build wording.

decisions.alias: Mario Kart DS - Custom Tracks Grand Prix Nitro (v1.1.0).nds
decisions.hook: CTGP Nitro 1.1.0 preserves the original Mario Kart DS courses while adding community tracks and battle stages. Custom music and driving aids accompany the new routes, making it a substantial extension for players who already know the original rather than a replacement campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the feature inventory into preserved content, new-course appeal and version-specific scope.

decisions.hook: Recruit Marvel heroes, support them with equipment, and spring Plot Twist cards to overturn a fight in this adaptation of the Vs. System card game. The rules offer substantial deck-building depth, but tiny text and an awkward interface make learning them harder than it should be.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Vs. System decisions while retaining interface criticism.

decisions.hook: Explore a nonlinear wasteland on foot or in tanks whose engines, weapons and armor compete for limited carrying capacity. Bounty hunting and vehicle tinkering are the draw rather than a tightly directed story; this edition includes an English fan translation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces absolute freedom claim with tank-building decisions; preserves translation.

decisions.hook: Roam a post-apocalyptic wasteland on foot or in customizable tanks, choosing bounties and building a party for turn-based fights. The freedom to tinker is the attraction; Metal Dreamers' playable English v1.0 translation still needs the old promotional passwords listed with the patch for keypad chests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies nonlinear play without losing the password caveat.

decisions.hook: Drill through colored blocks while watching both your air supply and the blocks about to collapse above you. Reaching an air capsule safely can matter more than digging quickly, giving these short descents a sharp risk-reward rhythm.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic quick-fun label with drilling risks.

decisions.hook: Each step through the dungeon is a turn, so surviving depends on using pots, scrolls and other supplies before a bad situation becomes fatal. This remake of the Super Famicom Shiren rewards careful improvisation, but its unforgiving runs are a poor choice for a relaxed power fantasy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported purest claim and explains survival appeal.

decisions.hook: Advance one square at a time through a ruined dwarven citadel, trading turns with monsters and searching for useful equipment. The brisk dungeon crawl is easy to get into, but offers less depth than its first-person role-playing presentation might suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains turn-based movement and shallow campaign caveat.

decisions.hook: Swap neighboring tiles to match colors while the stack rises, then arrange falling tiles into further matches. The pleasure is turning a simple clear into a sustained chain, with fast recovery and forward planning constantly competing for attention.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands unexplained Panel de Pon reference.

decisions.hook: Build a team from Unova's new Pokemon and work through turn-based type matchups, gyms and Team Plasma's campaign. The unfamiliar creatures give team-building a fresh start, even though the catch-train-battle structure remains familiar.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why the new roster matters.

decisions.hook: Catch and train a team through Johto, then continue into Kanto, with your lead Pokemon following beside you. The long two-region journey is the attraction if you want to spend time with a team rather than rush to the first championship.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces fan-favourite claim with concrete remake appeal.

decisions.hook: Platinum expands Diamond and Pearl's Sinnoh journey with the Distortion World and a Battle Frontier of postgame challenges. Choose it for a substantial turn-based Pokemon campaign with more to tackle after the main story, not a reinvention of catching and training.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces version-only label with actual additions.

decisions.hook: Train a Pokemon team through Johto and Kanto, with a companion following you through the world. It shares HeartGold's expansive campaign but changes some available Pokemon and the legendary focus, so there is little reason to play both for the story alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes SoulSilver useful without reading HeartGold first.

decisions.hook: This White 2 difficulty hack rebuilds trainer battles and rebalances a large Pokemon roster for Nuzlocke-style runs. Extra encounters and infinite Rare Candies put the emphasis on planning teams and surviving fights rather than grinding levels.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses feature inventory around Nuzlocke preparation.

decisions.hook: Pair warlords with Pokemon and conquer kingdoms through small grid-based battles where positioning and type matchups matter. This Nobunaga's Ambition crossover offers an approachable campaign of recruitment and territorial expansion rather than a conventional gym journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains tactical appeal instead of light-but-real shorthand.

decisions.hook: This HeartGold overhaul restricts you to low-stat Pokemon and delays or removes many evolutions, forcing weaker creatures to carry demanding battles and no-heal gauntlets. Level caps and Rare Candies support deliberate Nuzlocke-style planning, while a post-war Johto story and Kanto wasteland change the setting too.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains trashlocke restriction and keeps difficulty context.

decisions.hook: HeartGold's story stays intact, but Galar Pokemon replace the familiar encounters and trainer teams, with newer moves and abilities changing how you build a party. Reusable TMs and fewer required field moves reduce chores; this is a roster-focused refresh rather than an extreme difficulty challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces jargon-heavy feature list with audience distinction.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Explorers of Darkness (USA).nds
decisions.hook: Become a Pokemon and explore randomly arranged dungeons with a partner, making each step and attack part of a turn-based expedition. The friendship-driven story is the main pull; Explorers of Sky later expands this campaign, so Darkness is not necessary for an additional story.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes misleading blanket easy claim and explains dungeon play.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Explorers of Fortune.nds
decisions.hook: Explorers of Fortune expands Sky's familiar dungeon adventure with many more Pokemon, regional forms, new dungeons and side quests. Optional direct team control and shared experience let you reshape the expedition management without replacing the original story's spirit.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses expanded roster and control choices into recommendation.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Explorers of Sky (USA).nds
decisions.hook: Lead a Pokemon exploration team through turn-based dungeons and a substantial story about your partnership. Sky expands Time and Darkness with extra playable choices and Special Episodes, making it the fuller route into that adventure rather than an entirely new campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what the definitive edition actually offers.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Explorers of Time (USA).nds
decisions.hook: Travel as a Pokemon with a partner, managing moves and supplies through randomly arranged, turn-based dungeons. Time shares its central story with Darkness; choose one for the adventure, or Sky for the expanded version with additional episodes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces edition-only label with independent recommendation.

decisions.alias: Pokemon Mystery Dungeon - Explorers of the Spirit (v1.01).nds
decisions.hook: A full-length fan-made story uses Explorers of Sky's turn-based dungeon engine to revisit familiar characters in a changed situation. Redesigned dungeons remove traps, random monster houses and item loss on failure, but this v1.01 edition does not offer manual control of every teammate.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps failure and control caveats while removing award/list padding.

decisions.hook: Built on Volt White, this story hack replaces major trainers and mixes new Pokemon with conspicuous crossover creatures in a darker Unova adventure. Item-based Omega and Mega evolutions are permanent, and starter choice affects difficulty; choose it for an eccentric remix rather than a faithful expansion.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses grim premise and explains unconventional evolutions.

decisions.hook: Start in Kanto and work toward Johto in a quest-heavy HeartGold overhaul that mixes characters from the anime, manga and Origins. Shared experience supports the expanded journey, but crude mature humor and an AI-assisted English translation make it a less straightforward choice than the official adventures.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains story, mature-content and translation caveats in readable prose.

decisions.hook: Capture Pokemon by drawing loops around them, then borrow their abilities to overcome obstacles during ranger missions. It is a direct stylus-action alternative to turn-based battling, though repeated circling supplies much of the challenge and variety is limited.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces dismissive thin label with the actual stylus loop.

decisions.hook: Draw capture loops around Pokemon, then spend their assistance on obstacles as you work through Almia's ranger missions. Temporary helpers and a persistent partner make choosing what to bring useful, but the repeated stylus-circling still needs to appeal to you.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes sequel independently informative.

decisions.hook: Renegade Platinum preserves Sinnoh's story while making all 493 Pokemon obtainable and rebuilding trainers for much tougher battles. Expanded learnsets, Fairy typing and changes to weaker species widen team-building options, while trade-free evolutions remove a practical obstacle to experimenting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces dense specification list with challenge and team-building payoff.

decisions.hook: Drayano's HeartGold overhaul opens all 493 Pokemon to collection and gives gym leaders full six-member teams for a harder Johto and Kanto campaign. Trade-free evolutions and fewer field-move chores ease team-building; this Complete edition also changes Pokemon stats and types rather than preserving their original balance.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Complete patch and six-member bosses without exhaustive list.

decisions.hook: This SoulSilver counterpart to Sacred Gold offers the same harder Johto and Kanto campaign, with all 493 Pokemon obtainable and full-team gym battles. The Complete patch includes Pokemon balance changes; encounter differences are a reason to choose between the pair, not a reason to expect two new stories.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains shared campaign and preserves Complete edits.

decisions.hook: Rebuild a team from the first three generations in a much harder White campaign, with altered types, stats and learnsets disrupting familiar assumptions. This is the early v1.5 Plus release, not the creator's later expanded revisions, so use version-matched expectations and documentation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves early-version warning while making redesign legible.

decisions.hook: Redux reworks Volt White 2 with all 649 Pokemon, expanded difficulty options and new legendary quests, while Complete adds further species and moveset changes. Dedicated training helpers make rebuilding teams less laborious; the documentation recommends an emulator because its Fairy-type implementation can fail on original hardware.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies Fairy compatibility warning and Complete balance changes.

decisions.alias: SNK vs. Capcom - Card Fighters DS (USA) (Rev 1).nds
decisions.hook: Collect SNK and Capcom characters as cards, combining their abilities to build a stronger battling deck. The pleasure is finding effective combinations rather than performing fighting-game inputs; this Rev 1 release fixes the original North American version's progression-blocking bug.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves Rev 1 fix and explains card combinations.

decisions.hook: Summon objects by typing their names, then improvise ways to solve small physical puzzles instead of following one prescribed solution. This collection includes Scribblenauts and Super Scribblenauts, making experimentation with the object vocabulary the main reason to play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces literal any-noun claim and clarifies compilation.

decisions.hook: Move teams around tactical maps, then use demon abilities and fusion to build stronger battle groups. A seven-day schedule makes choosing whom to visit part of the strategy, so the appeal lies in balancing relationships and preparation rather than only winning isolated fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces anime-wrapper shorthand with meaningful time pressure.

decisions.hook: Explore a hostile Antarctic anomaly in first person, recruiting and fusing demons for turn-based battles. Matching allies' alignments enables cooperative attacks, making party composition matter beyond raw strength; the grim science-fiction campaign is a lengthy commitment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes vague adult endorsement and explains alignment choice.

decisions.hook: Lift and throw enemies with a small mech while taking jobs across a world of floating islands. The expressive characters and setting carry the adventure, but the easy combat makes it a gentler action RPG than the machinery suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains mech throws and preserves easy difficulty caveat.

decisions.alias: Super Robot Taisen OG Saga - Endless Frontier (USA).nds
decisions.hook: Time attacks to keep enemies airborne and extend your party's combos within turn-based battles. The juggling adds execution to RPG planning, but the long campaign and conspicuous anime fan service will not suit everyone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands combo-juggling into a useful combat description.

decisions.hook: Fight across both screens using a deck of ability pins, dividing attention between partners rather than controlling one conventional action hero. Adjustable difficulty and level-based drop-rate tradeoffs make chasing loot a deliberate risk, while the Shibuya style gives that experimentation a strong identity.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains systemic shorthand through risk and divided attention.

decisions.hook: Build decks from more than a thousand cards and duel through an early DS interpretation of Yu-Gi-Oh. The period card pool is the point: choose it to explore older deck combinations, not to reproduce later generations of the trading-card game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces relative small-card-pool dismissal with concrete scope.

decisions.hook: Construct a deck for tournament-style duels or explore Duel World's events to meet opponents and obtain cards. It is a good choice when experimenting with the era's card combinations matters more than following a television-story adaptation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds Duel World context to bare duelling summary.

decisions.hook: Humans and robots share a futuristic baseball field, and money earned through play can strengthen your team during the match. Choose it for an arcade sport that turns player upgrades into part of the contest, not a faithful simulation of professional baseball.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces future-baseball label with upgrades and roster appeal.

decisions.hook: Wear down an opposing wrestler with strikes and power moves, then secure a three-count pin rather than simply emptying a health bar. Head-to-head and tag matches give the oversized wrestling spectacle more variety than the terse fighting-game presentation suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre-only text with pinning and match structure.

decisions.hook: Choose a jet with its own speed and weapon pattern, then dodge through compact vertical shooting stages. Bombs can erase incoming fire as well as hurt enemies, making timely survival decisions more valuable than hoarding them for a perfect run.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains pilot choice and bomb use.

decisions.hook: Propeller planes and an eccentric cast take over the vertical shooting, with route choices and multiple endings giving repeated runs different destinations. Pick it for brisk aircraft combat and replay variety rather than a serious military setting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sequel-name shorthand with routes and aircraft identity.

decisions.hook: Collect armor equipment to change your ship's capabilities as you shoot through vertically scrolling stages. Choosing and managing those loadouts is the reason to try it: the appeal lies in learning the equipment system, not just dodging with one fixed gun.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains armor selection rather than naming a mechanic.

decisions.hook: Switch among four weapons to match the direction and shape of incoming threats, then charge a stronger shot when the opportunity opens. That flexibility is the main interest in an otherwise fairly ordinary horizontal shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes weapon-switching useful while retaining modest appraisal.

decisions.hook: Large fighters and a camera that zooms with their distance make every exchange feel theatrical. The original Art of Fighting is worth sampling for that close-up impact, but its stiff bouts are harder to recommend as an introduction than the later entries.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds a reason to sample the stiff original.

decisions.hook: The sequel opens its larger cast to single-player selection instead of restricting the story to Ryo and Robert. There is more room to find a preferred fighter, but the punishing opposition still makes it a demanding place to learn the series.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains roster improvement and retains difficulty warning.

decisions.hook: Detailed, fluidly animated fighters trade blows in a reworked close-combat system with an emphasis on combinations. The small roster limits character variety, but gives the striking animation and individual matchups room to be the attraction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces visual shorthand with animation-versus-roster tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Return a ball to break the stars behind your opponent, then send one final shot through the exposed goal. Sliding saves and character-specific power shots give this Pong-like duel its bite; it is not simply Windjammers with different characters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects disc-sport misdescription to ball-and-star rules.

decisions.hook: Fast baseball mixes cartoon reactions with power-ups that strengthen pitching and batting. Automatic fielding in the easier mode makes it a welcoming arcade match, while manual fielding leaves more of the defense in your hands.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported best claim; explains assisted fielding.

decisions.hook: Pick a colorful fictional team and play straightforward baseball, with exaggerated comic-style presentation around the familiar pitching and batting. It suits a direct match against another player better than a search for elaborate management systems.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces baseball-only note with actual scope.

decisions.hook: Choose among six ships and decide when to release a concentrated charge shot or split it into wider coverage. Those choices make the spectacular horizontal shooting more flexible than Pulstar's harsher approach, without turning it into an easy ride.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces best claim with charge-shot decisions.

decisions.hook: Stun enemies with a leaf, then pick them up and throw them at other foes while collecting flowers to spend in shops. That mix of enemy handling and shopping gives the colorful platforming more character than a simple run to the exit.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects flower-smashing to leaf stun and enemy throws.

decisions.hook: A compact cast trades familiar projectile, jump-in and close-range attacks in a fast, responsive one-on-one fighter. It is a good detour when you want straightforward Street Fighter-style exchanges rather than a large system of meters and team rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported underrated ranking and explains accessible appeal.

decisions.hook: Fight through Osaka with fists and scavenged weapons, smashing street furniture for supplies before taking on each boss. The Final Fight-style crowd brawling is familiar rather than inventive, so choose it for a straightforward street-clearing session.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces clone-only dismissal with Osaka combat description.

decisions.hook: Aim colored bubbles into matching groups, using wall rebounds to reach awkward gaps. Cutting away a support cluster can drop everything beneath it, making placement more important than simply taking the first available match.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces alternate-title-only note with aiming and collapse decisions.

decisions.hook: Fire matching bubbles into the ceiling and use bank shots to dismantle its hanging clusters. Puzzle boards and competitive play give the same simple aiming rule different pressures, so this is more bubble-placement experimentation rather than a new genre.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces alternate-title-only sequel note with playable appeal.

decisions.hook: Read an enemy's windup through your knight's transparent outline, defend, then answer with a sword strike. Alternate routes and weapon purchases support the journey, but learning the rhythm of each close-range duel is the real attraction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains defense and progression behind the perspective label.

decisions.hook: Block and counter enemies from behind a transparent swordsman, with jumping and dashing adding ways to evade and strike. This is a cartridge conversion of the Neo Geo CD sequel, not a separate arcade-designed adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves cartridge-conversion caveat and supplies actual gameplay.

decisions.hook: Billy, Jimmy and a wider cast face off in one-on-one bouts rather than clearing streets together. Double jumps, counters and combos make it a surprisingly busy fighting game, so approach it for matchups rather than the usual Double Dragon brawling.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies fighting-game identity and its movement options.

decisions.hook: Punch through robot enemies in side-scrolling stages, including chases where the scenery races past as you fight. The superhero speed is the spectacle, but the uncomplicated attacks offer limited depth once that novelty fades.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes running-brawler shorthand legible and retains shallowness.

decisions.hook: Tengai Makyou characters exchange exaggerated attacks in a colorful one-on-one fighter, while items arriving mid-match can disrupt the duel. The pickups supply some welcome unpredictability even if you have no attachment to the role-playing series.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains mid-match pickups and crossover accessibility.

decisions.hook: Take one of the original Fatal Fury heroes through a tournament of one-on-one fights. The cast and presentation introduce South Town's appeal, but stiff early-series combat makes this more compelling as an origin story than a first choice for versus play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces historical label with audience-relevant caveat.

decisions.hook: Move between three fighting planes to evade an attack or change the angle of your approach, then work attacks into combinations. That extra layer gives Fatal Fury 3 a distinctive spatial game, though learning the plane shifts is part of the price.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes three-plane shorthand understandable.

decisions.hook: A broad cast fights across foreground and background planes, letting movement change the terms of an exchange. Choose this expanded Fatal Fury 2 for traditional one-on-one battles with an extra positional wrinkle, not for modern tag-team systems.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces legacy ranking with the actual two-plane appeal.

decisions.hook: Swordplay shares the stage with a grappling hook that lets you swing through hazards and find new approaches. The appeal is that blend of ninja movement and close combat rather than a complex character-building adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds concrete grappling traversal to generic ninja-platformer note.

decisions.hook: Block at the last moment with Just Defend to turn precise defense into an advantage, then use the T.O.P. system to choose where in your health bar a power boost activates. Garou rewards careful timing and planning without needing a huge roster to sustain interesting fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Just Defend instead of relying on acronym and superlative.

decisions.hook: Pilot a seaplane through vertical waves of aircraft and ground threats, saving bombs for moments when ordinary fire cannot clear a safe route. Branching routes offer some replay variety, but the central appeal is straightforward military shooting rather than a complicated weapon system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects helicopter to seaplane.

decisions.hook: Pick a national team and work through a quick arcade football tournament, charging the shot button for a powerful attempt on goal. Finding enough space to charge gives the attack a clear decision beyond merely running toward the net.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces football-only label with charged-shot decision.

decisions.hook: Repeated hits to a character's vulnerable piece of clothing can stun them and open a damaging follow-up. That targeting game gives this otherwise familiar Street Fighter-style fighter a specific reason to learn its matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies weak points cause stun rather than generic armor destruction.

decisions.hook: Choose a fixed three-fighter team and win successive one-on-one bouts, managing a different set of moves as each teammate steps in. The crossover cast is the attraction, but you cannot freely assemble favorites as in later King of Fighters games.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands fixed-team shorthand into selection tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Build a three-person team from the roster instead of accepting the original game's fixed groups. Mixing familiar Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting characters with KOF's newcomers gives you a useful reason to experiment across several fighting styles.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why team editing matters.
