decisions.hook: Running and more mobile close-range exchanges push this team fighter toward an aggressive rhythm. It is an interesting turning point if you enjoy learning how to close space and sustain pressure rather than relying only on distant projectile exchanges.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains movement changes rather than using modern-KOF jargon.

decisions.hook: Select Advanced or Extra mode to change the team's movement and power-management rules before fighting through three-person matches. The choice supports different habits, while the Orochi saga finale gives the arcade campaign more narrative payoff than a plotless dream match.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains selectable systems and story significance.

decisions.hook: Returning fighters from earlier entries form a large roster without a new story restricting who can meet. Choose it for building three-person teams and learning traditional KOF matchups, rather than chasing a new plot or tag-switching system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes universal-consensus claim and explains dream match.

decisions.hook: Pick three active fighters and a fourth teammate who can jump in as a support attack. Timing those striker calls adds a new layer to the familiar team battles, making this more interesting as a systems change than a simple roster update.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains striker role rather than four-person shorthand.

decisions.hook: Striker assists can turn a small opening into a long, chaotic attack sequence in this four-member team fighter. It is appealing when you enjoy experimenting with support combinations, less so when you want the cleaner exchanges of the three-on-three entries.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces broken-but-fun shorthand with assist consequence.

decisions.hook: Allocate your four-person team between active fighters and striker support, changing how much of the match rests on your chosen lead combatants. That flexibility is the reason to explore this entry, though its rough presentation is less inviting than the stronger-looking earlier games.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces rough label with flexible team allocation.

decisions.hook: Three-person teams return without striker assists, while MAX-mode combinations reward careful attack sequencing. The large dream-match cast makes it a strong choice for sustained matchup practice rather than following a story campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes competitive-favourite assertion and explains MAX appeal.

decisions.hook: Switch between teammates during a round instead of waiting for a fighter to lose, keeping reserve characters relevant to the current exchange. The resulting tag rhythm is a substantial change from traditional KOF, not merely another annual cast update.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains tag switching and its strategic difference.

decisions.hook: Giant monsters grapple in cities that break apart beneath them, with scenery becoming part of the spectacle. Choose it for destructive wrestling theatrics rather than a precise martial-arts duel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains monster wrestling and environmental destruction.

decisions.hook: Smash through stages as a giant monster, destroying buildings for power-ups before wrestling a boss creature. It turns the first game's city-sized fights into a more directed brawling journey, with destruction doing as much of the entertaining as the combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains sequel progression beyond kaiju label.

decisions.hook: Move your gun pod around the ship, lock it in place for cover, or launch it into a threatening target. That flexible shield-and-weapon role makes this horizontal shooter a satisfying positioning problem, but the demanding stages punish careless routes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains pod positioning and preserves difficulty warning.

decisions.hook: Choose a bowler and ball weight, then refine the direction and delivery of each shot. It is a compact arcade bowling game for repeating and improving a line, rather than managing a team or sporting season.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre-only note with concrete bowling adjustments.

decisions.hook: Pull matching balloons down into your hands, then throw them back to make vertical groups and trigger further clears. Working quickly while planning the next chain gives this puzzle game a more physical rhythm than placing falling blocks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains pull-and-throw rather than using genre shorthand.

decisions.hook: Grab and throw colored marbles to build chains while the ceiling presses down on your playfield. Character-specific attacks give versus matches a combative edge, making fast improvisation as important as spotting the next match.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes best claim and explains competitive chains.

decisions.hook: Collect power-ups to transform a wizard into forms with different attacks and movement options. The changing abilities and fantastical scenery are worth seeing, but the harsh stages demand more memorization and precision than the magical variety might suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains transformation benefit and keeps harshness caveat.

decisions.hook: Blocked attacks and taking hits build a Stress Gauge that can fuel powerful attacks, turning a bad exchange into a possible comeback. The eccentric Power Instinct cast makes this a comic alternative to solemn tournament fighters, not a game to choose for restraint.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Supplies stress-system hook instead of goofy label.

decisions.hook: Run, jump and fire through dense enemy lines, collecting weapons and climbing into armored vehicles when the opportunity appears. Expressive animation turns even brief firefights into little comic scenes, but survival still depends on reading threats rather than admiring them.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces perfect-pixel-art superlative with gameplay purpose.

decisions.hook: Branching routes, strange transformations and unusual vehicles keep changing the run-and-gun journey. The variety is generous, but the enormous final stage turns the finish into an endurance test rather than a quick victory lap.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves branching and endurance caveat in full sentences.

decisions.hook: Familiar Metal Slug shooting gains a timed medal system that rewards rapid destruction without dying. It offers another run through the formula, but conspicuously reused material makes it a weaker pick when you want the series at its most inventive.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains score-system distinction while retaining recycling criticism.

decisions.hook: A sliding move lets you duck through danger while firing as the series shifts toward darker enemies and scenery. That new movement option is worth trying, but the uneven campaign makes it a less convincing starting point than the earlier Slugs.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains slide utility and retains uneven assessment.

decisions.hook: Metal Slug X revisits Metal Slug 2's run-and-gun stages with changed enemy placements, weapons and pacing. Choose it for a reworked version of that campaign, not a completely new adventure after finishing the original.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies reworking rather than claiming a fully fixed game.

decisions.hook: Punch through mutated street enemies and charge special attacks to break up dangerous crowds. The grotesque enemies give the ordinary side-scrolling brawling some character, but the combat is more straightforward than the transformations suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains charged specials instead of average-only judgment.

decisions.hook: Aim a cursor into the battlefield while moving your soldier across the foreground to avoid incoming fire. Running and evasive rolls mean you must manage the gun sight and your own body separately, giving the gallery shooting its tension.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces reference-only description with aiming-versus-evasion decisions.

decisions.hook: Clear blocks and enemies with delayed bombs, opening routes without trapping yourself in the blast. Rideable creatures add a little protection, but the arcade adventure still rewards careful escape planning more than dropping explosives everywhere.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains bombs, routes and mount protection.

decisions.hook: Slide a rally car around compact isometric courses and reach the finish before time expires. Learning when to start a drift is the main satisfaction; this is a quick route-mastery game rather than a car-setup simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands rally label into timed drifting appeal.

decisions.hook: Dig through the playfield, drop apples onto pursuers and decide whether to clear the collectibles or eliminate every enemy. The latter route opens bonus stages, giving this Mr. Do! remake a reason to vary how you solve a screen.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces remake label with alternative clearing goals.

decisions.hook: Choose a club and line, then time the swing to send the ball around hazards toward the cup. The quick arcade presentation makes each shot inviting, while course judgment gives you more to improve than the timing alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague sports endorsement with shot-planning appeal.

decisions.hook: Keep throwing flames until a monster becomes a giant fireball, then launch it through the others to clear a screen. Positioning a chain reaction is the satisfying part of this compact, spooky platform game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the Snow Bros comparison through actual fire mechanics.

decisions.hook: Throw shuriken through a ninja invasion, using health-consuming special attacks when the screen becomes dangerous. Ranged weapons give the brawling a different rhythm, but clunky combat makes it a harder sell than the premise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains ranged combat and costly specials while keeping criticism.

decisions.hook: Choose a ninja with distinct attacks and special techniques, then shoot through enemies across different historical eras. The changing settings and oversized historical monsters provide the appeal, rather than a serious treatment of the time-travel story.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds character attacks and era variation to vague fun claim.

decisions.hook: Pick a vehicle and steer through a rapid sequence of corners viewed from an isometric angle. The appeal is learning the road and finding a vehicle that suits your reactions, not treating the course as a conventional track simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces isometric-racer label with vehicle and corner learning.

decisions.hook: Match falling colored pieces to generate bombs, then ignite them with a lit bomb to clear a larger area. Setting up that second-stage explosion gives this Bomberman spin-off a different planning rhythm from ordinary falling-block puzzles.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains bomb chains instead of naming the genre.

decisions.hook: Pilot a helicopter through dinosaur-infested city and wilderness stages, shooting threats while rescuing stranded civilians. The rescue scoring gives you a reason to move toward danger instead of simply finding the safest firing lane.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains civilian rescue as meaningful risk.

decisions.hook: Charge shots and position your supporting pod to work through tightly arranged horizontal shooting stages. The pre-rendered spectacle is striking, but harsh recovery and memorization-heavy routes make this a commitment to practice rather than a casual sightseeing run.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps demanding memorization caveat in useful prose.

decisions.hook: Pair two fighters and use tag-team combinations to turn an opening into a coordinated attack. Its dragon-themed martial artists echo Double Dragon, but the appeal here is learning partner synergy rather than clearing streets together.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains tag play and removes reliance on Double Dragon recognition.

decisions.hook: Chain attacks together while pushing an opponent toward an arena edge where a ring-out can decide the round. Position is therefore more than a question of move range, giving the fast Fatal Fury bouts an extra source of danger.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains ring-out consequence and chain-combo appeal.

decisions.hook: Fast chain combinations meet a two-plane arena, letting evasive movement change the angle of a close-range exchange. It is a strong choice for learning Fatal Fury's spatial fighting without reducing every round to a contest of raw damage.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes absolute best claim and explains two-plane rhythm.

decisions.hook: A broad returning cast trades fast chain attacks in Fatal Fury's multi-plane arenas. Choose it for trying different characters and learning the rhythm of plane shifts, rather than expecting a new story to carry the tournament.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces dream-match-only note with concrete fighting appeal.

decisions.hook: Smash enemy robots with metal fists and scavenged limbs, with transformations briefly changing how you plow through the opposition. The mechanical mayhem is the attraction; underneath it remains a direct side-scrolling brawler.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains robot weapons and transformations.

decisions.hook: SNK and Capcom characters meet in one-on-one fights rather than the team spectacle of the rival crossover series. Seeing familiar fighters interpreted by SNK is the draw, but the awkward, slower exchanges make the novelty easier to recommend than the combat itself.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns odd-and-slow dismissal into an intelligible recommendation.

decisions.hook: Long-reaching weapon attacks make spacing and patience more important than rushing into a flurry of punches. Choose the first Samurai Shodown for deliberate, threatening duels where committing to one swing can matter as much as a combination.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces original-weapons-fighter label with tactical identity.

decisions.hook: Choose Slash or Bust to change a fighter's move set before entering a dark, high-damage weapon duel. The alternative styles reward experimentation, but a small mistake can erase a large part of your health.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Slash/Bust choice and retains severe damage caveat.

decisions.hook: Heavy weapon strikes, defensive parries and weapon-breaking attacks make each exchange a substantial gamble. It is a strong choice when you want patient spacing and punishment to matter more than maintaining a long combo.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes series-peak claim and explains high-stakes defense.

decisions.hook: More elaborate combinations shift the weapon duels toward sustained offense without removing the danger of a heavy slash. Its unusual voluntary-defeat mechanic adds another rule to learn, making this a more system-heavy choice than the earlier entries.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains combo emphasis while contextualizing suicide mechanic.

decisions.hook: A large cast fights weapon duels where spacing and a well-timed heavy strike can decide the round quickly. The deliberate pace rewards patience, but brutal finishing moves make this an explicitly violent choice even within Samurai Shodown.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces hardest-hitting superlative with meaningful combat warning.

decisions.hook: Fight from ruined streets into a supernatural realm, calling on rescued spirits to transform and gain different attacks. The shifting forms and scenery are imaginative, but clunky brawling makes the journey less satisfying than its premise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains spirit transformations and retains clunky caveat.

decisions.hook: Fight through different eras as a samurai warrior, meeting supernatural enemies instead of one continuous street gang. The time-travel spectacle is the reason to sample this side-scrolling brawler, rather than expecting the later Sengoku 3's combo emphasis.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands time-travel-brawler label into a recommendation.

decisions.hook: Separate attacks and directional special moves let you build longer combinations than the usual crowd-clearing brawler. Character choice and throwable weapons support that experimentation, making this the Sengoku to choose for learning a fighting system rather than changing forms.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces best-on-system assertion with combat explanation.

decisions.hook: Shoot through branching overhead routes as a lone fighter or a switchable three-person squad. Rotating injured teammates and choosing their attacks makes the team mode more than a cosmetic character selection.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces peak-Saurus praise with team-management decisions.

decisions.hook: Choose one of four soldiers and use shot locking, evasive movement and vehicles to clear overhead battlefields. Route choices keep repeat runs varied, while pre-rendered characters give this a visibly different feel from the first Shock Troopers.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains actual sequel changes rather than still-good shorthand.

decisions.hook: Cybernetic footballers fire arm weapons and powerful shots across an enclosed pitch where wall rebounds stay in play. With no fouls to restrain the violence, this is about creating space by force rather than recreating the real sport.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces football-only text with cybernetic combat rules.

decisions.hook: Attack cartoon enemies with a yo-yo while jumping through bright side-scrolling stages. The playful weapon and exaggerated animation make this a lighter alternative to military run-and-gun games, not a complex adventure to settle into for days.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds yo-yo identity to generic run-and-gun label.

decisions.hook: Three-on-three basketball teams trade quick possessions, with different strengths in dunking, three-point shooting, speed and defense. Pick a team that suits your preferred way to score; the compact matches favor immediate court play over management.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces streetball-only label with team-selection decisions.

decisions.hook: Wear down the opposing dodgeball team with throws, catches and fighting-game-style special shots. Eliminated players move outside the opposing court and can still assist, keeping positioning and possession important after a teammate loses all their health.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Kunio-only shorthand with fighting-style throws.

decisions.hook: Guide a rod through narrow courses without touching the walls or moving obstacles. The original trackball design makes this a test of controlled, nervous precision, so its appeal depends heavily on how naturally the movement feels.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains trackball maze risk instead of novelty label.

decisions.hook: Choose stronger individual blows or faster combinations, then use deflections to turn an opponent's committed swing against them. The beautifully drawn weapon duels reward understanding timing and distance rather than simply picking the longest sword.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Power/Speed choice and defensive deflection.

decisions.hook: Power and Speed styles shape whether your swordsman relies on heavy blows or linked attacks, with a hidden EX style adding another option. Deflections keep defense active, making the elegant duels worth learning beyond their attractive animation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains style choice instead of refined-sequel shorthand.

decisions.hook: Punch through a skyscraper in first person, conserving scarce bullets and a knife that wears down with use. Hostages and equipment give the search some structure, but the repeated close-up fighting is a more unusual premise than a varied action campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces novelty-only dismissal with resource-management hook.

decisions.hook: Race from above through rally stages under a strict time limit, balancing acceleration against the next bend or obstacle. Progress depends on reaching the next section efficiently, not merely overtaking the cars visible on screen.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces rally-only text with checkpoint pressure.

decisions.hook: Move between foreground and background paths while grabbing and throwing enemies through a cartoon bounty-hunting adventure. The shifting planes give the brawling and platforming a useful spatial puzzle instead of one flat corridor to clear.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains two-plane movement and grabbing utility.

decisions.hook: Lead a national side through an arcade football tournament while possession builds a meter for a powerful shot. Keeping the ball therefore prepares a scoring opportunity as well as denying the opposition a turn to attack.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces football-only label with possession-powered shots.

decisions.hook: Guide a ship through diagonally scrolling scenery, using charge shots and bombs to break through dense threats. The distinctive isometric view is beautiful but makes reading safe space demanding; expect a punishing shooter rather than a relaxed visual tour.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes local ZIP reference and explains diagonal navigation.

decisions.hook: A small cast of anime parodies fights with oversized special moves and conspicuous windups for its biggest attacks. The humor gives it personality, while choosing when to risk those theatrical moves supplies a more practical reason to learn the matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains eccentric cast and commitment to big attacks.

decisions.hook: Throw a flying disc past an opponent using angles, speed and lobs while covering your own goal. The simple court supports a lively game of feints against another person; solo opponents offer practice without the same human guessing game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces perfect-versus claim with a clear duel description.

decisions.hook: Choose a ship and configure its weapon coverage before flying through horizontal shooting stages. Experimenting with that loadout is the main reason to try this otherwise fairly generic shooter, with a pounding dance soundtrack giving it extra personality.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains modest assessment while explaining configurable weaponry.

decisions.hook: Clear enemies from compact single-screen stages as the bright little Zupapa or Zupipi. Simple controls and two-player cooperation make it an inviting room-by-room arcade diversion rather than a long exploratory platform adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces genre-only note with contained co-op appeal.

decisions.hook: Humans and robots share a futuristic baseball field, and earnings from play can strengthen your team during the match. Choose it for the way upgrades reshape an arcade sporting contest, not a faithful professional-baseball simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces future-baseball shorthand with in-match upgrades.

decisions.alias: ASO II - The Last Guardian ~ Alpha Mission II (Japan) (En,Ja).chd
decisions.hook: Collect armor equipment to alter your ship's capabilities while fighting through vertically scrolling stages. Learning which loadout fits the next threat is the attraction, giving the shooting more equipment management than a fixed-weapon game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes armor equipment an understandable reason to play.

decisions.alias: Art of Fighting - Ryuuko no Ken Gaiden ~ The Path of the Warrior - Art of Fighting 3 (World) (En,Ja,Es,Pt).chd
decisions.hook: Detailed fighters trade blows in a reworked combination-based combat system, with unusually fluid animation drawing attention to each exchange. The small roster limits character variety, so choose it for learning a handful of distinctive matchups rather than a vast cast.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains animation and roster tradeoff instead of shorthand.

decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes absolute visual ranking while preserving CD load caveat.

decisions.hook: Fast baseball mixes cartoon reactions with power-ups that strengthen pitching and batting. Easier play handles fielding automatically, while manual defense leaves more responsibility with you; the appeal is an accessible arcade match rather than season management.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sports dismissal with fielding and power-up decisions.

decisions.hook: Read incoming attacks through a transparent knight, block them, then answer with your sword. Weapon purchases and branching routes add progression, but the appeal rests on mastering close-range duels rather than freely exploring a large role-playing world.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains block-counter rhythm and route progression.

decisions.hook: Jumping and dashing expand the first game's block-and-counter sword fights, letting you evade or launch a different strike from behind a transparent character outline. This Neo Geo CD sequel includes an English option, making its unusual duels easier to approach without Japanese.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects vague more-RPG-structure claim to documented movement changes.

decisions.alias: Dunk Dream ~ Street Slam ~ Street Hoop (World).chd
decisions.hook: Three-on-three teams race through short basketball matches, with ratings that favor dunks, long shots, speed or defense. Choosing a team shapes how you should attack, making this a direct court rivalry rather than a management simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sports-only dismissal with team differences.

decisions.hook: Reposition a supporting pod, lock it in place for protection, or launch it at a dangerous target while flying through ruined cityscapes. Its shield-and-weapon role gives the horizontal shooting depth, but the hard stages demand deliberate routes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains orbiting pod decisions and preserves hard difficulty.

decisions.hook: Draw or sheathe your weapon to change a fighter's move set during a bout. That choice gives the ninja duels two related toolkits to explore, making it worth trying for combat variety rather than merely another feudal-Japan backdrop.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains weapon switching instead of underrated label.

decisions.alias: Samurai Spirits - Zankurou Musouken ~ Samurai Shodown III (World) (En,Ja,Es,Pt).chd
decisions.hook: Select Slash or Bust to change your fighter's attacks before entering a dark, high-damage weapon duel. The alternate styles invite experimentation, but a small defensive error can cost a large share of your health.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Slash/Bust and high-damage tradeoff.

decisions.alias: Shin Samurai Spirits - Haoumaru Jigokuhen ~ Samurai Shodown II (World) (En,Ja).chd
decisions.hook: Heavy weapon strikes, parries and weapon-breaking attacks make each exchange a substantial risk. Choose it for patient spacing and punishing a badly timed swing, not for maintaining a constant stream of long combinations.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes series-peak ranking while explaining defensive stakes.

decisions.hook: The Samurai Shodown cast moves into a role-playing adventure built around stories from the first two fighting games. This unpatched Japanese edition is text-heavy and slow-paced, so it is a poor substitute if what you want is immediate sword dueling.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains role-playing adaptation and retains language/pacing caveat.

decisions.hook: Search a skyscraper from a first-person view, punching terrorists while conserving bullets and a knife that wears with use. Hostages provide supplies and repairs, giving the repetitive close-up combat a small resource-management layer.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains weapon wear and hostage support instead of novelty-only label.

decisions.hook: A Contra remix built on Revenge of the Red Falcon, aimed at players already comfortable with the original’s jump-and-shoot rhythm. Easy, shortened and full-length variants exist, so the challenge depends on the patch version rather than the name alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes filename-dependent wording while preserving the hack's revision caveat.

decisions.alias: Dai-2-ji Super Robot Taisen (Japan) - Castellano v1.0.zip
decisions.hook: Move a crossover robot squad through turn-based battles, using different weapon ranges and pilot abilities to cover one another. This Spanish-translated edition is a pick for mecha tactics rather than direct cockpit action.

decisions.hook: A profitable cargo run is also a bet on surviving the trip and docking safely. Trade cautiously, smuggle or turn pirate, then spend the proceeds on better ship equipment; the freedom comes with a cockpit worth learning.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies that trade profits improve the existing ship rather than imply buying replacement ships.

decisions.hook: Fight through side-view platform stages with a combat-trained crow that can make short work of bosses. The partnership is distinctive, but long stages and punishing restarts demand more patience than the straightforward jumping and fighting might suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a vague partnership pitch with crow-assisted bosses and demanding restart friction.

decisions.hook: Fight through monster generators while health drains even when you avoid being hit. Collected treasure can raise your maximum health, while food restores it, making efficient routes more useful than clearing every corner for its own sake.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies that the manual's maximum power means health capacity, not stronger attacks.

decisions.hook: The Monkey King and his travelling companions jump and fight through a Chinese-made platform adventure in pursuit of an impostor Monkey King. This English translation offers an unusual Journey to the West adaptation to explore, rather than a text-heavy retelling of the novel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague adaptation claims with the impostor hunt and identifies the English translation.

decisions.hook: Basketball becomes a vehicle for Globetrotter trickery rather than a sober league simulation, with support for up to four players. Choose it for a shared exhibition of court antics rather than a season-long management commitment.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces a vague friends recommendation with the supported four-player basketball option.

decisions.hook: Search elemental landscapes for the shattered Ironsword while seeking help from animal kings. Despite Kuros's heavy armor, finding routes and required objects matters more than simply overpowering everything in your way.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace the misleading fighting-game comparison with concrete exploration priorities.

decisions.alias: Jay and Silent Bob Mall Brawl.zip

decisions.hook: Jump through robot-filled stages while choosing which weapon deserves your limited ammunition. The appeal is learning enemy positions and conserving the right shots for difficult encounters, rather than the thin revenge story.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace abstract mechanical-resistance wording with clear weapon and ammunition decisions.

decisions.hook: Leap far above the treetops, cling to trunks and cut down incoming attacks. Kage's extravagant movement feels freeing until one hit costs a life; landing safely matters as much as taking the shot.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct one-hit loss of a life being described as the end of the entire run.

decisions.reason: Editorial review: Give the eight-bit adaptation an explicit play description rather than only a port comparison.

decisions.hook: Arcade-inspired graphics dress up Arthur's fragile armor, weapon choices and unforgiving platform combat. The visual makeover is the reason to try this Makaimura variant; it should not be confused with a promise of the separate Fair Play revision's easier rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove filename and audit language; preserve the distinction between a graphics makeover and easier rules.

decisions.hook: Origin rebuilds Metroid's routes, puzzles and secrets, so familiar equipment leads into an unfamiliar exploration challenge. decisions.reason: Editorial review: Resolve the unverified enhancement placeholder using documented Origin and Enhanced changes.

decisions.hook: Search enemy bases for captives while managing armed encounters along the way. The rescue work gives this side-scroller a purpose beyond rushing to the exit; this is a Chinese-language translation, not an English edition.

decisions.hook: A tiny platform-fighter distills the contest to movement, spacing and knocking a rival out of the arena. Its online cartridge edition uses special networking hardware, so do not assume every version includes online play.

decisions.hook: Eight plays keep each snap readable, while substitutions and season statistics give the arcade football some longer-term texture. Choose it for a season you can follow without giving up the quick play-calling and direct action of Tecmo Bowl.

decisions.hook: Claw attacks consume Wolverine's energy, making his signature weapon something to ration rather than use on every enemy. Contact with enemies can drain health continuously instead of granting the usual brief immunity, so careless close-range fighting is especially punishing.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace vague superhero praise with claw energy cost and dangerous sustained contact.

decisions.reason: Editorial review: Avoids implying earlier turtles differed only by colour; retains health-cost warning.

decisions.hook: Earn coins at festival mini-games, then decide whether to spend them on more attractions or on collecting Bikkuriman stickers. Unlocking attractions gives the short challenges a longer goal, but the Japanese menus make this less inviting without reading knowledge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces misleading adventure shorthand with festival economy and sticker collection.

decisions.hook: Dungeon expeditions supply materials for building new robot weapons, and arena battles test whether those upgrades work together. Choose it for the repeated gather-build-fight loop rather than a story-led journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how dungeon materials feed robot construction and arena progress.

decisions.hook: Grow and evolve living weapons while exploring an overhead world of monsters and gothic ruins. Experimenting with the arsenal is the main attraction; the brief story and limited conversations make this a better equipment project than a rich role-playing journey.

decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces version-only pointer with combat and pacing guidance.

decisions.hook: Cotton's broomstick shooting builds experience toward stronger attacks, while charged shots and fairy support widen your options. The colourful witch-and-monster scenery is inviting, but developing and using that firepower is the stronger reason to keep flying.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains shooter progression rather than calling the port good.

decisions.hook: Queue a sequence of commands for your mech, then watch allies and enemies carry out their turns together. Predicting where everyone will end up makes movement as important as firepower; impatient orders can leave a powerful machine attacking empty ground.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces rare/brilliant praise and unexplained comparison with simultaneous planning.

decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies indirect pet interaction and mini-game rewards.

decisions.hook: Rotate the board to guide a green ball to the red goal, arranging groups of three coloured tiles to remove obstacles. Permanent grey blocks make the route matter: clearing a colour is only useful if the ball can still reach its destination.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces homebrew label with board rotation and colour-clearing rules.

decisions.hook: This Japanese visual novel belongs to the Infinity series, with reading and story choices taking the place of action or exploration challenges. Choose it for the narrative connection; without Japanese reading skills, its central attraction is largely inaccessible.

decisions.hook: Travel around Japan photographing yokai, then use those pictures in card battles. Collecting is part of building a fighting toolkit rather than a separate album task, although the Japanese RPG text makes this a demanding import for non-readers.

decisions.hook: Win football matches to earn points for equipment that improves your team. That shopping loop gives the monochrome matches a longer-term goal, so choose it for gradually building a stronger side rather than only playing disconnected fixtures.

decisions.hook: Clear the maze while keeping an escape route around the four ghosts, saving power pellets for moments when the chase can turn in your favour. The fixed layout rewards learning routes, but chasing a bonus ghost too far can undo a safe plan.

decisions.hook: Sonic 2's visual themes return in newly arranged stages built around momentum, branching paths and ring collecting. It is a fresh pocket adventure rather than a straight port, with hidden puzzle pieces giving you a reason to slow down and search.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects port implication and replaces unsupported excellence claim.

decisions.hook: Match flower cards to form scoring sets in Koi-Koi, deciding whether to bank a win or keep playing for more. Tournament and certification modes give that risk-taking a longer goal, but learning the card sets is essential if you are new to hanafuda.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Names Koi-Koi play and explains scoring risk.

decisions.hook: Win mahjong hands to unlock strip scenes, with dialogue choices steering the story toward a particular woman. The adult artwork is the distinguishing reward rather than a substitute for knowing mahjong, and the Japanese text matters for following a chosen route.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds mahjong and dialogue structure while retaining adult-content caveat.

decisions.hook: Manage a team and play out its matches through pitching, batting and fielding, with individual statistics shaping the players. The cartoon presentation keeps the baseball approachable, but choosing and using the lineup gives it more substance than a reflex-only batting game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds team-stat and active baseball context to genre label.

decisions.hook: Pitch, bat and field with a cartoon team whose players have their own statistics. The colour presentation is cheerful, while the useful decisions come from matching that lineup to the job rather than treating every player as interchangeable.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains colour baseball edition without treating colour as its whole appeal.

decisions.hook: Work toward a wrestler's finishing-move conditions rather than simply throwing out the strongest attack. Coffin and reward matches change what winning requires, giving the small roster more variety than a succession of ordinary pins.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces surprisingly good with finishing conditions and alternate match goals.

decisions.hook: Fire bubbles into groups of three matching colours, using wall rebounds to reach awkward gaps. Removing a cluster that supports others can clear much more than one shot, so planning the angle is more rewarding than firing at the nearest match.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces alternate-title shorthand with aiming and collapse strategy.

decisions.hook: Guide a snowboarder through an isometric obstacle course rather than the series' usual chase-camera slopes. Free Ride is about reaching the goal, while Survival makes collisions eat into the health needed to keep going; reading the course matters more than scenery.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains isometric obstacle course and survival pressure.

decisions.hook: Build a band through rhythm challenges whose controls change with the instrument, rather than repeating one universal note pattern. The variety is the attraction, but the Japanese adventure-style story makes this less immediate than a simple song-selection rhythm game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains instrument-specific rhythm and reading-heavy story.

decisions.hook: Flip a two-sided triangle across the board so that the right face reaches each target, planning around obstacles and hazardous tiles. Orientation makes a short route surprisingly tricky, and the English menus mean the Japanese release is more approachable than its title suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects generic tile-sliding and Japanese-barrier framing.

decisions.alias: densha de go 2 on neo geo pocket (japan).zip
decisions.hook: Balance speed against the timetable, obey signals and brake to stop at the correct place on each platform. This train-driving game turns punctual, accurate operation into the challenge; treating it like a race is a good way to lose your allowance for mistakes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains schedule and stopping precision without copying console-specific route claims.

decisions.hook: Short and long button presses select lighter or heavier attacks in compact Real Bout-style duels. The Fatal Fury lane-switching system is absent, and the sparse modes make this better for a quick fight than a long unlock hunt.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects false two-plane dodge claim and notes sparse modes.

decisions.alias: kikou seiki unitron - sono tsuide. hikari umareru chi yori. (japan).zip
decisions.hook: Upgrade a Unitron robot with weapons and accessories, then test the build in top-down dungeons and menu-driven battles. It continues Biomotor Unitron's equipment-focused appeal, but Japanese text makes understanding the upgrades more demanding than simply recognising a stronger-looking machine.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains sequel robot loop without unsupported more-parts claim.

decisions.hook: Build a three-fighter team for compact KOF battles, then try Making mode to customise an individual fighter. That extra project gives solo play a reason to continue beyond clearing the standard ladder, while the team format rewards learning more than one character.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains team fighting and Making mode without vague levelling shorthand.

decisions.alias: last blade, the - beyond the destiny (europe).zip
decisions.hook: Power and Speed styles change how you approach the sword duels, while repelling an attack creates the opening for a reply. Unlockable power-up scrolls and mini-games add solo goals without turning the careful weapon fighting into an RPG.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague RPG-ish modes with sword styles and actual unlocks.

decisions.hook: Raise and care for the little girl Melon-chan in a monochrome virtual-life game. The reward is watching her development through repeated attention, so it suits patient caretaking more than someone looking for a clear action challenge; the text is Japanese.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains care focus and Japanese dependence instead of virtual-pet label.

decisions.hook: Follow Tomoya, Ayaka and Yue through a Japanese visual-novel prequel to Memories Off. Returning to later scenes from different viewpoints is the main reason to replay, so the appeal depends on reading the relationships rather than mastering a separate gameplay system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains viewpoint replay and series-prequel appeal.

decisions.hook: Run, jump and shoot through branching missions, switching to a tank or aircraft when the route calls for it. Alternate progressions give repeat runs a purpose beyond chasing a better score; this is a pocket campaign of its own rather than the arcade stages squeezed down.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns branching-stage shorthand into routing and vehicle appeal.

decisions.hook: Choose between two soldiers and follow a nonlinear path through infantry, tank, aircraft and submarine missions. The larger campaign and hostage collection reward revisiting routes, making this a richer exploration of the pocket formula rather than simply more enemies per screen.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported best-action-game superlative and explains replay value.

decisions.hook: Judge whether to hit, stand, split or double down as you try to beat the dealer without exceeding twenty-one. Those choices give the casino loop more agency than slots, but the entire attraction is practising blackjack rather than unlocking a broader adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains blackjack risk and active choices.

decisions.alias: neo cherry master - real casino series (japan, europe) (en,ja).zip
decisions.hook: Bet on fruit-machine reels and watch the combinations settle, with chance doing most of the work. Original mode adds a saved name and high scores to the basic loop, but it cannot supply the tactical decisions missing from plain slots.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds honest minimal-interaction caveat and Original-mode distinction.

decisions.alias: neo cherry master color - real casino series (world) (en,ja).zip
decisions.hook: Spin colour fruit-machine reels in Simple or Original mode and chase a higher virtual payout. The presentation is brighter, but the appeal remains the anticipation of a result; skip it if you want a game driven by decisions rather than repeated wagers.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands colour-only note while retaining narrow casino appeal.

decisions.hook: Choose horses and stake types, then see whether your race prediction pays off. This Japanese horse-betting simulation is about reading the odds and risking a virtual bankroll, not steering a jockey through a race.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains horse-betting role rather than suggesting direct racing.

decisions.hook: Manage a 1999 Japanese baseball team and take control of its pitching and batting. The four stadiums have different field dimensions, giving venue choice some interest beyond the real-team roster, although the Japanese presentation is less welcoming to newcomers.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds real-team and field-size context to baseball label.

decisions.hook: Choose a golfer for their strengths, line up a shot and judge power, hook and slice across three courses. The satisfaction is turning a considered approach into a clean shot, with enough differences between golfers to make course planning more than a timing test.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces good-one praise with club, aim and shot-planning appeal.

decisions.hook: Take on odd jobs, recruit companions and earn licences that unlock stronger skills in a quest-driven RPG. The job system offers some freedom, but vague directions and repeated errands can make progress feel like work; Japanese reading is essential in this edition.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects puzzle-escape misclassification to quest-driven RPG and adds grounded friction.

decisions.hook: Use the numbers beside each row and column to deduce which squares belong in a hidden picture. The small grids favour self-contained logic sessions, and a coloured reveal helps identify the finished image; this is the Japanese edition of Picture Puzzle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains nonogram deduction rather than naming another series.

decisions.hook: Reproduce the Azteca pachislot machine, then consult its pattern database and record results in a machine notebook. Those tools make sense for studying a particular gambling machine, but offer little to someone seeking varied arcade play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains machine analysis and narrow audience.

decisions.hook: Play a reproduction of the CR Fever Casino RX pachinko machine, with commentary and a gallery explaining its near-win sequences. The value is learning how that machine presents its chances, not exercising the direct ball control of a pinball game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains specific-machine simulation and reference-gallery purpose.

decisions.hook: Fill a grid by reconciling the number clues along each row and column until a picture emerges. The emphasis on smaller puzzles makes a complete deduction a manageable sitting, while the final colour reveal helps otherwise ambiguous pixel pictures make sense.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Picross shorthand with deduction and session appeal.

decisions.hook: Surround opposing discs to flip them, but avoid a greedy capture that hands over a stable corner. Short lessons, visible move hints and take-backs make this a useful place to learn Reversi before tackling the tournament opponents.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains corner control and existing beginner aids.

decisions.alias: pocket tennis - pocket sports series (japan, europe) (en,ja).zip
decisions.hook: Move into position, place the return and choose a player whose strengths suit your game. Exhibition lets you set up an isolated match, while the three-round tournament gives the monochrome tennis a compact progression without elaborate career management.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Gives tennis decision and mode distinction.

decisions.alias: pocket tennis color - pocket sports series (world) (en,ja).zip
decisions.hook: Use lobs and smashes to pull an opponent out of position instead of merely returning every ball. Exhibition and tournament play keep the focus on the rallies, while trophies provide a modest record of progress rather than a complicated career system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains shot selection and manageable competitive goals.

decisions.hook: Stack connected groups of four matching blobs, arranging the leftovers to fall into another clear and send nuisance pieces to your opponent. The interesting gamble is how long to build a larger chain before incoming garbage ruins the setup.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces great-version claim with chain building and competitive risk.

decisions.hook: Face Robot Masters directly, collecting their weapons and choosing the next opponent around those weaknesses. These pocket adaptations trade normal Mega Man stages for concentrated boss fights; the link feature exchanges database information, not cooperative play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains boss-rush weapon ordering and important no-coop caveat.

decisions.hook: Choose Slash or Burst variants for your sword fighter, then learn the reach and timing needed to punish an opening. Unlockable power-up cards add a solo collection goal, giving the colour sequel more to pursue than simply clearing its ladder.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces colour/sharp shorthand with styles and card progression.

decisions.alias: snk vs. capcom - the match of the millennium (world) (en,ja).zip
decisions.hook: Mix SNK and Capcom fighters in single, tag or team bouts, with three battle styles changing how you approach the contest. Unlockable characters and the Olympic mini-games give solo play variety, while the broad crossover roster is the stronger reason to settle in and learn matchups.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported best/masterpiece claims with concrete roster and mode appeal.

decisions.hook: Armour transformations support the platform fighting, while side-scrolling shooting stages interrupt the hand-to-hand routine. That shift makes this Cyber Cross sequel worth choosing for variety rather than expecting a single combat system to carry every stage.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic superhero comparison with transformations and shooting-stage variety.

decisions.hook: Stunning shots, a homing gun and a cape that knocks enemies into each other give Doraemon several ways through the platform stages. The scenery and tools keep changing, but the slow movement and uneven difficulty make this less breezy than the friendly artwork suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces plot and generic platform description with distinctive weapons and pace caveat.

decisions.hook: Mecha run-and-gun combat is paired with Metroid-like upgrades, giving the machinery more purpose than its striking Masamune Shirow designs alone. Choose it for that mix of action and developing abilities, though Japanese upgrade dialogue makes learning the equipment less straightforward.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds researched upgrade-based exploration instead of designer credit alone.

decisions.hook: An overhead racing career gives each circuit a place in your driver's progression rather than leaving every race isolated. The small cars look playful, but reading the bends and making clean passes is the real appeal, not the career framing on its own.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces irrelevant vehicle-combat comparison with useful overhead-racing guidance.

decisions.hook: Move robot forces between battlefields, then command them on hexagonal tactical grids. The split between campaign deployment and individual fights gives the heavy mechs a strategic role beyond simply looking impressive in combat animations.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces opaque six-neighbour wording with the familiar hex-grid term.

decisions.hook: Transformation pickups turn your spacecraft into a fighting robot during the side-scrolling stages. That change of form and armament is the attraction, rather than a fundamentally different structure from other fly-and-shoot campaigns.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the irrelevant robot-sandbox comparison with the transformation appeal.

decisions.hook: Headbutts, wall rebounds and tooth-powered climbing keep Bonk's whole body involved in the platforming. These familiar tricks return with quicker movement, making this a lively continuation rather than a reinvention of the caveman adventures.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Stops describing returning Bonk movement techniques as new additions.

decisions.hook: Santa shoots down enchanted decorations in this festive spin-off of Atlantean's Defender-style action. It is a short high-score challenge rather than a full campaign, suited to repeat attempts through the same holiday chaos.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains festive score-attack identity without the release-history preamble.

decisions.hook: Paint the floor squares while shooting enemies and navigating arrows that force you in particular directions. The challenge is finding a safe route through the board, not simply surviving until the last monster is gone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes nonsensical battle lines and the unsupported suggestion that your own shots hurt you.

decisions.hook: Defend underwater settlements by rescuing Atlanteans before enemy ships mutate them. The Defender-style shooting makes rescue compete with survival, while four worlds and an Endurance mode give the premise more room than a single score-attack stage.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces feature inventory and HuCard-history claim with the rescue decision.

decisions.hook: A 24-hour war branches according to the missions you accept, with demanding mech battles that expose weaknesses in your garage setup. Reworking a build for a particular opponent is the payoff; this is a punishing place to start learning Armored Core.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces hardest/most honest hype with the branching campaign and build demands.

decisions.hook: Heat and energy management make mech construction as important as aiming during Nexus's missions. This Evolution disc holds the new campaign; the separate Revolution disc revisits older missions, so the two discs are not interchangeable campaigns.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the heat overhaul and keeps the Evolution disc distinction.

decisions.hook: Tune a mech through training exercises and ranked arena duels rather than a story campaign. The focused tests are useful for diagnosing a build's weaknesses, but the lack of varied mission context makes this a narrow Armored Core spin-off.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands drill shorthand while retaining the thin-campaign warning.

decisions.hook: Build a mercenary mech for missions on Mars and test it against the arena ladder. Overboost gives you a powerful burst of movement, making the balance between mobility, weapons and energy an immediate garage decision.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains overboost rather than relying on generation jargon.

decisions.hook: Armored Core 2 mixes paid mech missions with an arena ladder, with weapons and movement systems chosen in the garage. VanLaser's True Analogs patch puts aiming on the right stick, easing the original control scheme without removing the need to manage your build.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the dual-analog patch distinction without ordering readers to reject the original.

decisions.hook: Work through a large collection of short mech missions using Armored Core 2's extensive parts selection. The sparse storytelling makes repeated sorties and garage adjustments the main attraction, rather than a dramatic campaign to follow.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes purest-entry hyperbole and clarifies mission-led appeal.

decisions.hook: Equip an adaptable mech for missions beneath the surface, using left-arm weapons and an AI consort to vary your approach. Short sorties make it easy to connect a garage decision with its battlefield result, even when the older control scheme takes practice.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces best-balanced claim and generation shorthand with concrete build choices.

decisions.hook: Rollers let your fragile Armored Trooper skate around locked-on targets, making momentum and safe firing angles central to survival. Escaping on foot and taking an abandoned machine adds a desperate recovery option. The v0.9 English patch is machine-translated, with some Japanese graphics and reported text clipping remaining.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the Votoms feature list while retaining machine-translation limitations.

decisions.hook: Choose a fighter, archer or sorceress, then turn dungeon loot and level-up points into a stronger action-RPG character. Shared-screen co-op and tactile hack-and-slash combat are the draw; the linear adventure offers much less freedom than the Baldur's Gate name might suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts act names and unlock lists while retaining co-op appeal and linearity.

decisions.hook: Five preset heroes bring different abilities to this shared-screen dungeon crawler, while runestones and gems let you tune weapons and armour. Crafting gives the loot hunt more purpose, but the familiar linear fighting makes this a refinement of Dark Alliance rather than a large departure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses the sequel on crafting rather than a long character inventory.

decisions.hook: Summon companions through music while fighting through an action-RPG parody led by a selfish, sarcastic bard. The quarrelsome narration is the main attraction; the lighter combat systems make it less rewarding if you do not enjoy the jokes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the summoning mechanic to the comedy-only dismissal.

decisions.hook: Explore a shifting tower with third-person combat, strange items and mutations that complicate each attempt to survive. This remake preserves Baroque's disorienting roguelike loop, so its surreal discovery is more inviting than its explanation of what to do next.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported original-versus-remake ranking and explains the death loop.

decisions.hook: Loud weapons and destructible cover make every firefight a spectacle as you push through eight substantial stages. The pleasure is in the impact of shooting and blowing open a position, not deep character building or a flexible campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces gun-porn shorthand with the concrete shooting appeal and limitation.

decisions.alias: Blood Will Tell - Tezuka Osamu's Dororo (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Defeat fiends to reclaim Hyakkimaru's stolen body parts, gaining strength and occasionally restoring senses or movement abilities. That bodily recovery gives the sword fighting an unusual sense of progression, though the awkward camera can interrupt the satisfaction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the implication that all 48 body parts change moves or presentation.

decisions.hook: Place traps before tactical fights and ration dragon power as the D-Counter rises toward a fatal limit. Restarts carry some progress forward, making another attempt part of learning the route rather than simply repeating a conventional RPG adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains D-Counter pressure and restart value without the anti-JRPG label.

decisions.hook: Your weapon choice shapes how summoned Innocent Devils evolve, while stolen materials feed equipment crafting. Those linked growth systems give Hector's sword fighting room for experimentation, but repetitive corridors and box-shaped rooms blunt the pleasure of exploring this 3D Castlevania.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps companion evolution and corridor criticism while trimming the systems catalogue.

decisions.hook: Latch a plasma chain onto green anchor points to swing and slingshot through 2.5D stages, then bring a large blade into close combat. The v1.0 English translation makes this unusual movement-led action game more approachable; its appeal is mastering a route rather than simply clearing every enemy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns movement-first shorthand into an explanation while keeping translation identity.

decisions.hook: Choose a character class and fight through the EverQuest planes, collecting equipment as you decide whether to destroy or restore an evil god. Up to four players can share the dungeon crawling locally with a multitap; the familiar loot-and-fight routine is the attraction rather than a surprising reinvention.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces clicking and zero-surprises dismissal with the co-op loot loop.

decisions.hook: Equip two Legions and decide when to summon them: their attacks add crowd control, but Sieg becomes slower and weaker while they are active. Developing those companions gives the battles meaningful preparation, though repeated enemy crowds and a short campaign limit the variety.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses Legion rules into their central tradeoff and preserves repetition criticism.

decisions.hook: Lead four soldiers through Vietnam missions, issuing orders and sharing supplies to keep the squad working together. Coordinating the group gives firefights more substance than lone-gun shooting, even when awkward handling makes those plans harder to carry out.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what squad control adds instead of ending on unexplained jank.

decisions.alias: Cowboy Bebop - Tsuitou no Yakyoku (Japan) (En) (v1.0.0 Translation).iso
decisions.hook: Rhythmic brawling and timed counters build a Cool meter, while shooting and ship chases break up an original Cowboy Bebop bounty story. Heavy cutscenes make this more appealing for the cast than for uninterrupted combat. The v1.0.0 translation covers text and graphics; its notes suggest software rendering if PCSX2 runs slowly.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims mode inventory while preserving the full-translation and rendering caveat.

decisions.hook: Build a deck of creatures, equipment and spells, then use it to claim and defend spaces on a board. Choosing which territory to strengthen and which fights to risk gives the card combinations a larger purpose than simply winning an isolated duel.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes misleading instant-matches claim and explains territorial card decisions.

decisions.hook: Recover town-building pieces from randomized dungeons and arrange them through Georama, while strengthening weapons along the way. Keeping equipment repaired matters because a neglected weapon can break permanently, giving the pleasant rebuilding loop a costly edge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Georama and weapon-breakage stakes rather than shorthand praise.

decisions.hook: Photograph ideas for inventions, improve equipment and rebuild settlements between trips into randomized dungeons. The overlapping crafting and Georama systems reward curiosity, but slow, talkative opening hours delay that freedom.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the hobby inventory with the relationship between photography, crafting and rebuilding.

decisions.alias: Devil May Cry 3 - Dante's Awakening (USA) (En,Ja) (Special Edition).iso
decisions.hook: Choose a combat Style and switch weapons during fights to build expressive, demanding combos. Special Edition adds playable Vergil and more forgiving continue options alongside extra challenges, making it easier to approach without removing the need to learn enemy openings.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts the Special Edition feature list and unsupported combat-peak assertion.

decisions.alias: Dirge of Cerberus - Final Fantasy VII (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Combine gun frames, barrels and accessories to balance Vincent's range, accuracy and movement, then choose whether stage rewards become levels or spending money. The equipment tinkering is more interesting than the often dull shooting encounters, making this primarily a Final Fantasy VII side story rather than a strong standalone shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves gun-building choices and weak-encounter criticism without review-score shorthand.

decisions.hook: Tune capsule skill loadouts, then manage ki through fast duels and Dragon Rush exchanges. Dragon Universe adds free flight between fights, while this Greatest Hits edition includes unlockable Japanese voices for a different presentation of the same campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes best-entry proclamation while keeping the Greatest Hits voice distinction.

decisions.hook: Dash and trade blasts across large 3D arenas with a roster packed with Dragon Ball characters and transformations. The spectacle and matchup variety are the attraction, especially if recreating a favourite fight matters more than a tightly restrained tournament roster.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces shallow fan-service shorthand with how arena space matters.

decisions.hook: Alternate between party-based ground brawling and dragon battles against airborne formations. Changing weapons and characters offers some variety, but repetitive combat and three endings tied to repeat playthroughs make this a substantial commitment for relatively thin action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps ground/dragon contrast and replay burden without the staff-history digression.

decisions.hook: Position Three Kingdoms officers so one tactic pushes an enemy into the next attack. Planning a long chain is the pleasure: the battles reward arranging the board before committing rather than simply sending the strongest unit forward.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands tactic-chain shorthand into a readable positional recommendation.

decisions.hook: Arrange officers and trigger tactics that knock enemies into further attacks, building long chains from careful positioning. More tactical options and branching campaigns give the sequel extra combinations to explore, but its appeal still rests on enjoying that deliberate setup.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the sequel understandable without requiring the first game's note.

decisions.hook: Pair pilots with mobile suits, then carve through enemy formations in large battlefield brawls. Experimenting with those combinations adds a Gundam-specific reason to replay, although the repeated crowd clearing remains closer to Dynasty Warriors than a detailed mech simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains pilot/suit mixing and the crowd-clearing limitation.

decisions.hook: Fight through standalone stories for characters outside Dynasty Warriors 3's main kingdoms, using the familiar crowd-clearing combat. Loading the original disc restores its content, so this expansion is a focused supplement rather than a complete replacement for the base game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces historic-but-rough shorthand and clarifies expansion dependence.

decisions.hook: Recruit officers, choose policies and take territory on a conquest map, then personally fight the resulting battlefield clashes. That strategic context gives familiar crowd-clearing combat a useful purpose beyond replaying a fixed officer biography.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how conquest decisions connect the battles.

decisions.hook: Choose among 48 officers and follow their campaigns through crowded Three Kingdoms battlefields. Bodyguards and character growth give repeated sorties continuity, but the pleasure remains broad, rhythmic crowd clearing rather than intricate duelling.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes peak/comfort-food labels in favour of the story-and-combat loop.

decisions.hook: Create officers, recruit a force and choose policies while expanding a kingdom across the conquest map. Deciding where to fight gives the repeated crowd battles a strategic frame, making this more appealing than the fixed stories if you want to direct the war yourself.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces best-entry and thinking-person hype with kingdom-management decisions.

decisions.hook: Keep attacks going to build the Renbu system's longer combo sequences across crowded battlefields. The change shifts the feel of familiar officers, and this PS2 edition adds scenarios and weapons rather than simply matching the higher-resolution versions; try it for that variation, not a refinement of Dynasty Warriors 5's exact combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unexplained skip advice with the divisive combo mechanic and PS2 distinction.

decisions.hook: Change visible equipment to alter your abilities as you explore an action-RPG world with little ceremony. Trying a new outfit can change how you handle the next encounter, though awkward combat makes the experimentation less smooth than its ideas deserve.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains equipment-driven growth without vague systemic praise.

decisions.hook: Program party members with Gambit conditions so healing, targeting and attacks happen according to your priorities. Revising those rules as encounters change is the distinctive pleasure, within a long, politically driven adventure that still has slow stretches.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes Gambits understandable and retains the lengthy pacing caveat.

decisions.alias: Front Mission 5 - Scars of the War (Japan) (En) (Patch 4 Translation).iso
decisions.hook: Build wanzers from individual parts and coordinate pilots through linked attacks in turn-based military missions. The Patch 4 English translation opens up a campaign whose appeal is preparing a complementary squad, not simply equipping every robot with the strongest available gun.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Drops series-peak and translation-quality absolutes while keeping the patch identity.

decisions.alias: Fullmetal Alchemist and the Broken Angel (USA, Canada).iso
decisions.hook: Transmute scenery into weapons and defences while Ed fights beside AI-controlled Al. The alchemy gives this Fullmetal Alchemist adventure its identity, but recycled dungeons, weak enemy AI and a short linear campaign make the story a stronger reason to play than the combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the alchemy mechanics and preserves substantive criticism.

decisions.hook: Build a persistent character while hacking through crowded fantasy worlds and collecting the runestones needed to advance. Local co-op turns the repeated monster clearing into a shared scramble, with a multitap needed for three or four players; solo runs expose the repetition more quickly.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims the attack inventory while preserving persistent characters and multiplayer requirements.

decisions.hook: Four heroes buy combos and specials as they fight through a short, linear fantasy campaign. Local co-op is the best reason to try it: simple key-and-switch obstacles and repeated battles offer little of Dark Legacy's broader progression loop.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the thin-solo warning without review-score and removed-feature inventory.

decisions.hook: Alternate between agile Yoshitsune and heavy-hitting Benkei, using their different abilities to fight and traverse the stages. Kamui slows incoming attacks into timed counter opportunities, giving the handsome but fairly simple samurai combat its most distinctive rhythm.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses on character contrast and the timed-counter hook.

decisions.hook: Swing chains, throw heavy punches and build a style rank high enough to break shielded enemies, with Hellcycle stages between the fights. One early combo handles much of the ordinary opposition, so repetitive demons and patterns undermine the apparent room for experimentation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unlock list while explaining why the combat becomes repetitive.

decisions.alias: Ghost in the Shell - Stand Alone Complex (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Alternate between Kusanagi's agile traversal and Batou's heavier shooting, occasionally possessing enemies through ghost-hacking. The Section 9 setting is appealing, but absent aim assist and an awkwardly spinning dodge camera can make otherwise conventional firefights frustrating.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses weapon and mode details while preserving camera and aiming friction.

decisions.hook: Recruit and equip a gladiator school, then use grid positioning and timed attack inputs to win arena battles. Building a complementary roster is rewarding, but the long campaign asks for more commitment than its individual bouts suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns systems-rich shorthand into the actual roster and combat tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Command goblin clans with waypoints or take direct control to join the fighting, using their different units and powerful Titans to break defences. The simplified scale works with a controller, making this an approachable action-strategy hybrid rather than a sprawling management game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why direct possession distinguishes this console strategy game.

decisions.hook: Build your own attack strings from a large move list, then dodge and punish enemies in close-range street fights. The difficulty rises when you perform well, keeping mastery tense rather than letting a stronger moveset turn every encounter effortless.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces zero-filler hype with the risk of its adaptive difficulty.

decisions.hook: Chain sweeping blade attacks, dodges and magic through encounters with Greek monsters, then finish major enemies through timed button sequences. Its tightly directed spectacle is the attraction; expect a designed action ride rather than a world of open-ended combat solutions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands genre-only praise with Kratos's actual fighting and the spectacle limitation.

decisions.hook: Kratos's new weapons and traversal tools feed larger fights and puzzles, including time-slowing and reflected attacks. The sequel expands the spectacle and combat options, but its linear routes and frequent timed finishers still favour a directed adventure over free-form experimentation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims the weapon and tool catalogue while preserving the linear spectacle caveat.

decisions.hook: Choose how your trailing Option satellites behave, then use that formation to attack while steering the main ship out of danger. Learning those firing angles is central to this demanding Gradius, with repeat runs rewarding route knowledge rather than simple reflex spraying.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes arcade-perfect rhetoric and explains Option control.

decisions.hook: Summon units from competing magical schools and use their counters to control a side-view tower. The layered battlefield gives this real-time strategy game a distinctive shape, while its illustrated story scenes interrupt rather than replace the tactical contests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the rune-school choice instead of dismissing the story as light anime.

decisions.hook: Four-player battles require you to turn your fighter manually, adding an awkward extra task to Guilty Gear's fast combat. Factory Mode is the more unusual attraction: build Robo-Ky II by learning and combining moves from other characters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the manual-facing caveat to a usable explanation of the unusual fighter.

decisions.hook: Take jobs and explore a compact Western landscape, then use kills to fuel Quickdraw's slow-motion shooting. Riding between towns and spending rewards on upgrades provides breathing room, but the appeal is an accessible gunfighter fantasy rather than a deeply simulated frontier.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts activity inventory and comparison quote in favour of the shooting loop.

decisions.hook: Destroy enemies and scenery in quick succession to maintain a Beat chain and earn powerful coffin attacks. A recharging shield encourages brief recovery between assaults, while the short campaign makes score improvement a stronger reason to return than discovery.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains chaining and recovery without a long feature list.

decisions.hook: Keep destruction chains alive through larger crowds, with additional playable characters bringing different close-range and ranged attacks. The longer campaign offers more Gungrave to master, but the pleasure is still stylish repetition rather than varied objectives or exploration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Keeps the sequel's extra characters without unsupported must-pick advice.

decisions.hook: Jump, strafe and aim from a mech cockpit while fighting tanks, aircraft and other machines across six battlefields. Ammo pickups and unlockable equipment support repeated attempts, but the small mission selection makes this a compact, fast action game rather than a sprawling military simulation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the slow military-simulation framing to the documented fast cockpit action.
