decisions.hook: Breed monsters and arrange them around your trainer, then rotate the formation to expose the attacks or healing you need. Protecting the trainer while keeping useful creatures active gives the battles real tactical substance, though repeated dungeon errands can wear thin.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the first game's appearance-merging emphasis with the sequel's formation decisions.

decisions.hook: Switch between paired DC heroes and fit collectible boosts into their powers to tune damage, efficiency and other effects. The first half chooses the pair for you, and similar basic combos limit the freedom promised by the superhero roster.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the boost catalogue while keeping constrained team selection and repetitive combat.

decisions.hook: Train a swordsman at a dojo, acquire techniques and assemble attack strings for measured sword duels. Unlike Bushido Blade, Kengo uses health bars rather than instant-kill combat; the stance and timing work is appealing, but repetitive training exercises slow the journey.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects false lethal-single-strike claim and notes the training grind.

decisions.hook: Switch between Arthurian knights and give simple squad orders while personally fighting through defensive missions. Combining melee with positioned archers is promising, but stuck allies, unstable combat timing and the lack of mid-mission saves can make a failed plan expensive.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts named-knight and review-score lists while preserving concrete control problems.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings, The - The Return of the King (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Upgrade familiar film heroes and fight together through battles from The Return of the King. Cooperative crowd clearing is the main attraction, with movie footage and set pieces supplying context rather than a freely explorable Middle-earth.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces fun-but-forgettable shorthand with what cooperative play offers.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings, The - The Third Age (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Lead a separate party in the Fellowship's wake, fighting turn-based battles through recognisable Middle-earth locations. The film setting gives a conventional RPG structure its appeal, but the deliberate pace and familiar battle routine offer little surprise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the turn-based appeal and formulaic limitation.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings, The - The Two Towers (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Choose Aragorn, Legolas or Gimli and use their different weapons and moves to cut through battles drawn from the films. The short, directed campaign makes this a concentrated action adaptation rather than a Middle-earth exploration game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds distinctive character decisions instead of only comparing the sequel.

decisions.hook: Build a four-hero Marvel squad and chase bonuses for particular lineups, switching characters as their powers suit the fight. Team composition and upgrades give the brawling purpose, but frequent button-mashing makes the roster more interesting than many individual encounters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims feature list to team construction and repetitive combat.

decisions.alias: Marvel Nemesis - Rise of the Imperfects (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Throw Marvel characters and the original Imperfects around destructible 3D arenas. Environmental mayhem is the attraction, but loose movement, projectile-heavy AI and an unappealing story mode make this a weaker choice for carefully balanced competitive fighting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Drops unrelated CPS2 comparison and dated online-service aside while retaining combat criticism.

decisions.hook: Hijack military vehicles and buy airstrikes to solve contracts in a war-torn open world. Working for competing factions gives destruction consequences, since pleasing one employer can make another less willing to help.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the anachronistic MGSV comparison and explains faction consequences.

decisions.hook: Take faction contracts, commandeer vehicles and demolish buildings in a separate PS2 adaptation of the Venezuelan campaign. Its map is smaller than the newer-console versions and there is no co-op; loose vehicle handling makes the destructive freedom less satisfying than it sounds.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the blanket bigger-sequel framing for this distinct PS2 version.

decisions.alias: Mobile Suit Gundam - Encounters in Space (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Use lock-on movement and ranged attacks to fight mobile suits in space, following several perspectives on Gundam's wars. Training a custom pilot adds a little progression, but the appeal is quick, recognisable battles rather than extensive mech engineering.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic arena-fighter shorthand with its campaign-and-pilot appeal.

decisions.alias: Mobile Suit Gundam - Federation vs. Zeon (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Fight two-on-two mobile-suit battles where destroyed machines consume a shared team budget. Choosing a powerful but costly suit changes how much risk you can afford, while boost management keeps positioning important during the shooting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the cost economy instead of calling it pure arcade mech.

decisions.alias: Mobile Suit Gundam - Gundam vs. Zeta Gundam (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Zeta-era suits expand the two-on-two mobile-suit battles, while the Universal Century campaign offers a broader set of encounters to pursue. Shared team costs and boost management remain the tactical core, so the larger roster is the reason to choose this continuation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the Zeta sequel intelligible without reading the previous entry.

decisions.alias: Mobile Suit Gundam - Journey to Jaburo (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Pilot Gundam through missions retelling the first television series, lining up shots and close-range attacks against enemy mobile suits. Familiar scenes are the attraction, but stiff movement makes this harder to recommend for responsive mech combat alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands stiff-but-atmospheric shorthand into a recommendation.

decisions.hook: Plan routes and timing for several Zeon mobile-suit teams before committing them to a mission. The satisfying work is coordinating a safe approach, making this a tactical alternative to Gundam games built around constant dashing and shooting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces the Carnage Heart reference with the actual planning payoff.

decisions.hook: Copy enemy abilities and bring them into Musashi's sword fighting across a cel-shaded adventure. Learning a useful move from an opponent gives encounters a purpose beyond clearing the route, though the straightforward action remains the main rhythm.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what ability copying changes without vague breezy praise.

decisions.alias: Nightmare of Druaga, The - Fushigino Dungeon (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Every step or attack advances the dungeon's turn, making movement and fighting part of the same positional puzzle. Equipment refinement gives expeditions a longer-term purpose, but this is a punishing dungeon crawl rather than a forgiving action adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies turn-based movement and avoids promising universal equipment persistence.

decisions.hook: Kill enemies in quick succession to maintain a Tate chain and strengthen Hibana's attacks, using airborne dashes and kicks to link targets. The resulting movement is exhilarating, but awkward camera angles and lethal gaps make learning the routes unforgiving.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes the misleading sword-survival shorthand and explains Tate chaining accurately.

decisions.hook: Bring Onimusha characters into side-view battles for up to four players, trading sword attacks in crowded arenas. The crossover roster is the main draw; this is a party-fighting detour rather than another atmospheric solo Onimusha campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces novelty-only dismissal with the multiplayer premise.

decisions.hook: Switch between two active characters to combine their abilities and improve weapons through a long action-adventure campaign. Partner management adds variety to the fighting, but the increased scope moves away from the earlier games' compact survival-horror pacing.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands biggest-entry shorthand into the partner-switching decision.

decisions.hook: Explore a compact, atmospheric castle adventure and fight demons with deliberate sword strikes. A precisely timed Issen counter can kill in one blow, giving the combat a demanding skill to master beneath its survival-horror pacing.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Issen rather than assuming the reader knows the term.

decisions.hook: Trade gifts with potential allies to change who accompanies Jubei and how parts of the adventure unfold. Sword fights still reward precisely timed one-hit counters, so the social choices add replay value without replacing the demanding combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains ally gifts and counters without relying on series shorthand.

decisions.hook: Alternate between demon-infested Japan and modern Paris in a linked, time-travelling adventure. Direct analog movement makes navigating sword fights less awkward than the earlier entries, while the two settings give the familiar combat a fresh frame.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces most-accessible assertion with its actual control and campaign distinction.

decisions.hook: Unlock a large collection of ships and experiment with their weapons and detachable Force units. The deliberate pace rewards memorising threats and choosing the right firing position; the catalogue is a reason to replay, not a shortcut around demanding routes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes misleading claim that every ship has a different Force and Dose system.

decisions.hook: Recruit a large cast whose daily schedules affect where you find them, exploring a town that feels busy beyond the main quest. The recruitment puzzle is the distinctive attraction, while the conventional RPG fighting is more familiar.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unhelpful world-sim and NPC-count shorthand.

decisions.hook: Modify weapons and fight through combat arenas with robot partners rather than spending much time exploring planets. That narrower focus suits quick shooting challenges, but it drops much of the wandering and discovery associated with other Ratchet games.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the arena focus and weapon tuning in complete prose.

decisions.hook: Move walking tanks and supporting infantry on a tactical map, then enter real-time duels where range and aim matter. The combination makes unit placement affect how the shooting unfolds, with a slow, deliberate pace rather than arcade mech speed.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the strategy/action interaction without grounded-and-unique hype.

decisions.hook: Choose a hero and follow an open-ended route through quests, learning new combat techniques during battles. The freedom makes different playthroughs rewarding, but hidden progression rules make it easy to miss opportunities without understanding why.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces opaque systemic terminology with the benefit and cost of open progression.

decisions.hook: Build an arena mech from weapons and defensive systems, including electronic countermeasures and optical camouflage. Experimenting with a loadout is immediately relevant to survival, making this a focused combat-and-garage game rather than a long story campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands garage and soundtrack shorthand into arena decisions.

decisions.hook: Deflect bullets and cut through gunmen in compact Western arenas, unlocking swords and stances as you progress. Turning gunfire into an opening for close combat gives the short missions their appeal, rather than a large world to explore.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes frame-data jargon and no-bloat hype while explaining bullet defence.

decisions.hook: Flashy warlords clear enemy crowds in an expanded roster, with two-player Conquest adding a strong cooperative reason to return. Heroes supplies new stories rather than including the original Basara 2 story campaigns, and the Japanese text remains a barrier to following their context.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects implication that Heroes contains the full original Basara 2 story content.

decisions.hook: Build and sustain a timed dual-blade mode through well-timed guards, dodges and attacks while cutting through a science-fiction retelling of Seven Samurai. Those timing systems promise more than the repeated crowds demand, with linear stages and weak pacing undermining the spectacle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the Nitou-Ryu system and keeps supported repetition criticism.

decisions.hook: Explore a hostile first-person dungeon with guns and blades, targeting body parts to change how monsters can attack. Control Type 4 supplies dual-analog movement and aiming, but the immediate freedom still comes with the vulnerability of a demanding dungeon crawl.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains locational damage and keeps the practical control distinction.

decisions.hook: Scavenge replacements as weapons break, use brutal attacks to excite the crowd and turn their gifts into an advantage in gladiator bouts. The arena fighting is the draw; mandatory Octavianus stealth sections, where being spotted means failure, repeatedly interrupt that momentum.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims gore and match inventories while preserving weapon scavenging and stealth friction.

decisions.hook: Travel a quiet landscape to find sixteen enormous opponents, then climb their moving bodies while managing your grip. Each fight is a spatial puzzle as much as a test of timing, with the empty journeys providing a deliberate contrast to the struggle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes inaccurate nothing-else claim and age-coded praise.

decisions.hook: Fight through enemy crowds while developing a fortress that also needs defending. Alternating outward expeditions with protecting home gives the hack-and-slash a useful structure, though the repeated fighting remains its main activity.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces mindless-loop dismissal with the base-defence decision.

decisions.hook: Develop Max through a Force Art upgrade tree while fighting crowds in real time. The growth system is the reason to stay, but anyone seeking the older Shining Force games' turn-based army tactics should expect a different kind of adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the action-RPG departure and upgrade appeal.

decisions.hook: Build on Armored Core 3's garage with new missions, hidden parts and trainable AI partners. Repeated sorties reward both piloting and loadout refinement. The original control scheme takes adjustment if you are used to later dual-analog entries.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves the stock-release control caveat without asserting whether a particular local copy has a fan patch.

decisions.hook: Weapon reach, sidesteps and ring positioning drive Soulcalibur's one-on-one duels. Create-a-Soul and the strategy-flavoured Chronicles of the Sword campaign add room to develop custom fighters, making this especially appealing for solo experimentation beyond standard arcade matches.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Adds the core weapon-duel appeal to the mode-only description.

decisions.hook: Fight inside large battles using single-target strikes, wide sweeps and shield shoves while allies and enemies clash around you. The scale distinguishes it from smaller brawlers, but unreliable targeting and frustrating bosses can make that spectacle harder to control than to admire.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses the battlefield scale and controls caveat instead of a weapon catalogue.

decisions.hook: Switch soldier classes and vehicles to capture command posts, or connect battles through Galactic Conquest. Large clashes make a good sandbox for battlefield roles, but predictable AI opposition limits the challenge and variety of solo play.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains class and vehicle decisions while keeping the weak-solo caveat.

decisions.hook: Build a walking Trotmobile from parts, then use it for travel, work and arena fights alongside music and trading. The mixture offers unusual freedom to decide what kind of life to pursue, though awkward handling makes it less polished than its open-ended ambitions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns mech-trotter jargon into the relationship between life-sim and machine building.

decisions.hook: Follow the same conflict through three protagonists, recruiting characters into a shared castle as their perspectives change your understanding of the war. Paired commands and area magic give battles distinctive complications, but switching storylines can slow the sense of forward progress.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims plot names and award claims while preserving viewpoint and paired-combat distinctions.

decisions.hook: Switch among companions in real-time fights and use Maia's guardian transformations, while royal decisions shape the realm between adventures. Those political choices give the RPG an unusual second layer, though limited ally AI makes the increasingly hard battles less dependable.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Focuses royal choices and character switching while preserving difficulty criticism.

decisions.hook: Develop fighters through branching skill choices that add moves and mechanics, then use guard cancels and spacing in arcade-style duels. The smaller, focused fighting format is the appeal rather than reproducing every Dragon Ball character and transformation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what skill trees add rather than simply declaring fighting depth.

decisions.hook: Launch enemies into the air and sustain Sword Time juggling attacks through selectable missions in a fantasy-China setting. The airborne combat is the distinctive reason to investigate, rather than expecting a broad adventure from this focused sword-action game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic stance claim with the documented Sword Time aerial hook.

decisions.hook: Scout patrols, grapple to useful positions and choose tools before committing to a silent kill. Three ninja perspectives give the missions variety, but the main satisfaction is completing a deliberate infiltration rather than improvising a prolonged open fight.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains stealth preparation instead of listing familiar Tenchu terms.

decisions.hook: Lure pursuers into combinations of pendulums, magnets and boulders instead of fighting them with direct weapons. Planning where a victim will land after each trap turns the rooms into grisly sequence puzzles, with positioning just as important as buying stronger devices.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes confusing Deception IV identity comparison while explaining trap chaining.

decisions.hook: Swing through a comic-styled city as Spider-Man, then switch to heavier, destructive Venom sections. Moving through the city is often more enjoyable than the thin mission objectives, so choose it for the characters' physical contrast rather than elaborate side activities.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands swinging-feels-good shorthand into the contrast between playable characters.

decisions.hook: Choose among seven protagonists and navigate board-like adventures where a spinning Reel resolves actions and combat strength. Skill Panels replace ordinary experience-based growth, creating unusual build decisions, but obscure rules and slow pacing make those systems difficult to enjoy without patient study.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses growth-panel instructions while keeping the opacity warning.

decisions.hook: Combine gunfire, blades and evasive rolls against movie monsters, spending collected orbs on combat and health upgrades. The short campaign offers straightforward action, but an awkward camera and uneven difficulty make it more of a diversion than a polished rival to Devil May Cry.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported rare-480p assertion and trims weapon inventory.

decisions.hook: Choose sides in a small samurai conflict, letting conversations or drawn swords change the route toward different endings. Short, repeatable runs and carried-over sword collecting make experimenting with another decision more appealing than treating one ending as completion.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes precise duration claims and explains replay structure.

decisions.hook: Take jobs and choose whether to support or betray the factions competing over Amahara. More swords and routes expand the replay possibilities, though the slower town-life rhythm is a different attraction from a succession of immediate duels.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces questionable ten-day claim with faction and sword decisions.

decisions.alias: Wizardry - Tale of the Forsaken Land (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Build a dungeon-crawling party whose trust unlocks coordinated actions, making relationships matter alongside classes and equipment. Those combinations give the slow grid exploration depth, but the opening hours demand patience before the party becomes flexible.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes best-console claim and explains party trust.

decisions.hook: Build a four-mutant team, switch heroes to combine powers and improve their abilities and equipment between missions. Local drop-in co-op makes those combinations more dependable than relying on the weak ally AI, with the X-Mansion providing a quieter break from the brawling.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Cuts unlock and level details while retaining party-building and weak-AI advice.

decisions.alias: X-Men Legends II - Rise of Apocalypse (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Combine X-Men and Brotherhood mutants in four-character teams, developing powers and gear to improve their combined attacks. The larger cast and cooperative play broaden the first game's appeal, but cumbersome menus and a dragging late game can tire even an enthusiastic team-builder.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses feature catalogue while preserving menu and late-game criticism.

decisions.hook: Dash and lock onto enemies in fluid 3D mech fights as Jehuty works through a short campaign. The movement is immediately appealing, but frequent dialogue and limited scope make this more of a compact introduction than a sustained combat challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces sequel-only dismissal with the first game's actual appeal and limitations.

decisions.alias: Zone of the Enders - The 2nd Runner (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Grab enemies, throw objects and switch subweapons while moving rapidly through large mech battles. The pleasure is combining those tools without losing momentum, making the compact campaign worth revisiting for cleaner, more expressive fights.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces benchmark and instant-start hype with concrete combat strengths.

decisions.hook: Build and tune a mech for extremely fast missions, including assaults on enormous mobile fortresses. The combination of high-speed combat and detailed assembly rewards experimentation, but keeping control at that pace is part of the challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands AC shorthand and removes device-specific performance advice.

decisions.hook: Classes, crafting and equipment drops give this alien-shooting action RPG a steady character-building loop. Repetitive corridors make it a weak choice if you want varied encounters rather than another round of loot collection.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the loot and corridor fragments into a useful trade-off.

decisions.alias: Armored Core - Formula Front Extreme Battle (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Assemble a mech and tune its AI for league battles, then watch whether your engineering survives contact with an opponent. Extreme Battle also lets you choose manual control before a match; the unusual attraction remains designing a machine that can win without you piloting it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Manual control is a choice at match start, not an unlock.

decisions.alias: Armored Core - Last Raven Portable (USA) (True Analogs v1.03).iso
decisions.hook: Build a mech for demanding missions, with VanLaser's True Analogs v1.03 patch giving movement and strafing to the left stick and turning and looking to the right. It requires PPSSPP and a mapped right analog stick; the controls are more flexible, but the demanding combat still rewards careful builds and practice.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains exact analog patch requirements without definitive-version hype.

decisions.hook: Explore a dungeon that rotates around you when you turn, making orientation part of each floor's puzzle. Equipment wear adds another resource to manage; the unusual viewpoint is the attraction and the initial hurdle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the rotating perspective rather than asserting immediate startup.

decisions.hook: Assemble a mech, then arrange logic chips to determine how it responds in combat. EXA also offers manual control, but the distinctive pleasure is diagnosing why an automated design failed and changing its program before the next battle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes programming and manual control understandable without shorthand.

decisions.hook: Arrange allies around your active character in the Magic Circle to shape their support, then test the setup in short action dungeons. Random dungeons extend the tinkering well beyond the initial stages; the draw is making builds work, not a sprawling story.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Magic Circle instead of listing its name.

decisions.hook: Run short action dungeons with one active adventurer supported by allies arranged in a Magic Circle. Much of the appeal comes from adjusting that formation between outings, making this a compact build experiment rather than a story-led RPG.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the first Cladun self-contained rather than sequel-relative.

decisions.hook: Build a street fighter from different martial-arts moves, then bet on the matches you fight. Choosing whether to win honestly or throw a bout gives the brawling a con-game twist rather than just another tournament ladder.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains betting stakes and drops unexplained creator shorthand.

decisions.alias: Dungeon Explorer - Warriors of Ancient Arts (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Take town quests, clear randomized dungeons and destroy monster generators for new gear. Job changes, weapon ranks, crafting and configurable AI allies make the build-and-loot routine the attraction. Repetitive dungeon work makes this easy to skip when you want varied tactical situations rather than another grind.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the crawler recommendation to three sentences.

decisions.hook: Dig and furnish a dungeon to attract different monsters, then venture inside to hunt what moves in. The pleasure is seeing your construction choices change the next expedition, though the build-and-hunt routine is a slow burn.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the construction-hunting relationship without comparison shorthand.

decisions.alias: Dungeon Maker II - The Hidden War (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Lay out corridors and rooms to attract monsters, then clear your own dungeon for materials and rewards. The sequel sticks closely to the original construction-and-hunting routine, so the ability to shape your hunting ground matters more than expecting a radically different game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported town-war claim with the documented construction loop.

decisions.hook: Take missions from a hub, craft weapons and use aerial Fury transformations to fight through enemy armies. The quest-and-upgrade structure gives this Warriors spin-off a different rhythm from the usual large battlefield campaigns.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Drops systemic superlative and explains the quest structure.

decisions.alias: Final Fantasy Tactics - The War of the Lions (USA) (Slowdown Fix).iso
decisions.hook: Build a tactical party through an interlocking job system while a political war story unfolds. This edition applies endrift's reverse-engineered slowdown fix to the PSP version's sluggish spell and skill animations, making repeated battles less laborious without replacing the underlying game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains slowdown-fix provenance while replacing genre apologetics.

decisions.hook: A mission-based action RPG lets you field a fourteen-member class through a war campaign, with military anime drama providing the framing. Sky's v2 fan translation merges both UMDs and includes retranslated lines plus glitch and freeze fixes. New Game is tucked into the Options menu, an easy obstacle to mistake for a missing feature.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses patch and interface caveats to three sentences.

decisions.hook: Target an opponent's head, arms or legs to strip armour away, then turn discarded weapons against them. Skill loadouts between bouts give the arena fighting a useful preparation layer beyond simply landing more hits.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns body-zone shorthand into a clear combat recommendation.

decisions.alias: God of War - Chains of Olympus (USA).iso
decisions.hook: A compact God of War campaign combines crowd-clearing combos with large-scale action spectacle. Choose it for a concentrated run of brawling rather than a long adventure or an elaborate character-building system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the appeal rather than only giving a duration.

decisions.alias: God of War - Ghost of Sparta (USA) (En,Fr,Es).iso
decisions.hook: Thera's Bane adds a fire-powered mode to God of War's close-range combo fighting. Strong pacing makes the compact campaign an appealing burst of spectacle, without the commitment of a much longer action adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains fire-mode appeal instead of relying on better-sequel shorthand.

decisions.hook: Hunt large monsters with transforming weapons and construct custom bullet patterns between missions. That ammunition editor gives loadout experiments a distinctive outlet, though the surrounding story leans heavily on anime conventions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes customization readable without assumed Monster Hunter knowledge.

decisions.hook: Customize mobile suits and take them through Gundam combat missions, using each sortie to try a different configuration. This English BETA patch is unidentified: the older public translation covered names, skills, parts and menus, not a fully English campaign. Choose it for suit experimentation only if substantial Japanese text is acceptable.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces mission-and-customization fragments with the preparation loop, retaining patch uncertainty.

decisions.hook: Position allies to exploit burning auras and use transformations to turn important fights. This approachable tactical RPG offers a gentler route into grid battles than Tactics Ogre, with a lighter tone rather than dense political complexity.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands named mechanics into the tactics recommendation.

decisions.alias: Kidou Senshi Gundam Gundam vs. Gundam NEXT PLUS (English Patched).iso
decisions.hook: Fight two-on-two mobile-suit battles and use NEXT dashes to cancel actions and reposition, making movement control as important as landing shots. The broad roster provides different matchups to learn rather than a single machine to perfect. The common MrShyCity v1.5 English patch covers unit and pilot names and the 25 PLUS missions, but little other mission text, and some lines overflow.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains NEXT dash cancels and team combat instead of compressed series shorthand.

decisions.hook: Fight from an isometric viewpoint, using cover and squad commands rather than charging through gunfire. A compact campaign and challenge missions make this an appealing choice for deliberate firefights without a long shooter campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces adjective fragments with a clear tactical attraction.

decisions.alias: Kurohyou - Ryu ga Gotoku Shinshou (Japan) (En) (v1.2 Translation).iso
decisions.hook: Fight street opponents by targeting different body zones and combining techniques from more than twenty martial-arts styles. Building a style around the attacks you enjoy is the distinctive attraction of this Yakuza spin-off. TeamK4L's v1.2 translation leaves some hostess content in Japanese, and the poker tutorial still crashes.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains style construction and targeted damage while keeping the critical patch warning.

decisions.alias: Kurohyou 2 - Ryu ga Gotoku Ashura Hen (Japan) (En) (v1.0 Translation).iso
decisions.hook: This sequel adds Osaka and more fighting styles to Kurohyou's body-part-focused street brawling. TeamK4L v1.0 translates the story, substories, minigames and menus, but leaves hostess side content and the Club SHINE job untranslated. Save before bosses, because level-ups can crash.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves translation gaps and level-up crash warning in three sentences.

decisions.hook: Take on monster-hunting missions and develop equipment for the next fight in this reworking of Lord of Arcana. The preparation-and-action loop is the reason to try it, but this is not a fully translated adventure. Serberker's v1.6 patch translates menus, missions, orbs and gear while leaving substantial Japanese text and occasional overflow.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces comparison-only praise with the hunting-and-equipment appeal.

decisions.alias: Lord of the Rings, The - Tactics (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Move film characters through grid-based battles in a straightforward tactical adaptation of The Lord of the Rings. The license is the strongest reason to choose it; the combat is competent but offers little distinctive tactical character.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the limited attraction rather than merely calling it flat.

decisions.hook: Every action, including moving and sneaking, depends on the cards in your deck and hand. That turns Metal Gear into a slow planning game where a good infiltration route is only useful if your cards can support it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the deckbuilding premise into complete useful sentences.

decisions.hook: Use cards to move, attack and sneak through turn-based Metal Gear missions. Smoother card flow and a faster pace make this a more approachable starting point than the first Acid, while the arena offers another place to test decks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the sequel self-contained and explains why to start here.

decisions.hook: Complete short stealth missions, extract soldiers with Fulton balloons and develop their equipment at Mother Base. Recruitment and research give even small outings a longer-term purpose, though base development is as central as the sneaking.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes prototype shorthand and explains the recruitment loop.

decisions.hook: Learn large monsters' attacks and turn repeated hunts into armour and weapon upgrades across an extensive quest list. Deliberate combat and deep equipment trees reward patience, but gathering the parts for a build can become a grind.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces no-story exaggeration with a clear hunting trade-off.

decisions.hook: Hunt large monsters for materials and turn them into equipment for the next fight, with the smoother handling of Portable 3rd's era. This English v6.3.0 patch uses the PS3 HD-derived build and completes Team Maverick One's work with AI-assisted, human-reviewed text. DLC quest details remain Japanese, and the build requires an emulator rather than a real PSP.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Unpacks hunting appeal while preserving HD-build and translation restrictions.

decisions.hook: Research equipment and configure mech loadouts before taking them into turn-based battles. The appeal is preparing a force that fits the mission, making this more interesting as a machinery-and-tactics game than as a quick action fix.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes ungrounded hex-grid and popularity claims.

decisions.hook: Dig a dungeon and cultivate its food chain so that slimes, lizardmen and larger monsters can fend off invading heroes. Building a healthy ecosystem rather than directly commanding an army is the distinctive challenge, and careless digging can undermine your own defence.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the food-chain mechanism without inflated Dwarf Fortress comparison.

decisions.hook: Run action-RPG missions for equipment and character growth, with a solo campaign alongside its multiplayer-oriented structure. The steady loot chase is the attraction; repeated mission work wears thin if you need frequent changes of scenery or objectives.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what the repetitive missions offer.

decisions.hook: Infinity includes Portable 2's story plus a new campaign, with customizable Infinity Missions providing a more open-ended loot hunt. Weyu and JamRules' v2 English patch fixes a post-mission freeze, but its Sony PSP font assumptions can cause misaligned text with PPSSPP's default font. DLC missions require a separate SAVEDATA installation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the expansion overview while preserving font and DLC requirements.

decisions.alias: Rengoku II - The Stairway to H.E.A.V.E.N. (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Climb a tower as an android whose head, torso and limbs can carry different weapons. Managing heat and replacing body parts makes each loadout a small engineering problem, while the repeated climbs put the emphasis on combat builds rather than varied adventures.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces comparison pile and unsupported skip instruction with the actual trade-off.

decisions.hook: Items supply combat skills but have limited uses, so choosing what to carry and when to spend it matters. Its menu-driven exploration gives this RPG an unusual structure, though the character writing is strongly anime-styled.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains finite-use equipment decisions in complete sentences.

decisions.alias: SD Gundam G Generation Over World (Japan) (En) (v1.1 HQ Translation).iso
decisions.hook: Develop mobile suits through branching unit trees in a large crossover Gundam tactics campaign. Repeated battles are part of building the force you want, so the appeal depends on enjoying that grind. Izzul95's v1.1 HQ English patch covers story, units and menus, but the extensive in-game database remains Japanese.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes every-series exaggeration and preserves untranslated database caveat.

decisions.alias: Star Wars - Battlefront II (USA) (Remastered Edition v8).iso
decisions.hook: AnthonyBF2's Remastered Edition v8 expands PSP Battlefront II with extra battlefields, heroes and hunt modes, including maps from earlier games and unreleased Pandemic material. Battles support up to 32 bots per team, making large skirmishes the reason to choose this variant. Campaign, Galactic Conquest and space battles are broken, so it is not a complete replacement for the original.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns a mod feature inventory into a clear skirmish recommendation and limitation.

decisions.alias: Super Robot Taisen A Portable (Japan) (En) (Plus v1.2).iso
decisions.hook: Crossover mech tactics with Super Rebalance Wars' AP Plus v1.2 reworks player units, adds accuracy and reduces full-upgrade costs so more favourites remain viable. Enemies are mostly unchanged, making this an easier rebalance rather than a harder challenge. Expect a long campaign with extensive anime dialogue.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses five sentences without losing the rebalance direction.

decisions.alias: Tactics Ogre - Let Us Cling Together (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Build and position a party through a long tactical campaign driven by political conflict. This is the unmodified PSP remake rather than One Vision, so choose it for the original rules and balance, with more grinding than the rebalance mod.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the unmodified release recommendation independent of the mod.

decisions.alias: Tactics Ogre - Let Us Cling Together (USA) (One Vision v1.11d).iso
decisions.hook: A political tactical RPG built around class choices and carefully positioned parties, here modified by One Vision v1.11d. The rebalance revises classes, AI and pacing; choose it for those changes rather than an untouched version of the PSP rules.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces definitive-version prescription with mod-specific choice.

decisions.alias: Tenchu - Time of the Assassins (Europe) (UNDUB v1.5c).iso
decisions.hook: Plan ninja infiltrations through a set of stealth missions, then build new assignments with the mission editor. Repeated map layouts limit the variety, so it is more attractive for refining approaches than discovering new environments. swosho's v1.5c undub restores Japanese voices, remuxes the videos and adds a modest draw-distance extension.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains stealth mission appeal rather than merely naming a mission pack.

decisions.alias: Untold Legends - Brotherhood of the Blade (USA).iso
decisions.hook: Clear dungeons for better equipment in a straightforward action-RPG loot loop. The repeated fighting and gear replacement provide little distinctive variety, making it hard to recommend unless that routine is exactly what you want.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the criticism instead of a one-word dismissal.

decisions.hook: Fight through action-RPG missions for new equipment, with shapeshifting providing a change from ordinary attacks. It remains a repetitive loot crawler, so the added forms do not make it a strong choice for varied encounters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the sequel without relying on the previous record.

decisions.hook: Take turns issuing squad orders, then directly move and aim each soldier during their action in a tactical campaign about a penal unit. akorov's v1.0.8 patch is a full English retranslation rather than the old 2014 patch. DLC episodes require separate patching on the memory stick.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Unpacks BLiTZ shorthand while preserving exact translation and DLC caveats.

decisions.hook: Build a WarCry deck and resolve Warhammer battles through card play rather than battlefield movement. The slow pace favours studying combinations, but makes it a poor substitute for a brisk tactics game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the slow card-game appeal rather than niche shorthand.

decisions.hook: Lead Space Marines through turn-based squad battles where attacks can destroy the cover you and your enemies rely on. That changing terrain gives positioning some bite, though the campaign is short.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why destructible terrain matters.

decisions.hook: Build decks and develop relationships with anime characters who become duelling partners. The large card pool offers plenty of experimentation, but the social framing adds dialogue between the card battles rather than replacing them.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Drops imprecise card count and dating-sim label in favour of partner duels.

decisions.hook: Build decks and choose partners for tag duels in the 5D's setting, with a broad card pool rewarding repeated experimentation. nzxth2's v1.1 retranslation redoes tier 1–2 story events and booster-pack text, retains the earlier card translations, and restores the original music and title menu.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes false largest-series claim and adds the game beneath the patch.

decisions.hook: Build a deck and develop a partnership with a GX character for tag duels. Choose this entry for the GX cast and card-battle setting rather than expecting a different core loop from the later Tag Force games.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the GX entry self-contained.

decisions.alias: Z.H.P. - Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman (USA) (En,Ja).iso
decisions.hook: Explore Mystery Dungeon-style runs and rebuild your hero with modular body parts and internal microchips. The absurd superhero comedy disguises a substantial upgrade puzzle, making experimentation between expeditions as important as surviving them.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Unpacks the body-upgrade premise into a clear recommendation.

decisions.hook: Explore three villain-controlled prison sections in a 2.5D Batman adventure, using gadgets to open routes and attack-and-counter fighting to handle guards. Light stealth and flexible section order offer some freedom, but confusing maps turn finding the next route into lengthy backtracking. Awkward targeting across different planes further weakens the compact action-adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces opening and closing fragments with a focused exploration critique.

decisions.hook: China, India and Russia form a trilogy of 2.5D stealth-platforming campaigns built around reading guards, hiding and using distractions. Performance ranks reward careful routes rather than indiscriminate fighting. The stealth is the attraction, but forced combat and timed chases periodically interrupt it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the trilogy to three sentences and preserves forced-action caveat.

decisions.hook: Switch between recruited companions to exploit different attacks and movement abilities through branching, boss-led stages. Recruiting or killing allies changes your options and ending, giving the short campaign a reason to replay. The deliberate 8-bit style includes punishing knockback, though an unlimited-lives option makes learning easier.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Reduces a feature list to party decisions and useful difficulty context.

decisions.hook: Choose a vault hunter, develop skill trees and chase randomized guns through a long quest-driven shooter. The Vita port includes selected extras rather than every console expansion and reduces co-op from four players to two. Reported slowdown during heavy fights on original hardware compromises an otherwise compelling loot loop.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses port caveats without implying all DLC is included.

decisions.hook: Push and pull blocks into escape routes before a tower collapses, then make evening dialogue choices that steer the story's endings. Full Body adds remixed puzzles and a Safety mode that removes threats and permits puzzle skipping. This Japan-only Vita release uses froid_san's v1.0 port of the PS4 English script and dub; trophies and the manual remain Japanese.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Retains English patch and untranslated content in three sentences.

decisions.hook: Pilot a mech through short sorties, salvage equipment and rebuild its parts and weapons for the next mission. The quick garage-to-battle loop is easy to dip into, but limited enemy variety and shallow encounters make it less satisfying as a long-term combat game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims the weapon list and keeps the short-mission limitation.

decisions.hook: Explore first-person dungeons with capturable demons filling out your party. Party development gives the dungeon work a clear purpose, but the heavy anime framing is a substantial part of the experience rather than incidental decoration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the recruitable-demon distinction in complete sentences.

decisions.hook: Shoot through randomized dungeon floors before a five-minute timer brings the Reaper after you. Tokens buy classes and equipment, but must be banked through a boss clear or escape rope; death leaves a recoverable tombstone. That extraction decision adds tension, though bland dungeons and shallow combat limit the appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Tightens the token rules into three sentences.

decisions.hook: Gather materials and build quest-driven towns in a block-based action RPG. Each story chapter starts a new area without your previous equipment or stat gains, providing fresh structure but interrupting the attachment to one growing settlement. Basic combat takes a back seat to construction, with a separate free-build mode available after the first chapter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves chapter-reset caveat while avoiding overstatement that all progress is erased.

decisions.hook: Choose one of six distinct classes and beat through lavishly drawn fantasy stages for equipment. The classes give the action different rhythms, but the endgame asks for many repeat runs and can become a loot treadmill.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes misleading randomized-route claim and explains class appeal.

decisions.hook: Choose a warrior, rogue or mage and clear dungeons for colour-tiered loot. Thin class customization and repetitive fighting make this Vita port a generic alternative to more distinctive action RPGs. Multiplayer is its stronger draw, not the solo campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes rating and long feature inventory while retaining grounded criticism.

decisions.hook: Mow through Three Kingdoms armies and spend battle gold on stratagems, or pursue territory on Conquest Mode's map of China. That campaign layer adds decisions between the crowd-clearing battles. Touch and gyro minigames interrupt the fighting, so the Vita features are not an uncomplicated improvement.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses territorial mode and hardware-feature caveat.

decisions.hook: Clear swarms of giant insects and alien invaders, collecting weapon and armour drops to prepare for harder missions. Ranger, flying Pale Wing and support-focused Air Raider offer different approaches to the same destructive battles. Clumsy vehicles and rough edges remain part of the bargain: choose it for escalating arcade carnage, not polish.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes incorrect six-difficulty assertion and condenses class list.

decisions.hook: Use a thorn grapple in hunting missions while working down an absurd million-year prison sentence and earning basic rights. Fast action contrasts with the oppressive dystopian framing, giving the equipment-and-mission loop a distinctive setting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the thorn and sentence systems without vague systemic praise.

decisions.hook: Shift gravity to fall in any direction across a floating city, treating walls and open air as possible routes. Learning to steer those falls is the delight; the thinner combat makes this a stronger choice for unusual movement and exploration than for elaborate fighting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the traversal-versus-combat recommendation explicit rather than aphoristic.

decisions.hook: Solve violent top-down rooms where one hit can kill you, choosing masks that alter the rules. Immediate restarts turn failure into route refinement, making it satisfying when you want fast experiments rather than a cautious campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes perfection claim and makes restart appeal concrete.

decisions.hook: Clear top-down encounters through lethal, fast-restarting gunplay and melee attacks. Larger spaces and heavier gun use make this sequel less tightly readable than the first Hotline Miami, so its expanded scope is also its main frustration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the sequel self-contained and explains the larger-level drawback.

decisions.alias: Injustice - Gods Among Us - Ultimate Edition (USA) (En,Fr,Es,Pt)(v1.01)[vita3k].zip
decisions.hook: DC characters fight with individual trait abilities and a meter-wager clash system that can alter a match after a life bar is lost. Ultimate Edition includes the six DLC fighters and extra solo challenges, giving it a substantial offering beyond versus play. Choose it for combo-heavy fighting and story content; reported Vita online lag is a caveat, not a promise of smooth multiplayer.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes CPS2 personal benchmark and condenses edition detail.

decisions.hook: Fight through demanding, dismemberment-heavy action with Ryu and additional character chapters. The Vita port adds Hero mode, AI-partner Tag Missions and Ninja Race, but its 30fps target and reported slowdown on original hardware compromise the precision the fighting demands.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses combat and port features while preserving slowdown concern.

decisions.hook: Weapon changes, Ninpo magic and demanding enemies make this a substantial sword-action campaign rather than a lightweight portable spin-off. Plus adds a gentler Hero mode and touch features, but original-hardware play runs at 30fps rather than the console version's 60. A troublesome camera and softer response make this a compromised way to play a precision game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses port extras and preserves framerate/camera caveats.

decisions.hook: Each clan member lives only two years, so expeditions and unions with gods must prepare the next generation. Passing down traits and equipment turns dungeon progress into a family-planning problem, presented with striking woodblock-inspired art.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains generational planning rather than a list and aesthetic adjective.

decisions.hook: A weapon-based fighter where spacing, deflections and punishing single hits matter more than long combos. This port restores the uncensored finishers and adds online play and a gallery, with blood and violence settings available. Choose it for tense sword duels rather than a fast tag-combo spectacle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses the port and avoids misleading replacement-roster description.

decisions.hook: Use rushing Hyper Attacks to clear crowds and switch between two officers working on separate fronts. Regional story campaigns and a created-warrior Chronicle Mode provide plenty of structured battlefield action, not deep strategy. The Vita version can reveal distant enemy waves late, making its crowd spectacle less convincing than the larger-console versions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses officer mechanics and Vita draw-distance caveat.

decisions.hook: Create a warrior and switch among up to four officers on different parts of Sengoku battlefields. This gives you more direct control over simultaneous objectives than staying with one crowd-clearing hero. Relationship-building dialogue between battles is a major part of the campaign, so expect conversation as well as action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Trims review attribution while preserving switching and dialogue trade-off.

decisions.hook: Take ninja contracts from three rival factions, using stealth, tools and assassinations to influence their conflict. Short missions and flexible approaches are the attraction, but reused maps, exploitable AI and finicky physics undermine the fantasy of precise infiltration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses tool inventory and retains grounded stealth criticism.

decisions.hook: Plan each step through turn-based dungeons where items and equipment combinations can rescue a failing run. Day-and-night rules and extensive post-game challenges give Shiren 5 Plus unusual longevity, but the shifting rules demand more attention than a casual loot crawl.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces definitive hype and unexplained Mixer reference.

decisions.alias: Sorcery Saga - Curse of the Great Curry God (USA)[NoNpDrm].zip
decisions.hook: Explore light Mystery Dungeon-style floors alongside a hungry mascot that consumes items. Feeding your companion adds a small inventory decision to an otherwise forgiving, silly dungeon crawl rather than a severe survival challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains hungry-mascot resource pressure without adjective fragments.

decisions.hook: Use expendable offerings to cast spells in monster-hunting missions, then choose whether to save or sacrifice defeated creatures. Those decisions shape your character's development, making the dark theme part of building a fighter rather than just decoration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the rescue-sacrifice trade-off without every-spell exaggeration.

decisions.hook: Choose a Street Fighter and Tekken pairing, extend combos through tags and use gems to modify your team. The Vita release includes the twelve extra fighters alongside the PlayStation roster. Its team systems reward setup and execution, while optional touch shortcuts offer a less demanding way to trigger combos.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses Vita roster and gem mechanics without private platform comparisons.

decisions.hook: Shoot through randomized basement rooms while stacking items that can radically transform a run. Unlocks expand the possibilities over repeated attempts, but the grotesque biblical and body-horror imagery is pervasive. This is base Rebirth: the Afterbirth expansions were not released for Vita.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses item enumeration while keeping base-game and imagery caveats.

decisions.hook: Explore turn-based dungeons with hunger, traps, equipment fusion and a companion whose orders you control. Varied dungeon rules and deep item interactions provide substantial play beyond the credits. Long tutorial exposition, fanservice and Touhou in-jokes make it less welcoming than its mechanical depth might suggest.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses dungeon systems and keeps onboarding caveat.

decisions.hook: Explore a semi-open world and use the Demon Hand to grapple onto oni and tear off limbs, combining weapons with skill-granting Mitama souls. The hunting has satisfying build choices, but repeated scenery and weak map guidance make the long campaign wear thin. The Vita version also has a sparser landscape than PS4.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses hunting systems while preserving repetition and navigation criticism.

decisions.hook: Build a team of three fighters and combine assists, tags and aerial combos into explosive attacks. X-Factor enables dramatic comebacks, making team synergy and knowing when to spend that advantage more important than simply choosing three favourites.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Avoids DLC-dependent roster total and explains three-character synergy.

decisions.hook: Fight quickly with a party of castaways while developing their island settlement. The combination of responsive action and a growing home base supplies momentum, though the long, anime-styled story is more prominent than in a pure action game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains village and combat appeal without empty anime label.

decisions.hook: Explore a top-down action adventure whose block puzzles and demanding jumps ask more patience than its Zelda-like appearance suggests. This is Working Designs' original US version, with its balance changes rather than the restored Japanese tuning.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported hardest-on-system claim while retaining localization caveat.

decisions.hook: A top-down action adventure built around intricate block puzzles, careful jumps and combat. The Un-Working Designs patch reverts the US version's damage and price changes to Japanese balance, making it the choice for that tuning rather than the original localized difficulty.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Makes the patched edition self-contained and replaces pick-this-one prescription.

decisions.hook: Break apart drifting asteroids while managing your ship's momentum, now with weapon power-ups and boss fights. The remake adds variety to the arcade survival loop, but the central attraction remains controlling a dangerous patch of space rather than a deep campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the remake rather than dismissing it as filler.

decisions.hook: Climb a randomized tower to find monster eggs and treasure, then raise familiars and develop the town between expeditions. Koh returns to level one on entry, but familiars raised outside retain their levels and successful escapes preserve carried equipment. That distinction makes securing an escape as important as pushing for another floor.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects false claim that only monster eggs persist between tower runs.

decisions.hook: Explore a hostile tower in first person, with death revealing more of a surreal story rather than simply erasing a failed attempt. Its unsettling world and repeated expeditions are the draw, but the punishing survival makes discovery slow and uncertain. Plissken's complete v1.0.2 English patch uses The Nerve Tower fan site's script.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains death-driven progression in complete prose and preserves the exact patch.

decisions.hook: Explore Gotham as Batman, Robin or Batgirl, collecting clues and decoding them to intercept crimes running on an in-game clock. Spending too long fighting street thugs can mean missing a heist, an ambitious detective idea for a movie tie-in. Clumsy fixed-camera combat and awkward movement make the execution much harder to recommend than the premise.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Condenses open-world detective premise and concrete control criticism.

decisions.hook: Explore as the vampire Kain, using spells and transformations to overcome obstacles and drinking enemies' blood to replenish steadily draining health. Those abilities make the dark campaign more than a straightforward sword adventure. Frequent loading disrupts the pace, so the atmosphere and vampire role are stronger reasons to play than fluid action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces mood adjectives with the vampire survival loop and loading trade-off.

decisions.alias: Brahma Force - The Assault on Beltlogger 9 (USA).pbp
decisions.hook: Pilot a heavy mech through first-person corridors, picking up weapons as you advance. Its stomping movement gives encounters a different feel from a nimble infantry shooter; choose it for that machinery fantasy rather than stealth.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces Metal Gear shorthand with mech-movement trade-off.

decisions.hook: Combine party magic in turn-based battles through a traditional, story-led RPG. The finely drawn animation is a strong attraction, but the conventional pacing means it is better suited to a long adventure than quick combat sessions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces generic JRPG label with combat and presentation distinction.

decisions.hook: Conquer a continent through hex-grid battles where knights command squads of summoned monsters. This Grand Edition release uses the Cross Mod v7.1 translation and rebalance, so it is not the original US ruleset. The slow campaign rewards army development and repeated strategic planning rather than immediate action.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes questionable added-nations claim and retains exact mod context.

decisions.hook: Choose a nation and conquer territory with knights leading summoned monster squads into tactical battles. This is the official English Legend of Forsena rather than the expanded Grand Edition, offering the original release's promotion and army-building systems without that edition's additions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Avoids unsupported promise of no patch quirks.

decisions.hook: Fight lethal weapon duels with a larger character and weapon selection and story campaigns following rival clans. Faster bouts make this less austere than the original Bushido Blade, but a single clean opening can still matter more than a long combo.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces duplicate local prose and makes sequel mechanics self-contained.

decisions.hook: Build a team within a ratio budget and choose a Capcom or SNK groove to change its fighting rules. Team construction is the interesting wrinkle, though the PlayStation conversion loses animation compared with the arcade game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains groove and ratio choices while keeping animation caveat.

decisions.hook: Choose mech parts and arrange logic chips to determine how each machine responds in battle. Combat plays out without direct control, so the satisfying work is tracing a failure back to your program and improving it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces original-game superlative with clear programming appeal.

decisions.hook: Explore a large castle where new abilities reopen routes and equipment can change how you fight. Dense secrets make revisiting rooms rewarding, though the generous RPG progression can soften the combat challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns fragment into a clear exploration recommendation.

decisions.hook: Explore Mystery Dungeon-style floors and improve Chocobo's claws and saddle between adventures. The Final Fantasy setting and gentler challenge make this a friendlier introduction to the format than Shiren, without abandoning equipment-building decisions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands equipment shorthand while retaining approachable positioning.

decisions.hook: Pilot space fighters through missions where victories and defeats send the war down different branches and endings. Switching between weapons suited to shields and hulls makes target selection part of each dogfight. The branching campaign is the reason to continue after a setback rather than automatically reload for a perfect record.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains campaign consequences and weapon selection consistently across all disc identities.

decisions.hook: Pilot space fighters through missions where victories and defeats send the war down different branches and endings. Switching between weapons suited to shields and hulls makes target selection part of each dogfight. The branching campaign is the reason to continue after a setback rather than automatically reload for a perfect record.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains campaign consequences and weapon selection consistently across all disc identities.

decisions.hook: Pilot the Swordfish through a short sequence of on-rails shooting stages. The limited freedom makes it more of a brief Cowboy Bebop action vignette than a space-flight game, and Japanese text remains a barrier to the presentation.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the rail-shooter constraint rather than only a fan label.

decisions.hook: Fight 3D duels by combining button sequences into projectile attacks rather than relying only on close-range punches. Reading space and incoming shots gives it the feel of a spell battle, a useful change from conventional hand-to-hand fighters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the projectile distinction in complete prose.

decisions.hook: Build Digimon decks and learn straightforward card-battle rules through a lengthy progression. The accessible battles are the attraction, but acquiring and developing a collection involves enough repetition to make the grind a real caveat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces hollow surprising-quality claim with the actual appeal.

decisions.hook: A 2D Dragon Ball fighter whose stiff movement makes exchanges less fluid than the animated source promises. Choose it only if the cast outweighs that friction; it is a weak option when responsive fighting is the priority.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Gives a concrete reason to skip rather than an unexplained command.

decisions.hook: Fight dragons with swords and magic across several generations, with your choices shaping the next protagonist and the strengths they inherit. That family progression gives decisions consequences beyond the current adventure. The combat is relatively simple, so exploring the branching lineage is a stronger reason to play than seeking a demanding action system.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains inherited progression and gives the modest combat a concrete place in the recommendation.

That family progression gives decisions consequences beyond the current adventure.
