decisions.hook: Fly through horizontal stages with option pods extending your firepower. Arranging useful coverage around the main ship gives encounters a different feel from a single forward gun, making the weapon setup more interesting than the hardware-showcase reputation alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains option-pod appeal instead of hardware-showpiece shorthand.

decisions.hook: Read the radar and fire guns and bombs at approaching enemies from a first-person cockpit. This is immediate arcade flight action, not a navigation-heavy space simulation, and a single hit can end a life.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects imprecise Space Harrier comparison with first-person cockpit action.

decisions.hook: Guide Arthur through Ghouls'n Ghosts with carefully committed jumps and weapon throws. The demanding patterns reward patient route learning, but repeated deaths are central to the experience rather than a minor obstacle to sightseeing.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes best-port claim and explains why the difficulty matters.

decisions.hook: Switch among three mech heroes at any time as you cross platforming zones and fight their bosses. Trying the available forms against each obstacle gives the anime-licensed action more to do than simply jumping and striking with one fixed character.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unsupported average verdict with the on-demand form-switching hook.

decisions.hook: Touko's RT2A is a short horizontal shooter built around timed score attacks, making efficient destruction more important than a long campaign. Originally a hidden ReVival Chase bonus, this 2016 SuperGrafx conversion uses sampled sound in place of music.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Drops irrelevant development duration and explains timed-score appeal.

decisions.hook: Buy weapons and repair supplies in towns, then pilot a mech through side-scrolling combat areas. The equipment-and-expedition loop gives the action long-term progression, but Japanese dialogue and shop text make this more demanding to navigate than a text-light shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes overconfident playable-by-feel assurance for a Japanese RPG.

decisions.hook: Walk, jump and hover through side-scrolling mech battles with a single straight-firing gun. Sluggish controls and demanding encounters make the attractive robot theme hard to enjoy consistently; this is not a transforming vertical shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects vertical transforming-shooter misidentification to side-scrolling mech action.

decisions.hook: Choose a fantasy class and fight through overhead dungeons in a Gauntlet-like action RPG. The different roles make co-operative play the natural attraction, though solo play is available if you want to work through the campaign alone.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains class appeal and avoids unqualified solo-quality claim.

decisions.hook: Explore towns from above, buy equipment and cast spells, then enter side-scrolling dungeons for the fighting. The short adventure's Crusades-era occult story gives this familiar RPG loop an unusual setting. The Un-Working Designs patch reverses the localization's inflated difficulty, making it the choice for restored balance rather than the original US tuning.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces mood fragments with the exploration-combat split and patch choice.

decisions.hook: Switch weapons to answer different formations in a fast horizontal shooter. The appeal is maintaining momentum while choosing useful fire coverage, backed by a forceful soundtrack rather than a long equipment-building campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces system-seller reputation with weapon choice and pacing.

decisions.hook: Fight through a short ninja action campaign using counters and special moves to interrupt enemies. Choose it for learning close-range exchanges and replaying the fighting, not for an extended exploration adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands brawler shorthand into a useful combat recommendation.

decisions.hook: Choose one of four elemental armours before each horizontal-shooting stage, then spend collected crystals on supplies. Matching the armour's attack style to the next level gives the heavy-metal spectacle a preparation layer beyond reflex dodging.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects purchased-armor claim: armor is selected before shopping.

decisions.hook: A single-plane mech brawler with fighting-game-style special moves and combos, rather than a succession of isolated duels. Learning how to turn an opening into a sustained attack is the draw; Japanese story scenes frame the robot combat.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the misleading one-on-one classification and replaces the unexplained engine reference.

decisions.hook: Switch between a fighter and an energy-consuming phantom that can repel bullets, then risk firing its focused attack to turn enemies into gold. The arcade game's pleasure is managing that temporary protection and cashing out safely, not the sword-launching system of the later Shin version.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the arcade/Shin conflation: original Phantom mode and gold, not bullet-to-blade conversion.

decisions.hook: Collect stars to advance an upgrade bar, then decide whether to take the highlighted improvement or save for something further along. Released elsewhere as Slap Fight, this vertical shooter makes building your arsenal an active decision rather than an automatic reward.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what Alcon's upgrade bar asks the player to decide.

decisions.hook: Choose a team of three aircraft and learn how their different attacks handle crowded urban battlefields. An adaptive difficulty system and hidden boss conditions give repeat runs much to investigate, but make this a demanding choice if you want transparent rules from the start.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands team and rank shorthand into a play recommendation without maximalist praise.

decisions.hook: Destroying enemies earns experience that levels up your ship's guns into increasingly extravagant firepower. The appeal is building and preserving that overwhelming offense through dense vertical-shooter battles, rather than managing an elaborate upgrade menu.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces historical shorthand with the distinctive experience-driven weapon growth.

decisions.hook: Medal collecting sits alongside a chain system that rewards destroying major targets in a carefully timed sequence. Deliberately spending lives can preserve that sequence, so serious scoring asks you to treat survival resources very differently from an ordinary shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes unsupported cleanest claim and explains Bakraid's central chain and life-spending tension.

decisions.hook: Building firepower also raises the game's adaptive difficulty, making restraint and even a planned death useful tools. Medal collecting and dismantling enemies create an absorbing scoring puzzle, but its obscure rules demand more study than simply learning to dodge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes deepest-ever superlative and explains rank without claiming literally every action increases it.

decisions.hook: Destroy enemies quickly and race across the screen to collect the cyborgs they release before any escape. Selectable ship speed and a disco soundtrack support a frantic collection rhythm: this is about fast movement and interception, not just squeezing through slow bullet curtains.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the cyborg collection loop instead of funniest-Cave shorthand.

decisions.hook: Fire left or right as monsters crowd in from both sides of a gothic horizontal shooter. Choosing each stage's difficulty lets you shape the challenge, making route selection part of the appeal rather than committing immediately to one fixed gauntlet.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns the genre and difficulty-select fragment into useful play guidance.

decisions.hook: This expanded Deathsmiles adds playable Sakura, the Ice Palace stage and the punishing Level 999 difficulty. Left-right shooting still demands attention to both sides of the screen; the new content offers another route through the game rather than merely another character to collect.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces extra ship shorthand with the actual character, stage and difficulty additions.

decisions.hook: Keep destroying enemies in quick succession to maintain a scoring chain while threading dense bullet patterns. Clearing the stages is one challenge; learning an uninterrupted attack route gives the same battles a much more exacting second life.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains what chaining changes rather than naming the mechanic alone.

decisions.hook: Firing shot and laser together raises a red gauge that makes enemy attacks more dangerous. Black Label turns its extra offensive power into a deliberate risk: knowing when to ease off matters as much as knowing when to unleash it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Translates red mode shorthand into its supported risk-reward mechanic; drops unexplained secret-boss name.

decisions.hook: A charged Hyper lets ordinary shots erase bullets and your laser push back large enemy beams. Those defensive tools make an imposing screen feel negotiable, but deciding when to spend them remains essential to both survival and maintaining a scoring chain.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Hyper's shot-cancel/laser-defense split instead of a vague approachable label.

decisions.hook: DaiOuJou adds temporary Hyper firepower to DoDonPachi's chain-driven shooting, but using it also raises the enemy difficulty. The resulting bargain is compelling and severe: a power surge can solve one passage while making the next more dangerous.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands punishing Hyper shorthand into the actual power-versus-rank tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Alternate spreading shots and a focused laser while building Hypers for bursts of extra firepower. Compared with DaiFukkatsu's bullet-cancelling emphasis, this is a sterner test of direct dodging, rewarding players who want to learn dense patterns rather than continually erase them.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces unexplained dolls and last-DDP claim with the game's mechanical emphasis.

decisions.hook: A tractor beam can carry enemies and even combine two players' ships into a stronger craft. That cooperation brings a larger collision target as well as extra firepower, giving this vertical shooter a more interesting bargain than simply collecting the next weapon.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces inaccurate weapon-lock-on summary with documented tractor beam and fusion tradeoff.

decisions.hook: Switch from mobile shooting to a concentrated laser that slows your aircraft, choosing reach and damage at the cost of evasive speed. Short enemy chains add a scoring challenge to Cave's first shooter without being the only reason to enjoy its military stages.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces developer-history shorthand with shot-versus-laser movement decisions.

decisions.hook: Tag enemies with lingering power shots before finishing them with normal fire to increase their reward. Flying psychic characters and a chargeable defensive barrier give the urban battles personality, while the two-step scoring system rewards more care than firing everything indiscriminately.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Distinguishes Power Shot scoring from the defensive barrier and removes empty purity praise.

decisions.hook: Collect gems to fuel a temporary mode that slows enemy bullets and turns destroyed enemies' shots into scoring items. It makes pressure something you can regulate, but spending the reserve too freely leaves less protection for the next difficult passage.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains Kakusei's resource and bullet-cancellation loop in ordinary language.

decisions.hook: Gem-powered awakening slows bullets, while the deeper Zesshikai mode spends both gems and gold and adds dangerous revenge fire. The sequel offers richer ways to turn crowded screens into score, but learning its overlapping resource states is a substantial part of the challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why the sequel is more involved instead of leaving Zesshikai and hard unexplained.

decisions.hook: Build a biplane's weapons into broad streams of fire, with the fully powered flamethrower providing the most extravagant coverage. The satisfaction is keeping that arsenal alive through a sustained vertical-shooter assault, not merely reaching the next boss with whatever remains.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces classic-Toaplan shorthand with the signature powered-up flamethrower appeal.

decisions.hook: Choose among eight characters for an overhead run-and-gun campaign fought on foot rather than in a freely flying ship. The roster gives you different ways to approach the shooting; choose this for ground-level combat rather than expecting another aerial Toaplan sortie.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands the character and on-foot distinction and avoids treating its Out Zone relationship as sufficient guidance.

decisions.hook: Pilot a biplane through ground defenses and enemy formations, preserving weapon upgrades and using bombs to escape trouble. It is a direct, demanding vertical shooter whose appeal lies in learning where to be before the next attack, not in a complicated scoring subsystem.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects misleading helicopter-era wording and replaces date-only context with play guidance.

decisions.hook: Switch among spreading, seeking and missile weapons while steering through a growing volume of enemy fire. Unlike Japan's V-Five, Grind Stormer uses direct weapon pickups and screen-clearing bombs rather than an upgrade bar, making it a distinct ruleset rather than just another title.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Clarifies Grind Stormer's bomb/pickup rules instead of conflating it with V-Five.

decisions.hook: Steer a summoned spirit into enemy fire to slow bullets while your walking character still has to negotiate the ground. The grotesque historical-Japan setting supports an unusual split-attention shooter: managing the spirit never removes the need to keep its owner safe.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the spirit-control tension and removes the inaccurate Edo-era label.

decisions.hook: Cycle between forward, backward, vertical and diagonal fire to reach enemies around your ship. The horizontal stages become a positioning puzzle: choosing the right angle early is often more useful than trying to dodge while stuck with the wrong weapon direction.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands four-direction shorthand into the central tactical appeal.

decisions.hook: Collecting medals and improving your arsenal feeds an adaptive difficulty system that can make success increasingly dangerous. This is a shooter for learning resource and scoring routes as well as dodging; its hidden pressures are a poor fit for an uncomplicated power fantasy.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces rank-and-medal hell and designer shorthand with an intelligible recommendation.

decisions.hook: A visible difficulty gauge and a new scoring system encourage keeping enemy pressure high rather than merely surviving it. Black Label is more than a faster Ibara: strong scores require deliberately facing dense attacks, so a clear and a scoring run can feel like different tasks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces vague rebalanced claim with visible rank and the high-rank scoring distinction.

decisions.hook: Kill an enemy up close with normal shot to earn high-value chips, then use lock-on fire to extend that reward from farther away. That push forward and retreat is Ketsui's attraction: scoring repeatedly tempts you into the space where the bullets are most dangerous.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Corrects the implication that close-range lock-on alone creates the high-value chips; removes cleanest superlative.

decisions.hook: Gather pigs to fill a fuel meter, spend it on a powerful attack that produces medals, then switch back to collect the payout. Beneath the absurd presentation is a readable cycle of gathering and spending, with keeping the medal chain alive providing the real scoring pressure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains lard-based scoring instead of relying on insider terminology and unsupported accessibility praise.

decisions.hook: Ride through giant-insect battles with modes that change the character of the enemy fire: Original uses fewer, faster bullets, while Maniac fills the screen more densely. Original is a sensible starting point, but its speed still demands attention; Ultra is for a much harsher challenge.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes best-for-learning superlative and explains the actual mode differences.

decisions.hook: Black Label revises the characters' weapons and replaces Ultra with God mode, whose dense patterns come with their own scoring demands. This international Another Version softens parts of the challenge further; choose it as a distinct Futari ruleset, not merely the same game with a different subtitle.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserves Black Label and international Another Version distinctions without fan-favourite shorthand.

decisions.hook: Choose Reco or Palm, then decide between Original's faster, sparser fire and Maniac's denser patterns and more involved scoring. Ultra escalates the challenge dramatically, but the other modes already offer substantial room to learn routes and improve a run without treating that extreme as the goal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces masterpiece/meme judgments with useful mode-selection guidance.

decisions.hook: Fight on foot through overhead stages while a draining energy meter keeps the advance urgent. The tension is finding a safe route without lingering: clearing every threat means little if you spend too long reaching the next refill.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains how energy drain changes the run-and-gun rhythm.

decisions.hook: Stop firing to build a protective shield and charge a Rose Cracker, then release it to break through enemy fire. Those tools are powerful, but using them and collecting items can drive up the adaptive difficulty; this is a demanding resource puzzle beneath the sugary art.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces divisive rank-experiment shorthand with the shield/charge loop and its difficulty cost.

decisions.hook: Four fantasy characters take the place of military aircraft in a vertical shooter full of magical machinery and monsters. Try different characters to find an attack style that suits you; the appeal is that fantasy battle spectacle rather than a role-playing adventure suggested by the setting.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands first-Raizing trivia into a clear fantasy-shooter recommendation.

decisions.hook: Your helicopter's shots reach only partway up the screen, forcing you closer to tanks and gun emplacements than you might like. Limited bombs provide an escape valve, but learning a safe approach is the real work in this early vertical shooter.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces title and year alone with the short-range weapon's positioning challenge.

decisions.hook: Build your firepower through a demanding vertical assault, using the enormous skull bomb when enemy attacks leave too little room. Its dramatic weapons are the reward, but surviving to keep them matters more than hoarding a bomb until it is too late.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Turns skull-bomb and difficulty shorthand into useful survival guidance.

decisions.hook: Six long stages ask you to choose between wide shots, homing lasers and close-range explosive coverage. The sustained difficulty makes it a test of endurance and weapon planning rather than a quick spectacle; approach it expecting to learn sections through repeated attempts.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removes hardest-Toaplan superlative and explains the long-stage and weapon-selection demands.

decisions.hook: Pilot a helicopter against ground guns and incoming aircraft, balancing sustained fire with limited emergency bombs. The appeal is direct military shooting: learning the next approach and clearing threats early matters more than an elaborate scoring trick.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces helicopter-classic shorthand with the attack-priority and survival appeal.

decisions.hook: Call in a formation of allied planes to multiply your forward firepower against ground targets. Helpers can be shot down, so choosing when to summon them turns an otherwise direct vertical shooter into a small exercise in spending support where it will matter most.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the expendable wingman formation instead of dismissing it as a gimmick.

decisions.hook: Hold fire to charge a shot that spreads in many directions, or keep tapping for ordinary forward attacks. A circling bomb can then be sent after enemies, giving this vertical shooter useful choices about when to defend your immediate space and when to reach outward.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Expands chargeups shorthand using the supplied charge and Circle Bomb mechanics.

decisions.hook: Use a tractor beam to capture small enemies, then throw them into other threats. That extra handling step gives the horizontal shooting a playful tactical wrinkle: an approaching enemy can become ammunition rather than just another target.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains why the capture-and-throw mechanic is worth trying.

decisions.hook: Cycle through swords as their power is spent, letting damaged blades recover while another keeps the fight moving. The hand-drawn landscapes make the journey striking, but repeated routes can wear thin; come for fluid sword combat more than varied exploration.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces clipped praise and criticism with the sword-cycling appeal and preserves the repetitive-route caveat.

decisions.hook: Build a two-fighter team and decide whether to spend recoverable health on a Baroque combo extension or save resources for a Mega Crash escape. Simple attack buttons make the crossover approachable, but those offensive and defensive trade-offs give the frantic fights more substance than button-mashing.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explains the health-and-meter trade-offs instead of unexplained system names and missing-link praise.

decisions.hook: Keep street fighters on one side and use dropped weapons to control the crowd. Sluggish responses can leave you trapped in repeated knockdowns, while the brawling becomes repetitive once you find a reliable position; this is a weak way to experience Double Dragon's arcade appeal.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace the evasive arcade comparison with sourced sluggish-control and knockdown criticism.

decisions.hook: This sideways space shooter is Hellenic's modified Delfox, not the PC Engine Gunhed. Its replacement soundtrack uses tunes by Black Sabbath and Europe, making it a curiosity for that altered presentation rather than a different shooting campaign.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace cryptic musical-identity wording with the sourced soundtrack modification and clear namesake distinction.

decisions.hook: A polygonal cockpit view puts you through a stunt loop and an open-bridge jump. Sensitive steering and graphics that can break up during busy moments make this a demanding technical curiosity, not a dependable choice for immediate racing fun.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace vague control-interest praise with sourced sensitive-steering and breaking-graphics caveats.

decisions.hook: Duels are decided through repeated knockdowns rather than a simple best-of-three round structure. Attacks depend on your direction when you release fire, with shorter presses producing harder kicks, so learning the input timing matters more than frantic button presses.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace the vague depth dismissal with the manual's direction-and-release attack mechanic.

decisions.hook: Pilot a craft through top-down scrolling firefights, learning the different attack patterns of successive opponents. This is the first half of a two-part combat trial, and completing it gives you the code needed to continue rather than a complete campaign on its own.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Name the top-down craft-shooting format instead of leaving the first combat trial abstract.

decisions.hook: The second half of Hypsys puts you in an aircraft with a separate missile attack alongside ordinary fire. The extra weapon adds a targeting decision to the top-down shooting, but you need the first half's completion code to enter this final combat trial.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Explain the second section's aircraft and separate missiles rather than merely calling it another trial.

decisions.hook: Climb the buildings, operate platform levers and deal with Kong's minions while barrels keep arriving. This first part asks for vertical route planning before the second part switches to side-scrolling gunplay.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The gunplay belongs to the second part of the same game, not a sequel.

decisions.hook: Recover talismans and return them to the cauldron, using magical stepping blocks to reach platforms and spells to stun enemies. The routes demand thought, but repeated trips over the same difficult hazards can make the quest more exhausting than its compact map suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The old note overlooks magical stepping blocks and the repetitive, demanding return trips.

decisions.hook: Small, cartoon-like fighters still have to manage crowds at punching distance in this Spectrum adaptation of Mighty Final Fight. The appeal is finding room to attack without letting the street gang close around you, rather than treating every encounter as a flurry of punches.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Remove the irrelevant bullet-arena comparison and centre the crowd-spacing appeal.

decisions.hook: Guide Monkey J through the gold temple's platform hazards in search of treasure. The cartoon setting invites exploration, but picking a safe landing in each room matters more than charging toward the next opening.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace the empty archaeology-simulation contrast with a concrete platforming recommendation.

decisions.hook: Dig weapon money out of blocks and spend it on the upgrades embedded in the landscape. This graphics-remastered version includes trainer options, but the underlying appeal remains deciding when to spend your crystals and when to keep saving.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replace archival trainer wording with a direct edition caveat and spending decision.

decisions.hook: Pac-Man trades maze corners for running jumps, springboards and a trip back home in magic shoes. This recoloured version keeps the platform journey's emphasis on judging momentum and gaps while ghosts complicate the route.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The recolour caveat is useful, but the redundant maze comparison can become movement advice.

decisions.hook: Fight through prehistoric, Egyptian, medieval and futuristic stages before each timer expires. The time-travel scenery supplies variety, but the loss of Target Renegade's two-player mode makes this a poor replacement for a shared street-brawling session.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Add the loss of two-player mode as a concrete reason to prefer Target Renegade.

decisions.hook: Catch an enemy with your wand and slam it from side to side, or let it go to clear your path. Collecting every flower before killing the final enemy opens a chance at an extra life, giving each small arena a useful risk-and-reward decision.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct the copied metadata's fruit claim: the manual explicitly requires flowers.

decisions.hook: Catch enemies with a wand and slam them from side to side, balancing quick kills against collecting every flower for a chance at an extra life. This colour-enhanced variant keeps Rod Land's compact arena decisions.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Correct fruit to flowers while retaining the colour-enhanced edition distinction.

decisions.hook: Choose tennis shots by direction, power and the moment of contact, adjusting to different court surfaces. The appeal is deliberate placement and timing rather than simply getting the racket somewhere near the ball.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The unexplained comparison to a similar title obscured otherwise useful stroke-control guidance.

decisions.hook: Fight through Amargol’s forest and collect six spell vessels to gain the strength to draw the Sword of Sablat. This is Sirwood’s first playable part, with collection giving the monster fighting a purpose beyond reaching the next screen.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The first playable part incorrectly promised the whole forest-to-castle journey; clarified its six-vessel objective.

decisions.hook: Take the Sword of Sablat into a cave maze, using it against enemies and to climb the walls while gathering pieces of a magic papyrus. This second part rewards mapping and searching: finding the castle entrance is not enough without the means to open it.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The second playable part incorrectly reused the whole-game summary; restored its cave maze and papyrus objective.

decisions.hook: Fight through Amargol’s castle with the Sword of Sablat, overcoming monsters and magical obstacles on the way to the stolen shield. This is Sirwood’s final playable part, a push toward the tower confrontation rather than the complete forest-and-cave adventure.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Preserved the final-part distinction while replacing plot-only framing with its castle-combat focus.

decisions.hook: Eight fighters bring different ranges and special attacks to one-on-one bouts, squeezed into fiddly single-button combinations. A human rival makes the move experimentation more rewarding; the repetitive solo fights are a weaker reason to choose this conversion.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaced vague conversion-curiosity framing with documented single-button complexity and the stronger two-player mode.

decisions.hook: Escort a shuttle through asteroid attacks, then fight through satellites to stop a geo-disrupter. Slow movement and sluggish firing make the changing action scenes more frustrating than heroic; skip it if responsive action matters more than the Superman licence.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaced vague power demonstrations with actual shuttle/satellite tasks and documented slow movement and firing response.

decisions.hook: Repeated one-on-one fights alternate with top-down chases and sliding-block repairs to the T-800. The variety is real, but the simple, repetitive combat makes this a weaker choice than the film’s premise suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Removed the misleading film-cutscene claim for Spectrum and identified the actual fights, chases and repair puzzles.

decisions.hook: Rotate falling shapes to complete horizontal lines and clear space before the stack reaches the top. Keeping a tidy surface buys flexibility, while leaving a deep gap for one particular piece can turn patient planning into a desperate wait.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The metaphorical stacking note never stated the line-clearing rule; made the central decision explicit.

decisions.hook: Rotate falling shapes to complete horizontal lines and clear space before the stack reaches the top. Keeping a tidy surface buys flexibility, while leaving a deep gap for one particular piece can turn patient planning into a desperate wait.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: The 48K note also omitted line clearing; clarified the same stacking trade-off without inventing edition differences.

decisions.hook: Raizing pares the series back to direct shooting, with a health bar and a charged attack that lifts you above the battlefield briefly invulnerable. It is a forgiving change from dense bullet-pattern games, though its simpler scoring offers less to dissect than 19XX or Raizing's more elaborate shooters.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Tag a large enemy with a charged marker, then keep homing fire on it while dodging and clearing the surrounding formations. Three planes change the balance of speed, firepower and lock-on strength, giving this brisk military shooter more tactical texture than its conventional appearance suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Tear through enemy mechs and replace your own arms, legs and weapons with the parts they drop. The pleasure is adapting your reach and movement as the available equipment changes, rather than repeating one brawler combo for an entire run.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Juggle Alien swarms with melee strings, grabs and gunfire, choosing between heavily armed humans and more acrobatic Predators. The large crowds reward keeping enemies on one side and weaving weapons into your attacks; there is considerably more to learn than the license suggests.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Earn coins in a fast, expressive brawler, then choose which attacks and health upgrades to buy between stages. Distinctive fighters and branching combo options reward practice, although a few bosses spoil the otherwise readable combat with abrupt off-screen attacks.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Tennis, basketball and football become short arcade tournaments with simplified rules and quick rematches. Tennis and basketball are the stronger diversions; football's clunky movement and awkward passing make it the weak link rather than a reason to choose the collection.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Pilot a fighting mech with a limited boost gauge and a main arm that opponents can knock off, forcing you to recover it before regaining most attacks. Managing movement and protecting that limb make the bouts feel distinct from Street Fighter; this is not a freeform parts-building game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Choose a genuinely different class, ration spells and consumables, and take branching routes through a brawler full of equipment tricks. The extra systems make repeat runs rewarding, but learning the inventory wheel and character-specific tools matters much more than simply mashing through the crowds.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Four classes bring different melee and magic options to a branching arcade adventure where spells and throwing items are resources to spend carefully. It is a leaner introduction to Capcom's D&D formula than Shadow over Mystara, but has fewer combat and equipment possibilities to explore.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Charge magical attacks and route enemy kills around an elaborate collection of hidden items rather than treating this as a straightforward fantasy shooter. There is a great deal to optimize, but the scoring rules are poorly explained in play; expect outside reading and deliberate practice before the collection system makes sense.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Cartoon monsters fight with elastic attacks and light-to-heavy chains, while a temporarily powered-up special gauge encourages spending your advantage quickly. The animation and unusual fighters remain appealing, but Night Warriors gives the same foundation a more flexible meter system and a fuller roster.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.

decisions.hook: Aim a rotating weapon arm independently of your ship to attack enemies approaching from awkward angles. That extra aiming task gives this colourful horizontal shooter its identity, but it also makes movement and weapon positioning fussier than a conventional forward-firing game.
decisions.reason: Editorial review: Replaces CPS II shorthand with explained play, decisions and a meaningful recommendation; corrects misleading distinctions where present.
